Why A is wrong: 1 month is too early — healing isn't complete enough for a stable margin. Why C is wrong: 6 months is longer than needed for gingival margin stability (though bone remodeling may continue). Why D is wrong: 12 months is excessive for gingival margin stabilization, and complete osseous fill doesn't always occur. Why E is wrong: 2 weeks only gets you early epithelial healing, not a stable margin.

Q79 How many months should elapse between root resection and placement of the final restoration?
A. 1–2 months
B. 3–6 months
C. 6–9 months
D. 9–12 months
E. Final restoration can be placed immediately after resection
Correct Answer: B

Per Eastman and Maynard, 3–6 months should pass between root resection and final restoration. This waiting period allows for complete soft tissue maturation (biologic width establishment at ~3 months per Gargiulo), bone remodeling at the resection site, and assessment of the tooth's long-term stability and prognosis. During this interim period, a provisional restoration is placed to evaluate function, hygiene access, and tissue response before committing to a definitive restoration. Rushing to a final restoration risks margin discrepancies and functional failures.

Why A is wrong: 1–2 months is too early for adequate tissue maturation. Why C is wrong: 6–9 months is longer than the recommended window. Why D is wrong: 9–12 months is excessively conservative. Why E is wrong: Immediate restoration doesn't allow for healing assessment.

Q80 After root resection, what is the recommendation regarding post and core placement, and which roots are typically retained for maxillary and mandibular molars?
A. Always place a post and core for maximum retention; retain MB root for maxillary, mesial root for mandibular
B. Try to avoid post and core due to risk of fracture; maxillary = retain palatal and distal roots; mandibular = retain distal root
C. Post and core is mandatory; maxillary = retain palatal root only; mandibular = retain mesial root
D. Try to avoid post and core due to risk of fracture; maxillary = retain palatal and mesial roots; mandibular = retain mesial root
E. Post placement has no effect on fracture risk after resection
Correct Answer: B

After root resection, you should TRY TO AVOID post and core placement because of the increased risk of root fracture. Resected teeth already have compromised structural integrity — adding a post increases internal stress and fracture risk. For maxillary molars, the preferred retained roots are the palatal (P) and distal (D) roots — recall the DB root is most commonly resected. For mandibular molars, the distal (D) root is typically retained. The distal root of the mandibular molar tends to be straighter and more conical (better for a single-rooted restoration), while the mesial root has the deep 100% concavity that complicates restoration.

Why A is wrong: You should AVOID post and core, not always place it. Why C is wrong: Post is not mandatory, and retaining only the palatal root eliminates too much support. Why D is wrong: For maxillary molars, it's palatal + distal (not mesial) that are retained; for mandibular it's distal, not mesial. Why E is wrong: Post placement absolutely increases fracture risk in resected teeth.

SUTURE TECHNIQUES & MATERIALS (3)
Q228 Which statement BEST describes the vertical mattress suture technique?
A. Needle passes through flap only, knot tied coronally
B. Needle penetrates through the flap AND through the periosteum still attached to bone; knot is tied apically where the needle first penetrated, securing the flap in an apical position
C. Used only for interproximal closure
D. Identical to the single interrupted suture
E. Used exclusively for GTR membrane fixation
Correct Answer: B

Directly from your lecture slides: "Needle penetrates through the flap and through periosteum that is still attached to bone. Knot is tied apically (where the needle first penetrated the flap), allowing flap to be secured in an apical position." This is the defining feature of the vertical mattress — it engages the periosteum, which anchors the flap apically. This is the suture of choice when you need to maintain an apically positioned flap (e.g., after APF for pocket elimination or crown lengthening). The apical knot placement is what distinguishes it from a simple interrupted suture where the knot is tied at the entry point.

Why A is wrong: The periosteum engagement is the critical feature. Why C is wrong: Vertical mattress is used on facial/lingual surfaces, not just interproximal. Why D is wrong: Completely different technique and purpose. Why E is wrong: GTR uses interrupted and sling sutures primarily.

Q229 Which of the following correctly pairs suture material with its classification?
A. Silk = resorbable; Vicryl = non-resorbable
B. PTFE = resorbable; gut = non-resorbable
C. Silk and PTFE = non-resorbable; gut, chromic gut, Vicryl (polyglactin 910), Monocryl (poliglecaprone 25) = resorbable
D. All sutures used in periodontics are resorbable
E. Chromic gut = non-resorbable; Vicryl = resorbable
Correct Answer: C

Directly from your slides: Non-resorbable = Silk, PTFE. Resorbable = Gut, Chromic Gut, Vicryl (Polyglactin 910 — braided multifilament), Monocryl (Poliglecaprone 25), Polysorb, Polydioxanone, Caprosyn (polyglytone 621). The distinction matters clinically: non-resorbable sutures must be removed at a follow-up appointment (typically 7-14 days), while resorbable sutures dissolve on their own. PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) is the same material as Gore-Tex — inert, non-reactive, excellent for periodontal surgery. Silk is easy to handle but has higher bacterial wicking potential.

Why A is wrong: Silk is non-resorbable. Why B is wrong: PTFE is non-resorbable; gut is resorbable. Why D is wrong: Both types are used. Why E is wrong: Chromic gut IS resorbable.

Q230 Which needle type has its cutting edge on the OUTER curve, and why is this preferred in periodontal surgery?
A. Taper cut needle — cutting edge on inner curve, preferred for dense tissue
B. Conventional cutting needle — cutting edge on outer curve, preferred for all soft tissue
C. Reverse cutting needle — cutting edge on outer curve, reducing risk of tissue tear-through
D. Half-curve needle — no cutting edge, used for mucosa only
E. All periodontal needles have identical cutting edge placement
Correct Answer: C

Directly from your slides: "Reverse Cutting — cutting edge is on the outer curve." The reverse cutting needle is preferred in periodontal surgery because the cutting edge faces AWAY from the wound edge. In a conventional cutting needle, the edge faces the wound, increasing the risk of the suture cutting through the tissue toward the wound margin. The reverse cutting design directs any tissue-cutting force away from the incision line, reducing tear-through. Needle shapes available per slides: 1 = half curve, 2 = straight needle, 3 = 5/8 circle. The taper needle (no cutting edge) is used for delicate tissues where minimal trauma is needed.

Why A is wrong: Taper cut has no cutting edge — it's atraumatic. Why B is wrong: Conventional cutting has edge on INNER curve. Why D is wrong: Half-curve needles can have cutting edges. Why E is wrong: Needle types have distinctly different cutting edge placements.

LASERS IN PERIODONTICS (6)
Q115 Which dental laser has the primary tissue target of water and hydroxyapatite, uses a photomechanical/photodisruptive mode of action, and can treat BOTH hard and soft tissue?
A. Diode laser
B. Nd:YAG laser
C. Er:YAG laser
D. CO\u2082 laser
E. Argon laser
Correct Answer: C

The Er:YAG laser (wavelength 2940nm, far infrared) targets water and hydroxyapatite — which is why it can cut BOTH soft tissue (high water content) and hard tissue like bone, enamel, and calculus (hydroxyapatite content). Its mode of action is photomechanical and photodisruptive (ablation), meaning it vaporizes water in the tissue causing micro-explosions that ablate tissue with minimal thermal damage. Your slides note it has shallow penetration (2–4 cell layers), minimal heat damage due to short pulses, and requires water spray for cooling. It's used for calculus removal, root detoxification, peri-implantitis, and crown lengthening.

Why A is wrong: Diode targets hemoglobin and melanin, works photothermal, soft tissue ONLY. Why B is wrong: Nd:YAG targets hemoglobin and melanin, works photothermal, primarily soft tissue. Why D is wrong: CO\u2082 laser targets water but not hydroxyapatite in the same way. Why E is wrong: Argon laser targets hemoglobin/melanin pigments.

Q116 Which dental laser targets hemoglobin and melanin, uses a photothermal "hot tip" mechanism requiring a blackened activated tip, and is most affordable and compact?
A. Er:YAG laser
B. Nd:YAG laser
C. Diode laser
D. CO\u2082 laser
E. Excimer laser
Correct Answer: C

The diode laser (wavelength 780–1064nm, near infrared) targets hemoglobin and melanin (pigmented tissues). It works via photothermal action with a "hot tip effect" and deep coagulation. Your slides specifically note it requires "tip activation" with a "blackened tip for heat concentration" — neither the Nd:YAG nor Er:YAG requires tip activation. The diode is the most affordable and compact unit, making it the most common laser in general dental practice. It's best for soft tissue surgeries, pocket disinfection, and minor aesthetic procedures like gingivectomy and frenectomy.

Why A is wrong: Er:YAG targets water/hydroxyapatite, uses photomechanical action, and is the most expensive. Why B is wrong: Nd:YAG also targets hemoglobin/melanin but does NOT require tip activation and is more expensive. Why D is wrong: CO\u2082 is a different wavelength and mechanism. Why E is wrong: Excimer lasers aren't used in periodontics.

Q117 Which laser has the HIGHEST hemostatic ability, and which has the LOWEST?
A. Highest = Er:YAG; Lowest = Diode
B. Highest = Nd:YAG; Lowest = Er:YAG
C. Highest = Diode; Lowest = Nd:YAG
D. Highest = Er:YAG; Lowest = Nd:YAG
E. All three lasers have equal hemostatic ability
Correct Answer: B

Per your laser comparison chart: Nd:YAG has "Very High" hemostatic ability due to deep coagulation. Diode has "High" hemostatic ability due to coagulation. Er:YAG has only "Moderate" hemostatic ability with minimal thermal effect. This makes logical sense — hemostasis requires thermal coagulation of blood vessels, and the Nd:YAG penetrates deepest with the most photothermal effect. The Er:YAG's photomechanical (ablative) mode doesn't coagulate as effectively because it's designed to MINIMIZE thermal damage, which is great for healing but bad for hemostasis.

Why A is wrong: Er:YAG has the LOWEST hemostasis, not the highest. Why C is wrong: Diode is high but not the highest — Nd:YAG is very high. Why D is wrong: Er:YAG is lowest, not highest. Why E is wrong: They have distinctly different hemostatic abilities.

Q118 The Nd:YAG laser is used in the LANAP (Laser-Assisted New Attachment Procedure) protocol. What are the three passes of the LANAP procedure?
A. First pass = calculus removal; Second pass = bone recontouring; Third pass = suturing
B. First pass = remove diseased epithelial lining from the pocket; Second pass = disinfect root surfaces and kill bacteria (especially P. gingivalis); Third pass = biostimulation and coagulation for fibrin clot formation
C. First pass = ablate bone; Second pass = place graft material; Third pass = close with membrane
D. First pass = incision; Second pass = flap elevation; Third pass = root planing
E. First pass = anesthesia; Second pass = tissue removal; Third pass = hemostasis only
Correct Answer: B

The LANAP protocol uses the Nd:YAG laser in free-running pulsed mode at 1.0–3.0W. The three passes from your slides: (1) First pass removes the diseased epithelial lining from the pocket — this is essentially de-epithelization, removing the pocket lining so epithelial cells can't form a long junctional epithelium. (2) Second pass disinfects root surfaces and kills bacteria, especially P. gingivalis — the Nd:YAG penetrates deeply and is highly effective against this keystone pathogen. (3) Third pass provides biostimulation and coagulation to form a stable fibrin clot. That fibrin clot acts like a biologic membrane, excluding epithelial cells and promoting new attachment — same GTR principle without a physical membrane.

Why A is wrong: Calculus removal isn't the first LANAP pass — that's SRP/ultrasonics (Step 3 of overall LANAP). Why C is wrong: LANAP doesn't involve bone ablation or grafting. Why D is wrong: LANAP is a flapless procedure — no incision or flap elevation. Why E is wrong: This oversimplifies and misrepresents the protocol.

Q119 The Er:YAG laser requires which specific cooling mechanism during use, and what is its unique clinical advantage over the other periodontal lasers?
A. No cooling needed; best for deep pocket disinfection
B. Air cooling only; best for frenectomy
C. Water spray cooling to prevent tissue overheating; can remove calculus and debride implant surfaces atraumatically
D. Cryogenic cooling; best for hemostasis during surgery
E. Chemical cooling agent; best for bone grafting procedures
Correct Answer: C

Your slides explicitly state: "Water spray needed for cooling (prevents tissue overheating)" for the Er:YAG. Its unique advantage is that it "Can be used to remove calculus and disinfect root surfaces atraumatically" and is "Effective for peri-implantitis treatment by gently debriding implant surfaces without damage." No other laser can safely remove calculus from root surfaces or debride implant surfaces without causing thermal/mechanical damage. The Er:YAG ablates calculus through micro-explosions of water within the calculus, popping it off the root surface without the shear forces of hand or ultrasonic instruments.

Why A is wrong: Er:YAG absolutely requires water cooling, and deep pocket disinfection is Nd:YAG territory. Why B is wrong: Air cooling alone is insufficient — water is mandatory. Why D is wrong: Cryogenic cooling isn't used, and hemostasis is actually the Er:YAG's weakest feature. Why E is wrong: No chemical cooling agent is used.

Q120 Regarding healing and post-operative comfort, how do the three periodontal lasers compare?
A. Diode = excellent healing; Nd:YAG = poor healing; Er:YAG = moderate healing
B. All three lasers produce identical healing responses
C. Diode = good healing (deep penetration but controlled thermal effects); Nd:YAG = moderate healing (some thermal damage); Er:YAG = excellent healing (minimal thermal damage, fastest healing)
D. Diode = excellent; Nd:YAG = excellent; Er:YAG = poor
E. Er:YAG = worst healing due to ablative tissue destruction
Correct Answer: C

Directly from your laser chart: Diode = "Good (Deep tissue penetration but controlled thermal effects)." Nd:YAG = "Moderate (Some thermal damage)." Er:YAG = "Excellent (Minimal thermal damage, faster healing)." The Er:YAG wins for healing because its photomechanical action minimizes collateral thermal damage — what you cut stays cut, and adjacent tissue stays healthy. The Nd:YAG's deep penetration means more thermal energy is deposited into surrounding tissue, causing more collateral damage. The diode falls in between.

Why A is wrong: Diode is good, not excellent, and Nd:YAG isn't poor. Why B is wrong: They have distinctly different healing profiles. Why D is wrong: Er:YAG has the BEST healing, not poor. Why E is wrong: Despite being ablative, the Er:YAG produces the least collateral thermal damage and the best healing.

PERIO EMERGENCIES (6)
Q156 In necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (NUG), what are the four histologic zones of the gingival lesion from most superficial to deepest?
A. Bacterial zone → PMN band → Tissue necrosis zone → Spirochete infiltration zone
B. Spirochete zone → Necrosis zone → PMN band → Bacterial zone
C. PMN band → Bacterial zone → Spirochete zone → Necrosis zone
D. Necrosis zone → Spirochete zone → Bacterial zone → PMN band
E. All zones contain equal concentrations of all organisms
Correct Answer: A

The four zones from superficial to deep: (1) Bacterial Zone = bacteria/spirochetes (most superficial, closest to root surface). (2) Band of Polymorphonuclear Neutrophils (PMN band) = the body's first-line defense against the bacterial invasion. (3) Zone of Tissue Necrosis = spirochetes have penetrated and destroyed tissue here. (4) Zone of Spirochete Infiltration = deepest gingival tissues — spirochetes have invaded furthest into viable tissue. The spirochetes being in the deepest layer tells you they're the most invasive organisms in NUG pathology.

Why B is wrong: The order is reversed. Why C is wrong: PMN band isn't the most superficial layer. Why D is wrong: Necrosis isn't the most superficial zone. Why E is wrong: The zones are distinctly organized, not uniform.

Q174 What are the characteristics of acute herpetic gingivostomatitis?
A. Occurs primarily in adults; slow onset; no fever; caused by bacteria
B. Occurs primarily in children; incubation period of 10–14 days; onset of high fever; lymphadenopathy
C. Occurs only in immunocompromised patients; caused by Candida albicans
D. Occurs in elderly patients; caused by traumatic occlusion
E. Occurs at any age equally; no incubation period; caused by anaerobic bacteria
Correct Answer: B

Acute herpetic gingivostomatitis (caused by HSV-1 primary infection): (1) primarily affects children, (2) the virus has an incubation period of 10–14 days, (3) sudden onset of high fever, and (4) lymphadenopathy (swollen lymph nodes). The oral lesions present as multiple painful vesicles/ulcers throughout the oral mucosa, gingiva, tongue, and lips. It's self-limiting (resolves in 7–14 days) but the virus remains latent in the trigeminal ganglion and can reactivate as herpes labialis (cold sores) later in life.

Why A is wrong: It primarily affects children, not adults, and is viral, not bacterial. Why C is wrong: Candida causes oral candidiasis, not herpetic gingivostomatitis. Why D is wrong: It primarily affects children and is caused by HSV-1, not trauma. Why E is wrong: It primarily affects children and has a definite incubation period.

Q175 What are the two initial clinical criteria required for diagnosing Acute Necrotizing Ulcerative Periodontitis (ANUP)?
A. Tooth mobility and bleeding on probing
B. Loss of clinical attachment and pain
C. Gingival redness and increased probing depth
D. Radiographic bone loss and halitosis
E. Pseudomembrane formation and lymphadenopathy
Correct Answer: B

The two INITIAL clinical criteria for ANUP diagnosis are: (1) loss of attachment and (2) pain. ANUP = ANUG (punched-out papillae, gingival bleeding, pain) PLUS attachment and bone loss. Your notes from the periodontal emergency lecture detail ANUG characteristics (infection characterized by gingival necrosis presenting with punched-out papillae, gingival bleeding, and pain), and ANUP adds clinical attachment loss and alveolar bone loss to those ANUG features. Predisposing factors include stress, poor diet, cigarette smoking, and HIV infection. Associated organisms are fusiform bacteria, Prevotella intermedia, and spirochetes.

Why A is wrong: Mobility and BOP aren't the two defining criteria. Why C is wrong: These are general inflammation signs, not specific to ANUP. Why D is wrong: These are secondary/supporting features, not the two initial criteria. Why E is wrong: Pseudomembrane and lymphadenopathy are secondary diagnostic features.

Q179 A gingival abscess is best described as:
A. A periapical infection draining through the marginal periodontium
B. An acute inflammatory response to a foreign body forced into the sulcus
C. A chronic infection of the furcation area
D. An endodontic lesion with a sinus tract
E. A lateral periodontal cyst
Correct Answer: B

A gingival abscess is an acute inflammatory response to a foreign body forced into the gingival sulcus — think popcorn hull, seed, broken toothpick, or calculus fragment pushed into the tissue. It's a localized, acute process in an otherwise relatively healthy sulcus (vs. a periodontal abscess which forms in a pre-existing pocket). Treatment involves removing the foreign body, draining the abscess, and irrigating. The gingival abscess is DISTINCT from a periodontal abscess (which involves deep pockets, bone loss, and specific organisms like P. gingivalis and Prevotella intermedia).

Why A is wrong: That describes a primary endo lesion with secondary perio involvement. Why C is wrong: Furcation involvement is a periodontal condition, not a gingival abscess. Why D is wrong: That's an endodontic abscess. Why E is wrong: Lateral periodontal cyst is a developmental cyst.

Q189 Pericoronitis most commonly involves which tooth?
A. Maxillary first molar
B. Mandibular first premolar
C. Third molar area
D. Maxillary canine
E. Mandibular lateral incisor
Correct Answer: C

Pericoronitis = third molar area. It's inflammation/infection of the operculum (gingival flap) partially covering an erupting or impacted tooth. Third molars are overwhelmingly the most common site because they're the last teeth to erupt and frequently have insufficient space, leading to partial eruption and a persistent operculum that traps food and bacteria. Pericoronitis can be acute (pain, swelling, trismus) or chronic (mild discomfort, occasional drainage) and is one of the most common indications for third molar extraction.

Why A is wrong: First molars fully erupt in childhood and rarely have pericoronitis. Why B is wrong: Premolars rarely have operculum issues. Why D is wrong: Canines can be impacted but pericoronitis is overwhelmingly a third molar problem. Why E is wrong: Lateral incisors don't typically develop pericoronitis.

Q190 The microbiological organisms most associated with periodontal abscess formation are:
A. Streptococcus mutans and Lactobacillus
B. Porphyromonas gingivalis and Prevotella intermedia
C. Candida albicans and Aspergillus
D. Staphylococcus aureus and MRSA
E. Herpes simplex virus and Epstein-Barr virus
Correct Answer: B

P. gingivalis and Prevotella intermedia are the organisms most associated with periodontal abscess formation. These are anaerobic, gram-negative organisms from the red and orange complexes (Socransky) that produce virulence factors promoting tissue destruction, including collagenase, proteases, and endotoxin (LPS). The periodontal abscess presents with increased probing, pain, pus, and sometimes incomplete root fracture.

Why A is wrong: These are cariogenic organisms, not periodontal abscess pathogens. Why C is wrong: These are fungal organisms associated with oral candidiasis, not abscesses. Why D is wrong: Staph is associated with skin/wound infections, not typical periodontal abscesses. Why E is wrong: Viruses are associated with NUG predisposition, not abscess formation.

CHEMOTHERAPEUTICS & ORAL HYGIENE (13)
Q100 The Bass brushing technique is characterized by:
A. Bristles directed 45 degrees toward the occlusal surface with a rolling motion
B. Bristles directed 45 degrees toward the gingival sulcus with a short back-and-forth vibrating motion
C. Bristles directed perpendicular to the tooth surface with a circular motion
D. Bristles placed horizontally with a long scrubbing motion
E. Bristles directed 90 degrees to the gingival margin with a sweeping motion
Correct Answer: B

The Bass technique: bristles are angled 45 degrees toward the gingival sulcus (not toward the occlusal surface), and you use a short, vibratory back-and-forth motion. The 45-degree angulation is specifically designed to get bristle tips INTO the sulcus, engaging and disrupting the subgingival plaque that sits in the first 1–2mm of the gingival crevice. The short vibrating motion dislodges plaque without traumatizing the tissue. This is THE technique we recommend most frequently for periodontal patients because it addresses subgingival plaque — the primary etiologic factor in periodontal disease.

Why A is wrong: 45 degrees toward the OCCLUSAL surface points bristles AWAY from the sulcus — opposite of what you want. Why C is wrong: Perpendicular bristle placement with circular motion is the Fones technique (used for children). Why D is wrong: Long horizontal scrubbing causes abrasion and recession. Why E is wrong: 90 degrees to the margin doesn't engage the sulcus.

Q101 A proxabrush (interdental brush) is most appropriately used in:
A. Tight contact areas between teeth
B. Open interdental spaces (embrasures)
C. Around orthodontic brackets only
D. Subgingivally to debride deep pockets
E. Only on anterior teeth
Correct Answer: B

Proxabrushes are designed for open contact areas — spaces where the interdental papilla has receded or is missing, leaving open embrasures. They're NOT for tight contacts (that's what floss is for). Open embrasures are common in periodontal patients because attachment loss causes papilla shrinkage. The proxabrush provides better plaque removal in these wide spaces than floss, which slips through without contacting the root surfaces. They come in various sizes to match the embrasure dimensions — always select the largest size that fits without forcing.

Why A is wrong: Tight contacts require floss — a proxabrush won't fit. Why C is wrong: They're useful around brackets but that's not their primary indication. Why D is wrong: They're for supragingival/interdental cleaning, not deep subgingival debridement. Why E is wrong: They work on any tooth with open embrasures, posterior included.

Q102 All of the following are reasons to clean interdental areas EXCEPT:
A. The interdental area is self-cleansing
B. Interdental areas harbor the highest concentration of plaque biofilm
C. Periodontal disease often begins in the interdental area
D. The toothbrush cannot effectively reach interdental surfaces
E. Calculus tends to form in interdental areas
Correct Answer: A

The interdental area is NOT self-cleansing — this is the exception. In fact, the interdental area is exactly the OPPOSITE of self-cleansing: it's a protected, stagnant zone where plaque accumulates undisturbed because the cheeks, tongue, and salivary flow don't reach it effectively. This is precisely WHY interdental cleaning (floss, proxabrush, etc.) is necessary. All other options are legitimate reasons to clean interdentally — plaque accumulates there, disease starts there, brushes can't reach there, and calculus forms there.

Why B is wrong (i.e., it IS a valid reason): Interdental areas do harbor dense biofilm. Why C is wrong (i.e., it IS a valid reason): Periodontitis typically begins interproximally. Why D is wrong (i.e., it IS a valid reason): Toothbrush bristles don't reach into closed contacts. Why E is wrong (i.e., it IS a valid reason): Calculus forms preferentially near salivary duct openings and in stagnant areas.

Q103 What oral hygiene device is best for cleaning the distal surface of a difficult-to-reach third molar?
A. Dental tape
B. Dental floss
C. End-tuft brush
D. Standard manual toothbrush
E. Proxabrush
Correct Answer: C

An end-tuft brush (also called a single-tuft or sulcabrush) is the best choice for the distal of a third molar. It has a small, concentrated tuft of bristles that can navigate into the tight space behind the last tooth in the arch — an area that a standard toothbrush head can't access and where floss has nothing to wrap around distally. Dental tape and floss are designed for interproximal contacts between teeth, not for the distal surface of the most posterior tooth. The end-tuft brush can also be used around orthodontic appliances and other hard-to-reach areas.

Why A is wrong: Dental tape is for flat, broad contact areas between teeth — not behind the last molar. Why B is wrong: Floss requires two adjacent tooth surfaces to work — the distal of a third molar has no tooth behind it. Why D is wrong: Standard brush heads are too large to access the distal of a third molar. Why E is wrong: Proxabrush needs an open embrasure between two teeth.

Q104 What is the concentration of chlorhexidine (CHX) prescribed in the United States?
A. 1.2%
B. 0.12%
C. 0.012%
D. 2.0%
E. 0.2%
Correct Answer: B

In the United States, CHX is prescribed at 0.12% (brand name Peridex/PerioGard). This is an important distinction from the European formulation, which is 0.2% (Hibitane). Your midterm slides list both: "Hibitane 0.2%" and "Hibitane 0.1%." The US concentration was reduced to 0.12% to minimize side effects (staining, taste alteration) while maintaining clinical effectiveness. CHX is still the gold standard antimicrobial rinse at either concentration — it's just that the US uses the lower one.

Why A is wrong: 1.2% is 10x the actual US concentration — that would be extremely irritating. Why C is wrong: 0.012% is too dilute to be therapeutically effective. Why D is wrong: 2.0% CHX is used for skin antisepsis (pre-surgical scrub), not as an oral rinse. Why E is wrong: 0.2% is the European concentration, not the US standard.

Q105 Which chemotherapeutic mouth rinse is considered the MOST effective antiplaque agent?
A. Chlorhexidine (CHX)
B. Listerine (essential oils)
C. Hydrogen peroxide
D. Cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC)
E. Stannous fluoride rinse
Correct Answer: A

CHX is the gold standard — the most effective antiplaque chemotherapeutic agent available. It has the broadest antimicrobial spectrum, the highest substantivity (see next question), and the most robust evidence base. Listerine is a solid second-line option but doesn't match CHX's effectiveness. Your midterm slides reinforce CHX as the top-tier agent. The downside is its side effects (brown staining, taste alteration, calculus formation), which is why it's typically used short-term (2–4 weeks post-surgery) rather than lifelong.

Why B is wrong: Listerine is effective but less so than CHX in head-to-head studies. Why C is wrong: Hydrogen peroxide has minimal sustained antiplaque effect. Why D is wrong: CPC has moderate effectiveness but inferior to CHX. Why E is wrong: Stannous fluoride has some antiplaque activity but isn't the most effective agent overall.

Q106 What is "substantivity" in the context of oral chemotherapeutics?
A. The overall effectiveness of the agent against all bacterial species
B. The sustained release of the agent at therapeutic levels over an extended period after initial application
C. The ability of the agent to penetrate biofilm
D. The concentration of active ingredient in the formulation
E. The speed at which the agent kills bacteria on contact
Correct Answer: B

Substantivity is the sustained release of an antimicrobial agent at therapeutic levels over an extended period after initial application. CHX has the highest substantivity of any oral rinse — it binds to oral surfaces (mucosa, teeth, pellicle) and is slowly released over 8–12 hours, maintaining bacteriostatic or bactericidal concentrations long after you spit the rinse out. This is what makes CHX so effective — you rinse for 30 seconds but get hours of antimicrobial activity. Other rinses wash out quickly and provide only transient effects.

Why A is wrong: That describes spectrum of activity, not substantivity. Why C is wrong: Biofilm penetration is a separate property. Why D is wrong: Concentration is a formulation characteristic, not substantivity. Why E is wrong: Speed of kill is a pharmacodynamic property, not substantivity.

Q107 What is the mechanism of action of chlorhexidine (CHX)?
A. Affects bacterial cell wall/membrane permeability, causing leakage of intracellular contents
B. Inhibits bacterial DNA synthesis
C. Blocks bacterial ribosomal protein translation
D. Disrupts bacterial folic acid metabolism
E. Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis like penicillin
Correct Answer: A

CHX works by affecting bacterial cell wall/membrane permeability. It's a cationic molecule (positively charged) that binds to the negatively charged bacterial cell membrane, disrupting it and causing leakage of intracellular contents. At low concentrations it's bacteriostatic (slows growth); at high concentrations it's bactericidal (kills outright). This membrane-disruption mechanism is why CHX has such a broad spectrum — virtually all bacteria have cell membranes that can be disrupted. It also explains why CHX binds to oral tissues (which are also negatively charged), giving it substantivity.

Why B is wrong: DNA synthesis inhibition is the mechanism of fluoroquinolones, not CHX. Why C is wrong: Ribosomal inhibition is how tetracyclines and macrolides work. Why D is wrong: Folic acid disruption is how sulfonamides and trimethoprim work. Why E is wrong: Cell wall synthesis inhibition is the mechanism of beta-lactam antibiotics.

Q108 Which oral chemotherapeutic agent is most commonly associated with stubborn extrinsic tooth staining?
A. Chlorhexidine (CHX)
B. Pyrophosphate
C. Phenolic compounds (Listerine)
D. Hydrogen peroxide
E. Cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC)
Correct Answer: A

CHX is notorious for causing brown/yellow extrinsic staining of teeth, restorations, and the tongue. The staining occurs because CHX (a cation) binds to dietary chromogens and tannins (found in coffee, tea, red wine) on tooth surfaces, creating a discolored complex. This is one of the main reasons CHX is limited to short-term use (2–4 weeks post-surgery). Your slides also note that CHX interacts with sodium lauryl sulfate (the detergent in toothpaste), so patients should wait at least 30 minutes between brushing and rinsing with CHX to maintain its antiplaque effectiveness.

Why B is wrong: Pyrophosphate is anti-calculus and doesn't cause significant staining. Why C is wrong: Listerine can cause some staining but nowhere near CHX levels. Why D is wrong: Hydrogen peroxide is actually used to BLEACH teeth. Why E is wrong: CPC causes minimal staining compared to CHX.

Q109 What are the active agents in Listerine mouth rinse?
A. Chlorhexidine and cetylpyridinium chloride
B. Thymol, menthol, and eucalyptol (essential oils)
C. Stannous fluoride and triclosan
D. Hydrogen peroxide and sodium bicarbonate
E. Pyrophosphate and zinc citrate
Correct Answer: B

Listerine contains essential oils: thymol, menthol, eucalyptol, and methyl salicylate. These phenolic compounds disrupt bacterial cell walls and have anti-inflammatory properties. Listerine is the most studied OTC (over-the-counter) antiseptic rinse and is the only ADA-accepted non-prescription antiplaque/antigingivitis rinse other than CPC rinses. It's a good second-line option when CHX is not indicated (for longer-term use when CHX staining is unacceptable). The alcohol in Listerine serves as a solvent for the essential oils.

Why A is wrong: Neither CHX nor CPC is in Listerine. Why C is wrong: These are completely different agents not found in Listerine. Why D is wrong: Peroxide-based rinses are separate products. Why E is wrong: These are anti-calculus/anti-halitosis agents, not Listerine components.

Q110 CHX's effectiveness and sustained antimicrobial activity are primarily attributed to its chemical nature as a:
A. Bisguanide that is bicationic (carries two positive charges)
B. Monovalent anion that binds to calculus
C. Neutral molecule that passes through cell membranes passively
D. Fluoride compound with antibacterial properties
E. Quaternary ammonium compound
Correct Answer: A

CHX is a bisguanide that is bicationic — meaning it carries two positive charges. This double positive charge is what gives CHX its remarkable properties: it binds strongly to negatively charged bacterial cell membranes (antimicrobial effect), to negatively charged tooth surfaces, pellicle, and oral mucosa (substantivity), and to anionic molecules like sodium lauryl sulfate in toothpaste (which is why you need to wait 30 minutes between brushing and rinsing — your slides state that even a 30-minute interval resulted in "significantly reduced antiplaque effect"). The bicationic nature is the molecular basis for everything CHX does.

Why B is wrong: CHX is cationic (positive), not anionic (negative). Why C is wrong: CHX actively binds electrostatically — it doesn't passively diffuse. Why D is wrong: CHX is not a fluoride compound. Why E is wrong: Quaternary ammonium compounds (like CPC) are a different class of antimicrobials.

Q111 Which fluoride compound is the most effective for plaque control?
A. Stannous fluoride
B. Sodium fluoride
C. Acidulated phosphate fluoride
D. All fluoride compounds are equally effective for plaque control
E. Sodium monofluorophosphate
Correct Answer: A

Stannous fluoride (SnF\u2082) is the most effective fluoride for plaque control. The "stannous" part (tin ion, Sn²⁺) is what provides the antimicrobial activity — it disrupts bacterial metabolism and reduces plaque formation beyond what the fluoride ion alone achieves. Sodium fluoride and APF are excellent for caries prevention (remineralization and fluorapatite formation) but don't have the same antiplaque properties. Stannous fluoride also has anti-gingivitis properties, which is why products like Crest Pro-Health (which contains SnF\u2082) can claim both anti-cavity AND anti-gingivitis benefits.

Why B is wrong: Sodium fluoride prevents caries but has no significant antiplaque effect. Why C is wrong: APF is a professional topical fluoride for caries prevention, not plaque control. Why D is wrong: They are NOT equally effective — stannous is superior for plaque control. Why E is wrong: Sodium monofluorophosphate is primarily anti-caries.

Q129 Which toothpaste product was the only one FDA and ADA approved for anti-plaque, antimicrobial, AND anti-gingivitis claims, and what was its active antimicrobial agent?
A. Crest Pro-Health; stannous fluoride
B. Colgate Total; triclosan
C. Sensodyne; potassium nitrate
D. Parodontax; sodium bicarbonate
E. Arm & Hammer; baking soda
Correct Answer: B

Your notes state: "Colgate Total the only one FDA and ADA approved to be anti-plaque, anti-microbial and anti-gingivitis" and "Colgate Total is the only one that has antimicrobial triclosan." Triclosan is a broad-spectrum antibacterial agent that was unique to Colgate Total's formulation. However, your notes also include the important caveat that triclosan is "supposed to be one of the most toxic elements on planet, can produce cancer" — which led to its removal from many consumer products. Newer Colgate Total formulations have replaced triclosan with stannous fluoride.

Why A is wrong: Crest Pro-Health uses stannous fluoride but wasn't the product with the FDA/ADA triple approval for anti-plaque/antimicrobial/anti-gingivitis. Why C is wrong: Sensodyne is for sensitivity, not antimicrobial claims. Why D is wrong: Parodontax is for bleeding gums but didn't have the FDA/ADA triple approval. Why E is wrong: Baking soda isn't an antimicrobial agent with these claims.

DIAGNOSIS, CLASSIFICATION, RISK FACTORS & CLINICAL PEARLS (71)
Q34 Which tooth is most commonly lost due to caries and periodontal disease?
A. Mandibular central incisor
B. Maxillary lateral incisor
C. First molar
D. Second premolar
E. Third molar
Correct Answer: C

The first molar is the most commonly lost tooth due to caries and periodontal disease. This makes clinical sense on multiple fronts: it erupts earliest of the permanent posteriors (~age 6), giving it the longest exposure time to caries risk. It also has complex anatomy with furcations that make periodontal maintenance difficult. Once furcation involvement occurs, prognosis drops significantly. Additionally, patients often don't recognize the first molar as a permanent tooth (confusing it with a primary tooth), leading to neglect during childhood.

Why A is wrong: Lower incisors are lost to perio but not as commonly overall. Why B is wrong: Max laterals are congenitally missing sometimes but aren't the most commonly LOST. Why D is wrong: Second premolars aren't the #1 lost tooth. Why E is wrong: Third molars are commonly extracted electively, but this question asks about loss due to disease.

Q35 After third molars, which tooth is the most commonly impacted, and in which population is it more prevalent?
A. Mandibular second premolar; more common in males
B. Maxillary canine; 3x more common in females
C. Mandibular first premolar; equally common in males and females
D. Maxillary lateral incisor; 2x more common in females
E. Mandibular canine; 3x more common in males
Correct Answer: B

After third molars, the maxillary canine is the most commonly impacted tooth, and it occurs approximately 3x more frequently in females than males. The upper canine has a long path of eruption (it develops high in the maxilla near the orbit and must travel a great distance to its final position), making it more susceptible to impaction. The female predilection may relate to differences in jaw size and timing of development. Impacted maxillary canines are a major clinical concern because canines are essential for occlusal guidance and esthetics.

Why A is wrong: Mandibular second premolars can be impacted but aren't #2 after third molars. Why C is wrong: Mandibular first premolars are rarely impacted. Why D is wrong: Maxillary laterals may be malpositioned but aren't commonly impacted. Why E is wrong: Mandibular canines are rarely impacted, and the gender ratio is wrong.

Q36 When managing an impacted maxillary canine, which clinical scenario would indicate using an open surgical technique (window exposure)?
A. Wide zone of attached gingiva with deep palatal impaction
B. Narrow zone of attached gingiva with a shallow labial or mid-alveolar bony impaction
C. Deep palatal impaction with thick keratinized tissue
D. Labial impaction with adequate attached gingiva and shallow position
E. Any impaction regardless of tissue or bony position
Correct Answer: B

The open technique is indicated when there is a narrow zone of attached gingiva combined with a shallow labial or mid-alveolar bony impaction. In this scenario, a closed technique (bonding a bracket under a flap) risks further compromising the already limited attached gingiva. By using an open window technique, the impacted canine is exposed and allowed to erupt through keratinized tissue, which is better for long-term periodontal health. The shallow position means the tooth is close enough to the surface that an open approach can effectively guide it.

Why A is wrong: Deep palatal impactions typically use a closed technique. Why C is wrong: Thick KT with deep palatal position favors a closed technique. Why D is wrong: Adequate attached gingiva with shallow position could use either technique but doesn't specifically mandate an open approach. Why E is wrong: Technique selection absolutely depends on tissue and bony factors.

Q37 What is the purpose of intramarrow penetrations made over the root prominence in bone between an impacted tooth and its correct position?
A. To create space for bracket placement and archwire activation
B. To stimulate osteopenia and reduce resistance to tooth movement
C. To remove cortical bone for direct surgical repositioning
D. To increase blood flow for graft placement
E. To facilitate membrane placement for GTR around the impacted tooth
Correct Answer: B

Intramarrow penetrations serve two purposes: (1) stimulate osteopenia (localized bone softening/remodeling) and (2) reduce tooth movement resistance. These small perforations create a Regional Acceleratory Phenomenon (RAP) — a transient burst of localized hard and soft tissue remodeling after surgical wounding of cortical bone. By poking holes through the cortical plate into the marrow space along the path of intended tooth movement, you kick-start an accelerated remodeling cycle that makes the bone more permissive to orthodontic forces. This is the same biologic principle behind corticotomy-assisted orthodontics.

Why A is wrong: Bracket placement doesn't require intramarrow penetrations. Why C is wrong: You're not removing cortical bone — you're perforating it to stimulate remodeling. Why D is wrong: This isn't about graft vascularity. Why E is wrong: GTR membranes aren't used in impacted canine management.

Q38 When performing ostectomy during crown lengthening or osseous surgery, how much bone should be preserved on the proximal surfaces of adjacent teeth?
A. 0.5mm
B. 1.0mm
C. 1.5mm
D. 2.0mm
E. 3.0mm
Correct Answer: C

You need to leave at least 1.5mm of bone on the proximal sides of adjacent teeth during ostectomy. This is a critical number — if you take too much bone from the neighboring teeth, you create iatrogenic attachment loss and compromise the periodontium of teeth that were otherwise healthy. Your midterm slides also discuss how bone of adjacent teeth may be removed during surgery to avoid a precipitous change in osseous morphology between teeth, but the 1.5mm minimum protects the biologic width and periodontal support of those neighbors.

Why A is wrong: 0.5mm is dangerously thin and would compromise the adjacent tooth's attachment. Why B is wrong: 1.0mm provides inadequate protection. Why D is wrong: 2.0mm is more conservative than needed — not the stated guideline. Why E is wrong: 3.0mm is excessively conservative and may prevent adequate recontouring.

Q39 When evaluating anterior gingival esthetics, the gingival crests of which teeth should be at the same level, and how should the lateral incisor compare?
A. Central incisors and canines should be at the same level; lateral incisor gingival crest should be slightly more coronal
B. All six anterior teeth should have gingival crests at exactly the same level
C. Central and lateral incisors should match; canine should be more apical
D. Canines should be the most coronal; centrals intermediate; laterals most apical
E. There is no established esthetic guideline for anterior gingival crest levels
Correct Answer: A

The gingival crests of the central incisors and canines should be at the same level — they form the "frame" of the smile. The lateral incisor gingival crest should sit slightly more coronal (about 1–1.5mm) than the centrals and canines. This creates the classic esthetic gingival architecture where there's a gentle dip at the laterals. This principle is essential for crown lengthening planning in the esthetic zone — if you need to correct a gummy smile or uneven gingival margins, you aim for this ideal relationship.

Why B is wrong: Having all six at the same level would actually look unnatural — the laterals need to be slightly coronal. Why C is wrong: The canine should match the central, not be more apical. Why D is wrong: This reverses the relationship. Why E is wrong: This is a well-established esthetic guideline used in both perio and restorative treatment planning.

Q40 When is a gingivectomy contraindicated for correcting a gummy smile or excessive gingival display?
A. When there is generalized gingival enlargement from medications
B. When there is risk of root exposure or when a single incisor is supraerupted
C. When the patient has thick biotype tissue
D. When the gummy smile is caused by altered passive eruption
E. When multiple teeth are involved
Correct Answer: B

Gingivectomy is contraindicated when there is a risk of root exposure (meaning the CEJ-to-bone distance is already minimal, so removing gingiva would expose root) or when a single incisor is supraerupted. In the supraerupted single incisor scenario, the problem isn't excess tissue — the tooth itself has over-erupted, so the gingival margin appears more coronal than its neighbors. A gingivectomy would remove tissue but create an asymmetric gingival contour because the underlying bone level is different. The correct treatment for a supraerupted incisor is orthodontic intrusion, not tissue removal.

Why A is wrong: Medication-induced gingival enlargement is actually a classic indication FOR gingivectomy. Why C is wrong: Thick biotype is actually more favorable for gingivectomy. Why D is wrong: Altered passive eruption is one of the primary indications for gingivectomy/crown lengthening. Why E is wrong: Multiple teeth can be treated with gingivectomy.

Q41 What is a fiberotomy procedure, and in which teeth is it most successful (lowest relapse rate)?
A. Cutting the transseptal fibers; most successful in mandibular premolars
B. Inserting a scalpel into the sulcus to sever gingival and transseptal fibers; most successful in maxillary anteriors with the least relapse
C. Removing supracrestal fibers with a laser; most successful in mandibular molars
D. Performing a full-thickness flap to sever PDL fibers; equally successful in all teeth
E. Severing only the free gingival fibers; most successful in mandibular incisors
Correct Answer: B

A fiberotomy involves inserting a scalpel blade into the sulcus to sever the supracrestal gingival and transseptal fibers that cause orthodontic relapse. After orthodontic movement (especially rotation), these fibers have "memory" — they pull the tooth back toward its original position. By cutting them circumferentially around the tooth within the sulcus, you eliminate the elastic recoil. It's most successful in maxillary anteriors, producing the least relapse. This makes sense because upper anteriors are commonly rotated teeth that are corrected orthodontically, and the procedure is technically easier to perform in the accessible anterior region.

Why A is wrong: It's not just transseptal fibers, and premolars aren't the most successful site. Why C is wrong: Laser isn't the described technique, and mandibular molars aren't the optimal site. Why D is wrong: No full-thickness flap is needed — it's a minimally invasive sulcular approach. Why E is wrong: Both free gingival and transseptal fibers are targeted, and mandibular incisors aren't the most successful location.

Q42 What is the optimal tissue location for placement of temporary anchorage devices (TADs)?
A. In the alveolar mucosa beyond the mucogingival junction
B. In the attached tissue at the mucogingival junction (MGJ)
C. In the interradicular bone within keratinized attached tissue
D. In the palatal rugae area only
E. Directly into the PDL space
Correct Answer: B

The optimal placement for TADs is in attached tissue at the MGJ. Placing TADs in attached/keratinized tissue reduces the risk of peri-implant inflammation and soft tissue complications compared to placing them in loose alveolar mucosa. Mobile mucosa around a TAD promotes inflammation, plaque accumulation, and potential failure. The interradicular areas are common anatomic sites, but the tissue type at the insertion point is what matters most — you want firm, immobile, keratinized tissue.

Why A is wrong: Alveolar mucosa is mobile and non-keratinized — worst location for TAD stability and tissue health. Why C is wrong: While interradicular placement is anatomically common, the question asks about tissue location, and the answer is specifically at the MGJ in attached tissue. Why D is wrong: Palatal rugae placement is used in some situations but isn't the universal optimal position. Why E is wrong: Placing a TAD into the PDL space would cause tooth damage and is never indicated.

Q43 What is the Regional Acceleratory Phenomenon (RAP)?
A. Permanent thickening of cortical bone after surgical insult
B. A transient burst of localized hard and soft tissue remodeling after surgical wounding of cortical bone that potentiates tissue reorganization and healing
C. Decreased bone metabolism following orthodontic force application
D. Permanent osteoporosis induced by corticotomy procedures
E. Increased mineralization density of bone surrounding implants after loading
Correct Answer: B

RAP is a transient burst of localized hard and soft tissue remodeling that occurs after surgical wounding of cortical bone. It potentiates tissue reorganization and healing. The key word is "transient" — it's temporary, lasting weeks to months, during which bone turnover dramatically increases in the surgical area. This creates a window of opportunity for accelerated orthodontic movement because the bone becomes temporarily more porous and less resistant to tooth movement. RAP is the biologic basis behind procedures like corticotomy-assisted orthodontics and the intramarrow penetrations discussed for impacted canine management.

Why A is wrong: RAP is transient, not permanent, and it causes temporary porosity, not thickening. Why C is wrong: RAP increases bone metabolism, not decreases it. Why D is wrong: It's transient remodeling, not permanent osteoporosis. Why E is wrong: RAP relates to surgical wounding, not implant loading.

Q83 A patient presents with 2–4mm probing depths, swollen blue-colored gingiva, and a radiograph showing the alveolar bone crest 1mm from the CEJ. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. Gingivitis
B. Necrotizing ulcerative periodontitis
C. Chronic periodontitis
D. Periodontitis Stage I
E. Periodontal health on a reduced periodontium
Correct Answer: A

This is gingivitis. Here's why: the bone crest is 1mm from the CEJ, which is NORMAL (healthy bone sits 1–2mm apical to the CEJ). So there's no bone loss. The swollen blue gingiva and 2–4mm probing depths represent inflammatory tissue enlargement (pseudopocketing from edema), not true attachment loss or bone destruction. Blue/cyanotic color indicates chronic venous congestion in inflamed tissue. Without bone loss, you cannot diagnose periodontitis — regardless of how angry the tissue looks.

Why B is wrong: NUP would show tissue necrosis, punched-out papillae, and bone loss — none of which are described. Why C is wrong: Chronic periodontitis requires bone loss — the bone is at a normal 1mm from CEJ. Why D is wrong: Stage I periodontitis still requires attachment loss — this case has none. Why E is wrong: Reduced periodontium implies prior attachment loss that has been stabilized — no prior loss exists here.

Q84 Plaque and calculus are causing what type of periodontal disease?
A. Congenital
B. Inflammatory
C. Reactionary
D. Traumatic
E. Neoplastic
Correct Answer: B

Plaque and calculus cause inflammatory periodontal disease. The entire pathogenesis of gingivitis and periodontitis is driven by the host inflammatory response to bacterial biofilm (plaque) and its mineralized form (calculus). Calculus itself isn't directly pathogenic — it provides a rough, retentive surface for additional plaque accumulation, which drives the inflammation. The bacterial products trigger the innate and adaptive immune responses, leading to tissue destruction. This is why SRP (removing plaque and calculus) is the foundation of all periodontal therapy.

Why A is wrong: Congenital conditions are present from birth and not caused by plaque. Why C is wrong: "Reactionary" isn't a recognized category of periodontal disease. Why D is wrong: Traumatic relates to occlusal forces, not plaque/calculus. Why E is wrong: Neoplastic means tumor-related — not caused by plaque.

Q85 Which of the following teeth has the BEST prognosis?
A. Maxillary molar with Class III furcation involvement
B. Two-wall intrabony defect
C. Mandibular molar with Class II furcation involvement
D. Three-wall intrabony defect
E. All have equal prognosis
Correct Answer: D

A three-wall intrabony defect has the best prognosis among these options. Three-wall defects are the most contained (bone on three sides), providing the greatest regenerative potential — they hold graft material well, maintain space for membrane placement, and have the best blood supply from surrounding walls. Two-wall defects are less contained and less predictable for regeneration. Furcation involvement (especially Class II and III) significantly worsens prognosis because of the anatomic complexity and inability to adequately debride. Class III furcation (through-and-through) on a maxillary molar is essentially the worst prognosis scenario.

Why A is wrong: Class III furcation = through-and-through bone loss = poorest prognosis of all listed. Why B is wrong: Two-wall defects have moderate regenerative potential, less than three-wall. Why C is wrong: Class II furcation on a mandibular molar is problematic due to narrow lingual furcation entrance and limited access. Why E is wrong: These absolutely have different prognoses.

Q88 A tooth has 2mm recession and 2mm probing depth (CAL = 4mm). This tooth most likely has:
A. Severe periodontitis
B. Moderate periodontitis
C. Mild periodontitis
D. Gingivitis
E. Periodontal health
Correct Answer: C

With 2mm recession + 2mm probing = 4mm CAL, this falls into the mild periodontitis category. In the 2018 classification staging system, Stage I periodontitis corresponds to 1–2mm CAL (interdental), and Stage II is 3–4mm CAL. In the older system, mild periodontitis was generally defined as 1–2mm CAL, and moderate was 3–4mm CAL. Either way, 4mm CAL with recession clearly indicates some attachment loss has occurred — this isn't gingivitis (which has no attachment loss). The probing depth is only 2mm (shallow), but the recession reveals that attachment was lost and the tissue receded rather than forming a pocket.

Why A is wrong: Severe periodontitis requires CAL ≥5mm (Stage III+). Why B is wrong: Moderate periodontitis is on the border but 4mm CAL with only 2mm PD is more consistent with mild-to-early-moderate disease. Why D is wrong: Gingivitis has NO attachment loss — this patient has 4mm CAL. Why E is wrong: There is measurable attachment loss.

Q89 What is the most reliable objective clinical feature for diagnosing gingivitis?
A. Color change of the gingiva
B. Loss of stippling
C. Change in gingival contour
D. Bleeding on probing (BOP)
E. Patient-reported pain
Correct Answer: D

Bleeding on probing is the most objective and reliable clinical sign of gingival inflammation. Color change, loss of stippling, and contour changes are all useful clinical observations, but they're more subjective — they depend on the clinician's perception and can be affected by pigmentation, tissue thickness, and biotype. BOP is binary (it either bleeds or it doesn't), reproducible, and directly reflects the histologic state of the sulcular epithelium. Your midterm slides on the 2018 classification define gingivitis as >10% of sites with BOP, reinforcing BOP as the diagnostic gold standard.

Why A is wrong: Color is subjective — varies with pigmentation and lighting. Why B is wrong: Stippling varies naturally between individuals and biotypes. Why C is wrong: Contour changes are visual assessments with interexaminer variability. Why E is wrong: Pain is subjective, unreliable, and most gingivitis is painless.

Q90 What percentage of tooth surfaces must be involved to classify periodontal disease as "localized" versus "generalized"?
A. Less than 10% = localized; more than 10% = generalized
B. Less than 20% = localized; more than 20% = generalized
C. Less than 30% = localized; more than 30% = generalized
D. Less than 50% = localized; more than 50% = generalized
E. Less than 40% = localized; more than 40% = generalized
Correct Answer: C

Less than 30% of sites involved = localized; more than 30% = generalized. This cutoff applies to both gingivitis and periodontitis in the 2018 classification. Your slides define it explicitly: "Localized is defined as 10%–30% bleeding sites" and "Generalized is defined as >30% bleeding sites." This is a straightforward memorization point, but the concept matters for treatment planning — generalized disease requires more comprehensive intervention than a few localized sites.

Why A is wrong: 10% is the threshold for gingivitis diagnosis (>10% BOP = gingivitis), not the localized/generalized cutoff. Why B is wrong: 20% isn't used as any classification threshold. Why D is wrong: 50% is not the cutoff. Why E is wrong: 40% is not a recognized threshold.

Q97 All of the following microbiological tests can identify specific periodontal bacteria EXCEPT:
A. DNA probes
B. Phase contrast microscopy
C. PCR (polymerase chain reaction)
D. Culture and sensitivity
E. Immunoassays
Correct Answer: B

Phase contrast microscopy CANNOT identify specific bacterial species. It can show the general morphology of bacteria (cocci, rods, spirochetes, motile vs. non-motile) and give you a rough sense of the microbial composition, but it can't tell you "this is Porphyromonas gingivalis" vs. "this is Treponema denticola." DNA probes, PCR, culture, and immunoassays can all identify bacteria to the species level. Phase contrast is useful for chairside patient education (showing them live bacteria in their plaque) but not for definitive microbial identification.

Why A is wrong: DNA probes can identify specific species by hybridizing with unique genetic sequences. Why C is wrong: PCR amplifies species-specific DNA — highly sensitive identification. Why D is wrong: Culture grows organisms for species identification and antibiotic sensitivity testing. Why E is wrong: Immunoassays use antibodies specific to bacterial antigens for identification.

Q98 Side effects of oral hygiene adjuncts (toothbrush, floss, interdental cleaners) include all of the following EXCEPT:
A. Abrasion of the teeth
B. Laceration of the gingiva
C. Transient bacteremia
D. Gingival recession
E. All of the above are potential side effects
Correct Answer: E

ALL of the listed options are potential side effects of oral hygiene adjuncts. Aggressive brushing causes tooth abrasion (especially at the CEJ) and gingival recession — remember, toothbrushing is one of the two major causative factors of recession from your mucogingival lecture. Improper flossing or interdental brush use can lacerate the gingiva. And any oral hygiene procedure that causes bleeding can introduce oral bacteria into the bloodstream, causing transient bacteremia. This is why we consider antibiotic prophylaxis for certain at-risk patients.

Why A–D individually are wrong as the "exception": Each one IS a legitimate side effect, so none can be excluded.

Q99 What are the benefits of orthodontic treatment for the periodontium?
A. Provides a better path of insertion for a removable partial denture (RPD)
B. Better root alignment to relieve crowding, improving access for oral hygiene
C. Both A and B, plus additional periodontal benefits from improved tooth position
D. Orthodontics has no periodontal benefit
E. Only option B
Correct Answer: C

Orthodontic treatment benefits the periodontium in multiple ways: (1) better path of insertion for RPDs (improved prosthetic support and reduced food impaction), (2) better root alignment to relieve crowding (which improves the patient's ability to perform effective oral hygiene — crowded teeth trap more plaque), and (3) additional benefits like eliminating traumatic occlusal relationships, reducing bony defects between malpositioned teeth, and improving the overall architecture for periodontal maintenance. Your slides on orthodontic tooth movement also show that moving a facially positioned tooth lingually increases labial soft tissue thickness, gingival height, and reduces bone dehiscence.

Why A alone is wrong: RPD path improvement is one benefit but not the only one. Why B alone is wrong: Root alignment is one benefit but not the only one. Why D is wrong: Orthodontics absolutely has periodontal benefits when properly planned. Why E is wrong: Both A and B plus additional benefits are correct.

Q121 What is the difference between a true periodontal pocket and a pseudopocket (gingival pocket)?
A. A true pocket has the base of the pocket at the CEJ; a pseudopocket has the base apical to the CEJ
B. A true pocket involves apical migration of the junctional epithelium (deepening of the sulcus with attachment loss); a pseudopocket has the base of the pocket at the CEJ (gingival enlargement without attachment loss)
C. A true pocket is always painless; a pseudopocket is always painful
D. A true pocket occurs only in posterior teeth; a pseudopocket occurs only in anterior teeth
E. There is no clinical difference between the two
Correct Answer: B

A true periodontal pocket represents pathologic deepening of the sulcus due to apical migration of the junctional epithelium — meaning there IS true attachment loss (the JE has moved down the root). A pseudopocket has the base of the pocket at the CEJ — the sulcus appears deep because the gingiva has swollen/enlarged coronally (think drug-induced gingival overgrowth or inflammation), but the JE hasn't migrated apically, so there's NO true attachment loss. This distinction is critical for diagnosis: pseudopockets have increased probing depth but NORMAL CAL, while true pockets have increased probing depth AND increased CAL.

Why A is wrong: It's reversed — in a pseudopocket the base is at the CEJ; in a true pocket the base has migrated apical to the CEJ. Why C is wrong: Pain is not the differentiating feature. Why D is wrong: Both can occur on any tooth. Why E is wrong: There's a fundamental difference in pathology and treatment.

Q122 What is the difference between the histological sulcus and the clinical sulcus?
A. They are identical measurements
B. The histological sulcus extends from the coronal aspect to the apical aspect of the junctional epithelium and cannot be clinically measured; the clinical sulcus can be measured with a probe
C. The histological sulcus is always deeper than the clinical sulcus
D. The clinical sulcus can only be measured radiographically
E. The histological sulcus includes bone; the clinical sulcus does not
Correct Answer: B

The histological sulcus is the true anatomic space from the coronal to the apical aspect of the junctional epithelium — but you CANNOT measure it clinically because a probe penetrates beyond the histologic base of the sulcus (it pushes through the JE into the connective tissue). The clinical sulcus is what you actually measure with a periodontal probe, and it's typically slightly deeper than the histologic sulcus because of probe penetration through the JE. In health, the histologic sulcus is about 0.5mm deep, but clinically you'll read 1–3mm because the probe goes past the JE base.

Why A is wrong: They are NOT the same — the clinical measurement overestimates the histologic one. Why C is wrong: It's the opposite — the clinical sulcus reading is typically deeper than the histologic sulcus. Why D is wrong: The clinical sulcus is measured with a probe, not radiographs. Why E is wrong: Neither sulcus measurement includes bone.

Q123 A patient has a 2mm probing depth that bleeds on probing and a 4mm probing depth that does NOT bleed on probing. Which site is of greater clinical concern and why?
A. The 4mm site because deeper pockets always indicate more disease
B. The 2mm site because bleeding on probing indicates active inflammation, which is more clinically significant than depth alone
C. Both are equally concerning
D. Neither is concerning — both are within normal limits
E. The 4mm site because it requires surgical intervention regardless of BOP status
Correct Answer: B

This is a classic Fleisher teaching point. The 2mm site with BOP is more concerning because bleeding indicates active inflammation — the tissue is diseased and potentially progressing. The 4mm probing depth without bleeding could be a stable, non-inflamed pocket (like a successfully treated reduced periodontium). Probing depth alone doesn't tell you about disease activity — BOP does. Your slides confirm that BOP is the cardinal diagnostic sign of inflammation and the basis for the 2018 gingivitis case definition (>10% BOP = gingivitis). A shallow site that bleeds needs attention; a deeper site that's stable and non-bleeding may just need monitoring.

Why A is wrong: Depth alone doesn't indicate active disease — you need signs of inflammation. Why C is wrong: The bleeding site is definitively more concerning. Why D is wrong: A 2mm bleeding site IS concerning. Why E is wrong: A 4mm non-bleeding site doesn't automatically require surgery.

Q124 How does probe tip shape affect probing depth measurements?
A. All probe tips give identical readings regardless of shape
B. Round probe tips penetrate more than flat or tapered tips
C. Flat and tapered probe tips penetrate more than round probe tips, potentially giving deeper readings
D. Only electronic probes give accurate readings; manual probes are unreliable
E. Probe shape only matters in furcation areas
Correct Answer: C

Your clinical notes state: "The shape and angulation of the probe interfere with the measurements. Flat and tapered penetrates more than round." This makes physical sense — a flat or tapered tip has a smaller cross-sectional area at the point of tissue contact, concentrating force over a smaller area (higher pressure per unit area), allowing it to penetrate more deeply through the junctional epithelium. A round-tipped probe distributes force over a broader surface, reducing penetration. This is one reason standardized probes (like the Williams or UNC-15 with defined tip diameters) are recommended for reproducible measurements.

Why A is wrong: Probe shape absolutely affects readings. Why B is wrong: It's the opposite — round tips penetrate LESS. Why D is wrong: Both electronic and manual probes are valid; shape affects both. Why E is wrong: Probe shape affects measurements at ALL sites, not just furcations.

Q127 The predominant pathogenic bacteria in periodontal disease are classified as:
A. Aerobic, gram-positive cocci
B. Anaerobic organisms
C. Fungi and viruses only
D. Facultative gram-positive rods
E. Aerobic spirochetes
Correct Answer: B

Your notes state: "Periodontal pathogens are anaerobes." The key periodontal pathogens — P. gingivalis, T. forsythia, T. denticola (the red complex), A. actinomycetemcomitans, and others — are anaerobic or microaerophilic organisms that thrive in the deep, oxygen-depleted environment of the periodontal pocket. As a pocket deepens, the environment becomes increasingly anaerobic, favoring these pathogens. This is the fundamental microbiologic shift from health (aerobic, gram-positive) to disease (anaerobic, gram-negative). SRP disrupts this by opening the pocket to oxygen and physically removing the anaerobic biofilm.

Why A is wrong: Aerobic gram-positive cocci are health-associated, not disease-causing. Why C is wrong: While viruses may play a role, the primary pathogens are bacterial anaerobes. Why D is wrong: Facultative gram-positive rods aren't the primary periodontal pathogens. Why E is wrong: Spirochetes (like T. denticola) are anaerobic, not aerobic.

Q128 Which of the following statements about mouth rinses and periodontal disease is CORRECT?
A. Mouth rinses can treat periodontitis and should be used as primary therapy
B. Mouth rinses are effective against plaque bacteria and gingivitis but do NOT treat periodontitis
C. Mouth rinses can replace scaling and root planing
D. All mouth rinses have equal antimicrobial effectiveness
E. Mouth rinses reach the base of deep periodontal pockets
Correct Answer: B

Your notes are emphatic: "Mouthrinses don't fix perio disease, only plaque bacteria and gingivitis" and "There is no mouth rinse that tx periodontitis." Mouth rinses can reduce supragingival plaque and treat gingivitis (a superficial, reversible condition), but they CANNOT penetrate into deep periodontal pockets to reach the subgingival pathogens causing periodontitis. Periodontitis requires mechanical debridement (SRP) to disrupt the subgingival biofilm. Rinses are adjuncts, not replacements for mechanical therapy.

Why A is wrong: No rinse is primary therapy for periodontitis. Why C is wrong: Rinses cannot replace SRP — mechanical disruption is essential. Why D is wrong: CHX is the most effective, as established earlier. Why E is wrong: Rinses don't penetrate beyond 1–2mm subgingivally.

Q131 Why can horizontal bone loss NOT be effectively treated with bone grafting alone?
A. Horizontal defects have too much blood supply for graft incorporation
B. Horizontal bone loss lacks bony walls to contain the graft — after suturing, the graft material will fall to the sides
C. Horizontal bone loss is always accompanied by ankylosis preventing graft take
D. Bone grafts only work in edentulous areas, never around teeth
E. Horizontal bone loss heals spontaneously and doesn't need grafting
Correct Answer: B

Your notes explain: "Horizontal bone loss can't be tx with bone graft because after suture it will fall to the sides." Horizontal bone loss creates a flat, broad defect with no containing walls — there's nothing to hold the graft material in place. Compare this to a vertical/intrabony defect (especially a 3-wall defect), which has bony walls on multiple sides that contain and stabilize the graft. This is exactly why we discussed earlier that 3-wall defects have the best prognosis for regeneration — containment is key. For horizontal bone loss, the treatment approach is resective (osseous surgery) rather than regenerative.

Why A is wrong: Blood supply isn't the issue — containment is. Why C is wrong: Ankylosis isn't a feature of horizontal bone loss. Why D is wrong: Bone grafts are used around teeth all the time (in appropriate defect morphology). Why E is wrong: Horizontal bone loss does NOT heal spontaneously.

Q132 Bleeding on probing (BOP) is a sign of:
A. Periodontitis specifically
B. Gingival inflammation (gingivitis), NOT a definitive sign of periodontitis
C. Normal healthy periodontium
D. Occlusal trauma
E. Root fracture
Correct Answer: B

Your notes state: "Bleeding on probing is not a sign of perio" — meaning BOP by itself doesn't diagnose periodontitis. BOP is a sign of INFLAMMATION (gingivitis). To diagnose periodontitis, you need evidence of attachment loss (CAL) and/or bone loss IN ADDITION to inflammation. BOP is extremely sensitive (good at detecting inflammation) but not specific for periodontitis. A site can bleed because of gingivitis alone without any attachment loss whatsoever. However, BOP is still the most important clinical sign to monitor — sites that consistently bleed are at higher risk of future attachment loss.

Why A is wrong: BOP indicates inflammation but doesn't specifically diagnose periodontitis. Why C is wrong: Healthy tissue does NOT bleed on probing. Why D is wrong: Occlusal trauma alone doesn't cause BOP. Why E is wrong: Root fracture may cause localized signs but isn't diagnosed by BOP.

Q133 In periodontal patients with mild-to-moderate disease, connective tissue turnover occurs in approximately how long, and how frequently should periodontal patients be seen for maintenance?
A. Connective tissue turnover in 3 weeks; maintenance every 6 months
B. Connective tissue turnover in 6 weeks; maintenance every 3 months
C. Connective tissue turnover in 12 weeks; maintenance every 6 months
D. Connective tissue turnover in 2 weeks; maintenance every month
E. Connective tissue turnover in 10 weeks; maintenance every 4 months
Correct Answer: B

Your notes state that "connective tissue turn over in 6 weeks" for mild-to-moderate perio cases, and "Any pt with perio intervention needs to be seen every 3 months." The 6-week CT turnover is why re-evaluation is timed at 6–8 weeks post-SRP — you're waiting for the new connective tissue to mature before reassessing. The 3-month maintenance interval is the standard for periodontal patients because it maintains the bacterial shift achieved by SRP before pathogenic organisms can recolonize to disease-causing levels. Compare this to the 6-month interval for healthy patients — perio patients need double the frequency.

Why A is wrong: 3 weeks is epithelial turnover for gingivitis, not CT turnover. Why C is wrong: 12 weeks is too long for CT turnover, and 6 months is the healthy patient interval. Why D is wrong: 2 weeks is too short for CT turnover and monthly visits are excessive. Why E is wrong: 10 weeks overestimates CT turnover.

Q136 After intrabony osseous resective surgery, approximately how much bone rebound (regrowth) can be expected?
A. 0mm — no rebound occurs
B. 1mm rebound
C. 3mm rebound
D. 5mm rebound
E. Complete regeneration to pre-disease levels
Correct Answer: C

Approximately 3mm of bone rebound occurs after intrabony cutting/resective osseous surgery. This is important for treatment planning — when you perform ostectomy, expect that the bone level won't stay exactly where you left it surgically. Some regrowth/rebound will occur during healing as the body partially fills in the surgical site. This 3mm number helps calibrate your surgical endpoints — if you need a final bone level at a certain position, account for the anticipated rebound.

Why A is wrong: Some rebound absolutely occurs — bone is biologically active. Why B is wrong: 1mm underestimates the typical rebound. Why D is wrong: 5mm overestimates it. Why E is wrong: Complete regeneration to pre-disease levels doesn't happen with resective surgery.

Q137 The prevalence of periodontitis at 47% represents which measurement methodology, and why is this figure considered incorrect for exam purposes?
A. 47% is the correct prevalence using 6-site measurements
B. 47% was derived from 3-site partial-mouth measurements and underestimates true prevalence; the correct figure using 6-site full-mouth measurement (Eke) is approximately 56%
C. 47% represents only gingivitis prevalence, not periodontitis
D. 47% is the worldwide prevalence; the US prevalence is higher
E. 47% is correct and no other figure should be used
Correct Answer: B

This is a Fleisher-flagged exam trap. The 47% figure came from older partial-mouth (3-site) methodology that underestimated true disease prevalence. The Eke study using 6-site full-mouth measurements found the prevalence is approximately 56%. On the exam, if they give you 47% as an answer choice, it's likely WRONG — the correct answer would be "none of the above" because 56% is the accurate figure. Your study notes confirm: "47% prevalence of periodontitis (FALSE!) — All of the above was the correct answer."

Why A is wrong: 47% uses the OLD 3-site methodology, not 6-site. Why C is wrong: 47% was a periodontitis estimate, just an inaccurate one. Why D is wrong: This isn't a US vs. worldwide distinction. Why E is wrong: 47% is explicitly marked FALSE in your materials.

Q138 Regarding chronic periodontitis and age, which statement is MOST accurate?
A. Older age directly causes chronic periodontitis by weakening the immune system
B. Chronic periodontitis is age-dependent because of accumulation of cases over time, but age itself does NOT make a patient high-risk
C. Chronic periodontitis only occurs in patients over 65
D. Age has no relationship whatsoever to chronic periodontitis prevalence
E. Chronic periodontitis prevalence decreases with age
Correct Answer: B

Chronic periodontitis appears "age-dependent" but it's really about CUMULATIVE disease burden — the longer you live, the more time there is for disease to develop and accumulate. Age itself is NOT an independent risk factor that makes you inherently more susceptible. An 80-year-old with pristine oral hygiene and no other risk factors isn't automatically at higher risk than a 40-year-old smoker with poor hygiene. This distinction matters for risk assessment: don't assume older = sicker.

Why A is wrong: Age doesn't directly cause perio — it's correlation, not causation. Why C is wrong: Chronic periodontitis occurs at any age. Why D is wrong: Age IS correlated with prevalence due to accumulation — just not causative. Why E is wrong: Prevalence increases with age, it doesn't decrease.

Q139 "Chronic apical periodontitis" is a term that refers to:
A. A combined endo-perio lesion requiring both endodontic and periodontal treatment
B. An endodontic term indicating a primary endo lesion only — it does NOT involve periodontal disease
C. Advanced periodontitis with furcation involvement
D. Aggressive periodontitis in an older patient
E. A periodontal abscess at the apex of a tooth
Correct Answer: B
