"Chronic apical periodontitis" is purely an ENDODONTIC term — it refers to a periapical lesion caused by pulp necrosis/infection, NOT periodontal disease. Don't be tricked by the word "periodontitis" in the name. A tooth with a sinus tract and "chronic apical periodontitis" is a primary endo lesion only. Treatment is RCT, not periodontal therapy. This came up in your study materials with the specific note: "chronic apical periodontitis is a simple endo term, nothing to do with perio."

Why A is wrong: It's not a combined lesion — it's purely endo. Why C is wrong: It has nothing to do with furcation involvement. Why D is wrong: "Chronic apical periodontitis" isn't related to aggressive periodontitis. Why E is wrong: A periodontal abscess originates from the periodontium, not the pulp.

Q140 During the proliferative phase of surgical wound healing, epithelial cells can migrate at approximately what rate?
A. 0.1mm per day
B. 0.5mm per day
C. 1.0mm per day
D. 2.0mm per day
E. 5.0mm per day
Correct Answer: B

Epithelial cells migrate at a rate of 0.5mm per day during the proliferative phase of wound healing. This is exactly why epithelial cells "win the race" to the root surface in GTR scenarios — they move fast. The three phases of surgical wound healing are: (1) Inflammatory phase, (2) Proliferative phase, and (3) Maturation phase. The 0.5mm/day migration rate is why GTR membranes are necessary — without a physical barrier, epithelial cells will cover the root surface before slower-moving PDL cells can regenerate attachment.

Why A is wrong: 0.1mm/day is too slow — epithelium is the fastest-migrating tissue. Why C is wrong: 1.0mm/day overestimates the rate. Why D is wrong: 2.0mm/day is too fast. Why E is wrong: 5.0mm/day is physiologically impossible.

Q143 Which condition is NOT related to non-plaque-induced periodontal diseases (per the 1999 Armitage classification)?
A. Pemphigoid
B. Lichen planus
C. Linear gingival erythema
D. Herpetic gingivostomatitis
E. Allergic reactions
Correct Answer: C

Linear gingival erythema was listed in the 1999 classification but has been REMOVED as a term in the 2018 updated classification. Your midterm slides confirm under "Key Changes": "Linear gingival erythema as a term is removed." Linear gingival erythema was originally described as an HIV-associated gingival condition, but the 2018 workshop eliminated it as a distinct entity. This is an important classification update to know for the exam.

Why A is wrong: Pemphigoid IS a non-plaque-induced gingival disease (mucocutaneous disorder). Why B is wrong: Lichen planus IS a recognized non-plaque-induced condition. Why D is wrong: Herpetic gingivostomatitis IS a viral non-plaque-induced condition. Why E is wrong: Allergic reactions ARE recognized non-plaque-induced conditions.

Q144 Regarding electric vs. manual toothbrushes, which statement is CORRECT?
A. Electric toothbrushes have greater efficacy than manual toothbrushes
B. Electric and manual toothbrushes have the SAME efficacy, but electric reaches that efficacy faster, making it more effective overall
C. Manual toothbrushes are superior to electric in all studies
D. Electric toothbrushes are only beneficial for patients with disabilities
E. There is no difference in effectiveness or efficacy between the two
Correct Answer: B

The distinction between efficacy and effectiveness matters here. Efficacy = the result under ideal conditions (both achieve the same endpoint of plaque removal). Effectiveness = the result in real-world conditions (electric gets there faster and more consistently). Your notes state: "Electric toothbrush INCREASES effectiveness better than manual (same efficacy, but electric reaches efficacy faster thus better effectiveness)." In practice, most patients don't brush perfectly with a manual brush — the electric brush compensates for imperfect technique.

Why A is wrong: The EFFICACY is the same — the EFFECTIVENESS differs. Why C is wrong: Manual is not superior. Why D is wrong: Electric benefits all patients, not just those with disabilities. Why E is wrong: There IS a difference in effectiveness (though not efficacy).

Q145 Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease can present with which of the following conditions?
A. Dental caries
B. Leukemia
C. Temporomandibular joint disorder
D. Bruxism
E. Dental fluorosis
Correct Answer: B

Leukemia is a systemic condition that can manifest with periodontal destruction — it falls under "Periodontitis as a Manifestation of Systemic Disease" in the classification system. Leukemic cells infiltrate the gingival tissues causing enlargement, and the compromised immune system (neutropenia) leads to rapid periodontal breakdown. Your notes reference the 1999 article classification system where systemic periodontitis types include hematologic disorders like leukemia. Other systemic conditions in this category include neutropenia, Down syndrome, Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome, and others.

Why A is wrong: Caries is a separate disease process, not a systemic manifestation of periodontitis. Why C is wrong: TMJ disorders are musculoskeletal, not periodontal. Why D is wrong: Bruxism relates to occlusal trauma, not systemic periodontitis. Why E is wrong: Fluorosis affects enamel development, not the periodontium.

Q149 A tooth has 4mm probing, bleeding on probing, and mobility of 1+. What diagnosis can you be CERTAIN of?
A. Both gingivitis and periodontitis
B. Periodontitis with a hopeless prognosis
C. Gingivitis only
D. Primary occlusal trauma
E. Combined endo-perio lesion
Correct Answer: C

You can only be certain of gingivitis. Here's the key reasoning: 4mm probing with BOP confirms inflammation (gingivitis). But 4mm probing depth could be a pseudopocket from gingival swelling — you DON'T know for certain that there's true attachment loss unless you measure CAL from the CEJ. And mobility of 1+ can be caused by inflammation alone (widened PDL from inflammatory edema) or occlusal trauma — it doesn't prove bone loss. Without confirmed CAL loss (radiographic bone loss or CAL measurement), you CANNOT diagnose periodontitis. You CAN diagnose gingivitis because BOP is present.

Why A is wrong: You can't confirm periodontitis without evidence of attachment loss. Why B is wrong: Hopeless prognosis requires far more severe findings. Why D is wrong: Primary occlusal trauma requires evidence of excessive force on a normal periodontium. Why E is wrong: No evidence of endodontic involvement is described.

Q152 What are the three components of the attachment apparatus?
A. Enamel, dentin, and pulp
B. Gingiva, alveolar mucosa, and oral mucosa
C. Cementum, alveolar crest (bone), and periodontal ligament (PDL)
D. Junctional epithelium, sulcular epithelium, and oral epithelium
E. Free gingiva, attached gingiva, and interdental papilla
Correct Answer: C

The attachment apparatus consists of three components: (1) cementum, (2) alveolar crest/bone, and (3) periodontal ligament (PDL). These are the three structures that actually ATTACH the tooth to the jawbone. Cementum covers the root and provides the anchorage point for PDL fibers. The PDL connects cementum to alveolar bone via Sharpey's fibers. The alveolar bone is the socket wall. When periodontitis destroys these structures, that's true attachment loss — and it's irreversible without regeneration.

Why A is wrong: These are tooth structures, not attachment apparatus. Why B is wrong: These are soft tissue categories, not the attachment apparatus. Why D is wrong: These are epithelial structures that line the gingiva but don't form the attachment. Why E is wrong: These are gingival landmarks, not the attachment apparatus.

Q153 What is the ideal distance from the most apical cell of the junctional epithelium to the alveolar bone crest?
A. 0.5mm
B. 1mm
C. 2mm
D. 3mm
E. 4mm
Correct Answer: B

The ideal distance from the most apical epithelial cell to the alveolar crest is 1mm. This is part of the biologic width concept (Gargiulo): the junctional epithelium measures about 0.97mm and the connective tissue attachment about 1.07mm, totaling approximately 2mm of biologic width. The 1mm distance from the base of the JE to the bone crest represents the connective tissue attachment zone — this is the "no man's land" that must be respected when placing restorative margins or performing crown lengthening.

Why A is wrong: 0.5mm is too close — would suggest bone is encroaching on the JE. Why C is wrong: 2mm is the total biologic width, not just the CT attachment component. Why D is wrong: 3mm would suggest excessive distance/bone loss. Why E is wrong: 4mm would indicate significant attachment loss.

Q154 Placing an implant adjacent to an active periodontal lesion or abscess is:
A. Acceptable if the implant is placed at least 2mm away
B. Acceptable with concurrent antibiotic therapy
C. NOT acceptable — the infection must be resolved before implant placement
D. Acceptable if the implant is immediately loaded
E. Only acceptable in the posterior region
Correct Answer: C

Implant placement next to an active perio lesion or abscess is NOT acceptable. Your notes state this directly. The rationale is that the active infection will contaminate the implant surface during and after placement, leading to peri-implant infection and likely implant failure. You must first resolve the periodontal infection (through SRP, abscess drainage, possible extraction of the hopeless tooth, and confirmation of healing) before placing an implant in or adjacent to that site. The site needs to be infection-free with healthy tissue.

Why A is wrong: Distance doesn't matter — the infection can spread. Why B is wrong: Antibiotics alone can't overcome local bacterial contamination of the implant surface. Why D is wrong: Immediate loading in an infected site is contraindicated. Why E is wrong: Location doesn't change the principle.

Q157 "Scaling" differs from "root planing" in that:
A. Scaling only removes plaque; root planing removes calculus
B. Scaling removes calculus and plaque from both the CROWN and ROOT surfaces; root planing specifically smooths the root surface to remove endotoxin-contaminated cementum
C. Scaling is performed only supragingivally; root planing is performed only subgingivally
D. There is no difference — the terms are interchangeable
E. Scaling requires anesthesia; root planing does not
Correct Answer: B

Your notes clarify: "Scaling is a term for removing calculus, plaques, on both CROWN and ROOT." Scaling is the broader term for mechanical deposit removal from any tooth surface — supragingival or subgingival, crown or root. Root planing is the additional step of specifically smoothing the root surface to a "glassy" finish, removing endotoxin-contaminated cementum and creating a biocompatible surface for tissue healing. Both require anesthesia in the subgingival environment.

Why A is wrong: Scaling removes BOTH plaque and calculus. Why C is wrong: Scaling can be performed both supra- and subgingivally. Why D is wrong: They are related but distinct procedures. Why E is wrong: Both require anesthesia when performed subgingivally.

Q159 Gingivectomy is indicated for which type of bony defect?
A. Infrabony (vertical) defects
B. Suprabony defects only
C. Three-wall intrabony defects
D. Through-and-through furcation defects
E. Any defect regardless of morphology
Correct Answer: B

Gingivectomy is indicated ONLY for suprabony defects. Your notes state: "Gingivectomy is done when SUPRABONY defect." The reason is that gingivectomy removes gingival tissue from the outside — it doesn't provide access to bone. If you have an infrabony defect, gingivectomy would just remove tissue without addressing the underlying bony crater, and you'd never see or treat the defect. Infrabony defects require flap surgery for access. This was also covered in your midterm slides: "Both Gingival Curettage and Gingivectomy are utilized with suprabony defects only."

Why A is wrong: Infrabony defects need flap access, not gingivectomy. Why C is wrong: Three-wall intrabony defects need regenerative surgery. Why D is wrong: Through-and-through furcations can't be treated with gingivectomy. Why E is wrong: Defect morphology absolutely matters.

Q160 Contraindications for gingivectomy include:
A. Gingival enlargement and shallow pockets
B. Infrabony defects and narrow zone of keratinized gingiva
C. Suprabony pockets with adequate keratinized tissue
D. Drug-induced gingival overgrowth
E. Generalized pseudopocketing from inflammation
Correct Answer: B

Your notes list gingivectomy contraindications as: infrabony defects and narrow zone of gingiva. Infrabony defects need flap surgery for bone access (as discussed above). Narrow keratinized gingiva is a contraindication because gingivectomy REMOVES tissue — if you don't have much to start with, removing it would leave inadequate keratinized tissue for gingival health (remember: minimum 2mm KT needed, per Lang & Löe). Your notes also specify: "gingival enlargement was NOT the answer" for contraindication — because gingival enlargement is actually an INDICATION for gingivectomy.

Why A is wrong: Gingival enlargement is an INDICATION, not a contraindication. Why C is wrong: Suprabony pockets with adequate KT is actually the ideal INDICATION. Why D is wrong: Drug-induced overgrowth is a classic indication FOR gingivectomy. Why E is wrong: Pseudopocketing from inflammation can be treated with gingivectomy.

Q161 A non-vital tooth #30 has a Grade 2 furcation involvement on the buccal. What is the FIRST treatment that must be performed?
A. Extract the tooth immediately
B. Perform periodontal flap surgery to debride the furcation
C. Perform root canal therapy (RCT) first to close all accessory canals in the furcation
D. Place a bone graft in the furcation
E. Hemisect the tooth immediately
Correct Answer: C

RCT first. Your notes state: "Tooth #30 having a furcation on buccal (grade 2 mobility), and it is non-vital. Tx must be: do RCT first to close all accessory canals in the furca." The endodontic infection is contributing to the furcation breakdown through accessory canals that communicate between the pulp chamber and the furcation floor. By performing RCT and sealing these accessory canals, you eliminate the endodontic contribution to the furcation defect. Only after endo is completed should you address the perio component surgically.

Why A is wrong: The tooth may be savable with combined endo-perio treatment. Why B is wrong: Perio surgery before endo means ongoing infection will undermine healing. Why D is wrong: Grafting before resolving the endo infection would fail. Why E is wrong: Hemisection might ultimately be needed but not before RCT.

Q162 The "unattached gingiva" or "free gingiva" encompasses which structures?
A. Only the interdental papilla
B. The papilla, free gingival groove, free gingival margin, and oral sulcular epithelium
C. Only the attached gingiva and alveolar mucosa
D. Only the junctional epithelium
E. The mucogingival junction and vestibular mucosa
Correct Answer: B

The unattached (free) gingiva includes: the papilla, the free gingival groove, the free gingival margin, and the oral sulcular epithelium. Your notes confirm: "'Unattached gingiva' involves: papilla, free gingival groove, free gingival margin, oral sulcular epithelium — Free gingiva was the answer." The free gingiva is the portion that isn't attached to the underlying tooth or bone — it forms the soft tissue wall of the gingival sulcus and can be deflected from the tooth with a probe or air.

Why A is wrong: The papilla is only one component. Why C is wrong: Attached gingiva is a separate zone, and alveolar mucosa is beyond the MGJ. Why D is wrong: JE is at the base of the sulcus — part of the attachment, not the free gingiva. Why E is wrong: The MGJ and vestibular mucosa are separate structures.

Q163 Localized aggressive periodontitis is defined as attachment loss affecting what percentage of sites?
A. 10% or fewer sites
B. 30% or fewer sites
C. 50% or fewer sites
D. More than 30% of sites
E. Any number of sites with rapid progression
Correct Answer: B

Localized aggressive periodontitis involves attachment loss at 30% or fewer sites. If it exceeds 30%, it's classified as generalized aggressive periodontitis. This parallels the localized/generalized cutoff used for gingivitis and chronic periodontitis — 30% is the universal dividing line in the classification system. Classic localized aggressive perio typically presents with attachment loss at first molars and incisors in young patients, often with relatively little plaque for the amount of destruction.

Why A is wrong: 10% is too restrictive — that's the threshold for gingivitis diagnosis, not localized aggressive perio. Why C is wrong: 50% is too high for localized. Why D is wrong: >30% would be GENERALIZED aggressive periodontitis. Why E is wrong: The definition includes a specific site percentage threshold.

Q166 An interdental crater-type bony defect involves how many bony walls?
A. 1 wall
B. 2 walls (buccal and lingual)
C. 3 walls
D. 4 walls
E. No bony walls
Correct Answer: B

An interdental crater involves 2 bony walls — the buccal and lingual cortical plates. The crater is the "scooped out" defect in the interdental septum between two teeth, with the mesial and distal walls being the tooth root surfaces (not bone). This 2-wall morphology gives moderate regenerative potential — better than a 1-wall defect but worse than a 3-wall defect. Your midterm slides confirm this when discussing osseous defect morphology.

Why A is wrong: 1-wall defects are a different morphology (hemiseptal defects). Why C is wrong: 3-wall defects are the most contained — different morphology. Why D is wrong: 4-wall defects would require an encircling bony wall (not typical of craters). Why E is wrong: Craters DO have bony walls — specifically the buccal and lingual plates.

Q167 "Reverse architecture" in osseous defects refers to:
A. Interproximal bone levels that are more coronal than buccal/lingual bone levels
B. Interproximal bone levels that are more APICAL than buccal and lingual bone levels
C. Equal bone levels on all surfaces
D. Complete absence of interproximal bone
E. Vertical bone loss only on the buccal surface
Correct Answer: B

Reverse architecture means the interproximal bone is more APICAL than the buccal and lingual bone — the opposite of normal healthy architecture where interproximal bone is the most coronal. In health, interproximal bone peaks between teeth (positive architecture). In reverse architecture, the interproximal bone has been lost while the buccal/lingual plates remain relatively intact, creating a "reversed" contour. This is a key indication for resective osseous surgery — you need to re-establish positive architecture by removing buccal/lingual bone to bring it level with the interproximal bone.

Why A is wrong: That would be NORMAL (positive) architecture. Why C is wrong: Equal levels are flat architecture, not reverse. Why D is wrong: Complete absence of interproximal bone is a more severe finding. Why E is wrong: This describes a localized defect, not reverse architecture.

Q168 According to Reiser et al. (1996), what is the distance from the CEJ to the greater palatine artery/nerve for a shallow palatal vault, average palatal vault, and high palatal vault?
A. Shallow = 5mm; Average = 8mm; High = 12mm
B. Shallow = 7mm; Average = 12mm; High = 17mm
C. Shallow = 10mm; Average = 15mm; High = 20mm
D. Shallow = 3mm; Average = 7mm; High = 10mm
E. The distance is the same (12mm) regardless of vault depth
Correct Answer: B

The 7-12-17 rule from Reiser et al. 1996 (directly on your slides under CTG donor site anatomy): Shallow palate = 7mm from CEJ to the greater palatine artery/nerve. Average palate = 12mm. High palate = 17mm. This is CRITICAL safety anatomy for palatal graft harvesting — if you go too deep, you'll cut the greater palatine artery and cause significant hemorrhage. A shallow palate gives you only 7mm of safe tissue depth, while a high vaulted palate gives you a luxurious 17mm. Always assess palatal vault depth before harvesting.

Why A is wrong: These underestimate the distances. Why C is wrong: These overestimate them. Why D is wrong: 3mm for shallow palate would be dangerously close. Why E is wrong: Vault depth absolutely changes the artery distance.

Q169 Regarding the types of floss, which statement is CORRECT?
A. Waxed floss is significantly more effective than unwaxed floss
B. Unwaxed floss is significantly more effective than waxed floss
C. Unwaxed floss has the SAME efficacy as waxed floss
D. Only waxed floss should be used in patients with tight contacts
E. Only unwaxed floss should be recommended by dental professionals
Correct Answer: C

Your notes state: "Unwaxed floss is the SAME efficacy as waxed floss." There is no clinically significant difference in plaque removal between waxed and unwaxed floss. The choice between them is based on patient preference and ease of use — waxed floss slides more easily through tight contacts, while unwaxed floss may provide slightly more tactile feedback. The most important thing is that the patient USES floss, not what type they use.

Why A is wrong: Waxed is NOT superior to unwaxed. Why B is wrong: Unwaxed is NOT superior to waxed. Why D is wrong: Both types can be used in tight contacts, though waxed slides easier. Why E is wrong: Both are appropriate recommendations.

Q170 What is the proper angulation of a curette blade to the root surface during scaling and root planing?
A. 0–20 degrees
B. 60–85 degrees (Gracey curette working angulation per lecture slides)
C. 90 degrees (perpendicular)
D. 10–30 degrees
E. 80–90 degrees
Correct Answer: B

Per your lecture slides, the angle formed between the instrument face and the tooth surface should be between 60°–85° for the Gracey Curette. This is the working angulation that allows the cutting edge to engage calculus and root surface effectively — too shallow and you'll burnish calculus rather than remove it, too steep and you'll gouge the root. The original study guide listed 40–60 degrees, but your slides explicitly state 60–85 degrees. The Gracey curette's built-in offset angle means you need to position the handle correctly to achieve this range.

Why A is wrong: 0–20 degrees is too flat — the blade won't engage. Why C is wrong: 90 degrees would dig the blade directly into the root, causing excessive cementum removal. Why D is wrong: 10–30 degrees is still too shallow for effective calculus removal. Why E is wrong: 80–90 degrees is too steep and would gouge the root.

Q171 To detect a vertical root fracture, you should:
A. Take a periapical radiograph from multiple angles only
B. "Walk the probe" around the entire circumference of the root in the sulcus
C. Apply percussion and cold testing only
D. Use transillumination only
E. Root fractures cannot be detected clinically
Correct Answer: B

"Walk the probe" — your notes confirm: "you must 'WALK THE PROBE' to detect any vertical root fractures — TRUE." When you walk the probe around the tooth, a vertical root fracture produces a characteristic narrow, deep, isolated probing defect that follows the fracture line. The probe will suddenly drop deep at one point and return to normal depths as you move away from the fracture. This is different from generalized periodontitis (where probing depths are elevated around the entire circumference). Radiographs help but may miss fractures unless the beam is parallel to the fracture line.

Why A is wrong: Radiographs are helpful but not sufficient alone — many fractures are missed radiographically. Why C is wrong: Percussion and thermal testing assess pulp vitality, not fracture detection. Why D is wrong: Transillumination works for crown fractures but not root fractures below the gingival margin. Why E is wrong: Walking the probe IS a clinical detection method.

Q172 When the junctional epithelium undergoes apical migration, it changes its attachment mechanism to:
A. Collagen fiber insertion (Sharpey's fibers)
B. Hemidesmosomes
C. Tight junctions
D. Gap junctions
E. Desmosomes only
Correct Answer: B

When the JE migrates apically, it attaches to the root surface via hemidesmosomes. Hemidesmosomes are the specialized adhesion structures that connect epithelial cells to non-epithelial surfaces (like the root surface via the internal basal lamina). This is fundamentally different from the connective tissue attachment of the PDL (which uses Sharpey's fibers inserted into cementum). The hemidesmosomal attachment of migrated JE represents REPAIR (long junctional epithelium), not regeneration — it's a weaker, less resistant attachment than the original CT/cementum/PDL complex.

Why A is wrong: Sharpey's fibers are the PDL's connective tissue attachment mechanism, not the JE's. Why C is wrong: Tight junctions seal adjacent cells together but don't attach cells to root surfaces. Why D is wrong: Gap junctions allow cell-to-cell communication, not surface attachment. Why E is wrong: Desmosomes attach epithelial cells to EACH OTHER, not to the root surface.

Q176 What is the best method to reduce pocket depth in a short duration (most efficiently)?
A. Scaling and root planing alone
B. Modified Widman flap
C. Guided tissue regeneration
D. Bone grafting
E. Laser therapy alone
Correct Answer: B

The modified Widman flap is the best method to reduce pocket depth in a short duration. It provides excellent access for debridement, allows precise flap adaptation to the root surface (reducing pocket depth by repositioning the soft tissue), and heals efficiently. It's designed primarily for debridement and pocket depth reduction rather than regeneration or resection. The modified Widman flap reduces probing depth effectively while also decreasing clinical attachment loss compared to more aggressive surgical approaches.

Why A is wrong: SRP alone may not adequately reduce deeper pockets. Why C is wrong: GTR aims for regeneration, which takes longer — not the fastest pocket depth reduction. Why D is wrong: Bone grafting targets defect fill, not rapid pocket depth reduction. Why E is wrong: Laser therapy alone may not address underlying defect morphology.

Q177 What effect does SRP have on a 2.5mm probing depth site?
A. Increases probing depth
B. Decreases probing depth and increases clinical attachment level
C. No change in probing depth; decreases clinical attachment level
D. Decreases probing depth but also decreases clinical attachment level (slight attachment loss)
E. Increases both probing depth and clinical attachment level
Correct Answer: D

At shallow probing depths (2.5mm), SRP can actually cause a slight DECREASE in clinical attachment. Your notes confirm: "2.5mm of SRP will decrease clinical attachment." This happens because at shallow depths, the instrumentation removes more cementum and connective tissue attachment than the inflammation was causing pocket depth. The probe was penetrating inflamed tissue before SRP; after SRP and healing, the tissue shrinks and attachment recedes slightly. This is why aggressive SRP at shallow sites (≤3mm) can be HARMFUL — you lose more attachment than you gain.

Why A is wrong: SRP reduces inflammation and probing depth. Why B is wrong: At 2.5mm sites, attachment can actually be LOST, not gained. Why C is wrong: Probing depth does change. Why E is wrong: Neither probing depth nor attachment increases at this shallow depth.

Q180 A patient's junctional epithelium is located 2mm CORONAL to the CEJ (gingival overgrowth), the probing depth is 4mm, and the distance from the free gingival margin to the mucogingival junction is 7mm. What is the clinical attachment loss?
A. 0mm (no attachment loss)
B. 2mm
C. 4mm
D. 6mm
E. 7mm
Correct Answer: B

When the JE is 2mm CORONAL to the CEJ, there's gingival overgrowth (pseudopocket) of 2mm. CAL = probing depth minus overgrowth = 4mm – 2mm = 2mm. Alternatively, think of it as: the probe goes 4mm from the gingival margin, but the first 2mm is through overgrown tissue above the CEJ (not real attachment loss). Only the remaining 2mm below the CEJ represents true attachment loss. The 7mm MGJ distance is a distractor — it doesn't factor into CAL calculation.

Why A is wrong: There IS some attachment loss — the probe goes 2mm past the CEJ. Why C is wrong: 4mm is the probing depth, not the CAL — you must subtract the overgrowth. Why D is wrong: 6mm isn't derivable from these numbers. Why E is wrong: 7mm is the FGM-to-MGJ distance, not CAL.

Q184 What is the maximum duration of Arestin (minocycline microspheres) release in the periodontal pocket?
A. 7 days
B. 14 days
C. 21 days
D. 30 days
E. 60 days
Correct Answer: B

Maximum duration of Arestin is 14 days. After placement in the periodontal pocket following SRP, the microspheres gradually dissolve and release minocycline over approximately 2 weeks. This sustained local delivery achieves antibiotic concentrations in the pocket far higher than systemic administration could achieve, while minimizing systemic side effects. After 14 days, the microspheres are fully resorbed and the antibiotic effect has concluded.

Why A is wrong: 7 days is too short — the microspheres last longer. Why C is wrong: 21 days exceeds the documented duration. Why D is wrong: 30 days is too long. Why E is wrong: 60 days far exceeds Arestin's delivery profile.

Q186 What is the external bevel incision angle used in gingivectomy?
A. 30 degrees
B. 45 degrees
C. 60 degrees
D. 90 degrees
E. 15 degrees
Correct Answer: B

The external bevel incision for gingivectomy is made at a 45-degree angle to the tooth surface. This angulation creates a thin, tapered tissue edge that allows the tissue to adapt smoothly to the tooth surface during healing. Your midterm slides on gingivectomy confirm this angulation. The blade is directed from the outer gingival surface inward at 45 degrees, creating a beveled cut that removes the pocket wall while producing an appropriate wound margin for secondary intention healing.

Why A is wrong: 30 degrees is too shallow. Why C is wrong: 60 degrees is too steep for the external bevel. Why D is wrong: 90 degrees would create a blunt, non-beveled wound edge. Why E is wrong: 15 degrees would create an excessively thin bevel.

Q187 What is gingivoplasty?
A. Removal of gingival tissue to reduce pocket depth
B. Reshaping of the gingiva without reducing the coronal-apical dimension
C. Surgical repositioning of the gingiva apically
D. Bone recontouring underneath the gingiva
E. Placement of a soft tissue graft to increase gingival volume
Correct Answer: B

Gingivoplasty is reshaping of the gingiva WITHOUT reducing the coronal-apical dimension. It's a cosmetic recontouring procedure — you're sculpting the tissue to create more physiologic architecture (proper scalloping, knife-edged margins) without actually removing tissue height. This is different from gingivectomy, which DOES remove tissue and reduce the coronal-apical dimension. Gingivoplasty is often performed as an adjunct to gingivectomy to create natural-looking gingival contours after the bulk tissue removal.

Why A is wrong: That's gingivectomy, not gingivoplasty. Why C is wrong: That's an apically positioned flap. Why D is wrong: That's ostectomy/osteoplasty. Why E is wrong: That's a soft tissue graft procedure.

Q188 What is "bone sounding"?
A. Tapping on teeth to assess percussion sensitivity
B. Passing a probe through anesthetized gingival tissue to the bone crest to determine the level of alveolar bone
C. Listening for changes in bone density with a stethoscope
D. Using radiographs to estimate bone levels
E. Vibrating the mandible to assess fracture
Correct Answer: B

Bone sounding involves passing a periodontal probe through anesthetized gingival tissue directly down to the alveolar bone crest. This gives you the most accurate clinical measurement of the bone level — more accurate than radiographs, which are 2D and subject to superimposition. Bone sounding is performed under local anesthesia (you're literally poking through soft tissue to bone) and is especially useful for treatment planning crown lengthening, implant placement, and assessing osseous defect morphology. It's the only way to know the true 3D bone topography without raising a flap.

Why A is wrong: That's percussion testing. Why C is wrong: Stethoscopes aren't used for bone density assessment in dentistry. Why D is wrong: Radiographs are 2D estimates, not "bone sounding." Why E is wrong: Mandibular fracture assessment is a different procedure entirely.

Q191 In periodontal wound healing, what is the FIRST cell type to arrive at the wound site?
A. Fibroblasts
B. Osteoblasts
C. Neutrophils
D. Macrophages
E. Epithelial cells
Correct Answer: C

Neutrophils are the first cells to arrive at the wound — your notes state: "1st cell to the wound healing = Neutrophils." Neutrophils are part of the acute inflammatory response and arrive within hours of tissue injury. They phagocytize bacteria and debris, release proteolytic enzymes, and initiate the inflammatory cascade. After neutrophils, macrophages arrive (which are the "cleanup crew"), then fibroblasts begin laying down new connective tissue, and eventually epithelial cells migrate to cover the wound surface.

Why A is wrong: Fibroblasts arrive later during the proliferative phase. Why B is wrong: Osteoblasts are involved in bone remodeling much later. Why D is wrong: Macrophages arrive after neutrophils (during the clearance phase). Why E is wrong: Epithelial cells migrate during the proliferative phase, days after the initial wound.

Q192 Regarding periodontitis and diabetes, which statement is CORRECT?
A. Diabetes has no relationship to periodontal disease
B. Periodontitis may be the first clinical presentation of undiagnosed diabetes
C. Diabetes only affects periodontal disease in patients over 65
D. Periodontal treatment has no effect on diabetic control
E. Only Type 1 diabetes affects the periodontium
Correct Answer: B

Your notes state: "Periodontitis may be the first presentation of diabetes." This is clinically important — if you see a young patient with aggressive, unexplained periodontal breakdown, undiagnosed diabetes should be on your differential. Diabetes impairs neutrophil function, collagen metabolism, and wound healing, creating an environment conducive to periodontal destruction. The relationship is bidirectional: diabetes worsens perio, and severe perio worsens glycemic control. Treating periodontitis can actually improve HbA1c levels in diabetic patients.

Why A is wrong: Diabetes is a major risk factor for periodontitis — the relationship is well-established. Why C is wrong: Diabetes affects the periodontium at any age. Why D is wrong: Periodontal treatment CAN improve glycemic control. Why E is wrong: Both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes affect the periodontium.

Q218 According to Tomar (2000), which of the following statements about smoking and periodontal disease is CORRECT?
A. Current smokers have a 2x greater risk; former smokers have no increased risk
B. Current smokers have a 4x greater risk; former smokers have a 2x greater risk; 53% of periodontitis is attributable to smoking; risk returns to non-smoker levels after ≥11 years of cessation
C. Smoking only affects gingival inflammation, not attachment loss
D. Smoking is a risk factor only in patients over age 60
E. There is no dose-response relationship between smoking and periodontitis
Correct Answer: B

Directly from your slides (Tomar, J Perio May 2000): current smokers = 4x greater risk, former smokers = 2x greater risk, and 53% of periodontitis is attributable to smoking (42% current, 11% former). There's a clear dose-response: ≤9 cigarettes/day = 3x risk, ≥31/day = 6x risk. Former smoker risk reduction: 0–2 years quit = still 3x risk, but ≥11 years quit = same risk as a non-smoker. Smoking is also a Grade modifier in the 2018 classification — it shifts a patient from Grade B to Grade C (≥10 cigarettes/day). In the PRA hexagon (Periodontal Risk Assessment), smoking is one of the 6 parameters along with %BOP, residual pockets >4mm, missing teeth, bone loss/age, and systemic conditions.

Why A is wrong: 2x is the former smoker risk, not current. Why C is wrong: Smoking directly increases attachment and bone loss. Why D is wrong: Age-independent. Why E is wrong: Strong dose-response exists.

Q219 In the 2018 classification system, when staging periodontitis, which parameter is used FIRST to establish the stage, and what is the backup if it's unavailable?
A. Radiographic bone loss (RBL) first; probing depth as backup
B. Clinical attachment loss (CAL) first; radiographic bone loss (RBL) as backup; tooth loss due to periodontitis may shift the stage higher
C. Bleeding on probing first; mobility as backup
D. Probing depth first; patient age as backup
E. Gingival index first; plaque index as backup
Correct Answer: B

Directly from your slides: "Initial staging should be determined using clinical attachment loss (CAL). If CAL is not available, use radiographic bone loss (RBL). Tooth loss due to periodontitis may shift the stage to a higher level (3 → 4)." Staging classifies severity and extent based on measurable destroyed/damaged tissue AND factors attributing to complexity of long-term management. Grading (Step 3) then assesses progression rate — Grade A (slow, <0.25 bone loss/age), Grade B (moderate, 0.25–1.0), Grade C (rapid, >1.0). Direct evidence for grading = radiographic bone loss over 5 years. Always assume Grade B first, then look for evidence to shift to A or C. Grade modifiers: smoking (≥10 cigs/day → Grade C) and diabetes (HbA1c ≥7.0% → Grade C).

Why A is wrong: CAL is first, not RBL. Why C is wrong: BOP isn't used for staging. Why D is wrong: PD and age aren't the staging parameters. Why E is wrong: GI and PI aren't part of the staging system.

Q220 Using the McGuire (1991) prognosis classification, a tooth with >50% attachment loss, Grade II+ furcation involvement, and Class II mobility would receive which prognosis?
A. Good
B. Fair
C. Poor
D. Questionable
E. Hopeless
Correct Answer: D

Per McGuire (1991) and McGuire & Nunn (1996) from your slides: Good = etiologic factors controllable, adequate support, adequate maintenance. Fair = up to 25% attachment loss, Grade I furcation. Poor = up to 50% attachment loss, Class I+ mobility, poor crown/root ratio. Questionable = >50% attachment loss, Grade II+ furcation, Class II+ mobility, endo-involved with poor root form. Hopeless = inadequate attachment, Grade III/IV furcation, Class III mobility. The Kwok & Caton (2007) system on your slides simplifies to: Favorable → Unfavorable → Questionable → Hopeless, based on whether local/systemic factors CAN vs. CANNOT be controlled. Prognostic factors at tooth level include: mobility, remaining attachment, PD, bone loss type, furcation, crown-root ratio, endo status, caries, remaining tooth structure.

Why A/B are wrong: >50% attachment loss exceeds Good/Fair thresholds. Why C is wrong: Poor maxes at 50% attachment loss. Why E is wrong: Hopeless requires Class III mobility or Grade III/IV furcation — this case hasn't crossed that threshold yet.

Q221 The 2025 bridge longevity study presented by Dr. Fleisher found what survival rate for cross-arch bridges in Stage III/IV periodontitis patients?
A. 50% success at 10 years
B. 65% success at 15 years
C. 76% success at approximately 20.4 years
D. 90% success at 25 years
E. 45% success at 5 years
Correct Answer: C

Directly from your slides: 94 participants, 111 bridges, average observation period 17.9 years (surviving bridges averaged 20.4 years, range 13–30 years). Of 111 bridges: 25 dropped out, 18 deceased, 16 failed, 52 still intact = 76% success. The fundamental concept: "Long span bridges constructed for patients with severe periodontal disease can last for many years and help stabilize the periodontal condition." This is a Fleisher-emphasized article. The takeaway: don't assume Stage III/IV patients can't have successful fixed prosthodontics — with proper perio management, cross-arch bridges can serve for decades.

Why all others are wrong: The specific numbers are 76% at ~20.4 years — no other combination matches the study data.

Q222 In the Cairo et al. (2011) recession classification that REPLACES the Miller Classification in the 2018 update, what defines RT1, RT2, and RT3?
A. RT1 = recession not reaching MGJ; RT2 = recession at/beyond MGJ; RT3 = recession with bone loss
B. RT1 = recession WITHOUT interproximal attachment loss (interproximal CEJ not clinically detectable); RT2 = recession WITH interproximal attachment loss where interproximal CAL ≤ facial CAL; RT3 = recession WITH interproximal attachment loss where interproximal CAL > facial CAL
C. RT1 = <2mm recession; RT2 = 2–4mm recession; RT3 = >4mm recession
D. RT1 = buccal recession only; RT2 = lingual recession only; RT3 = circumferential recession
E. RT1–3 are identical to Miller I–III
Correct Answer: B

Directly from your slides (Cairo et al. 2011): RT1 = gingival recession WITHOUT loss of interproximal attachment — the interproximal CEJ is clinically not detectable at both mesial and distal (meaning no interproximal bone loss). RT2 = recession WITH interproximal attachment loss, but interproximal CAL ≤ facial CAL. RT3 = recession WITH interproximal attachment loss, and interproximal CAL > facial CAL (worst prognosis for root coverage). Your 2018 Key Changes slide confirms: "The Miller Classification for recessions has been replaced with recession types 1–3." The clinical slide examples: RT1 shows an upper left canine with 3mm buccal CAL and no detectable interproximal CAL. RT2 shows 4mm buccal CAL with 3mm interproximal CAL. RT3 shows 6mm buccal CAL with 8mm interproximal CAL.

Why A is wrong: Cairo doesn't use the MGJ as a reference point like Miller does. Why C is wrong: It's not based on millimeters of recession. Why D is wrong: It's not surface-based. Why E is wrong: Cairo specifically replaces Miller — they're different systems.

Q223 Posterior bite collapse is characterized by which sequence of events?
A. Caries → extraction → implant placement → stable occlusion
B. Missing posterior tooth → super-eruption of opposing tooth → loss of contact and drifting → loss of posterior support → flaring of anterior teeth
C. Orthodontic treatment → molar intrusion → stable occlusion
D. Bruxism → enamel wear → posterior open bite
E. Posterior bite collapse is a specific disease entity requiring antibiotic treatment
Correct Answer: B

Directly from your slides: the posterior bite collapse sequence is Missing tooth → Super-erupted tooth → Loss of Contact/Drifting of Tooth → Loss of Posterior Support → Flaring of Anterior Teeth. Your slides explicitly state this is "a syndrome with many clinical findings and is NOT a disease entity." Treatment may require occlusal equilibration, orthodontics, or prosthetics (splinting) per the occlusal trauma treatment slides. This connects to secondary occlusal trauma — once posterior support is lost, the remaining teeth (especially anteriors) experience forces they weren't designed to handle, leading to pathologic migration and flaring.

Why A is wrong: This describes a treatment sequence, not the pathology. Why C is wrong: Orthodontics is a treatment, not the collapse mechanism. Why D is wrong: Bruxism causes wear but not the specific posterior collapse sequence. Why E is wrong: The slides explicitly say it is NOT a disease entity.

Q225 The Löe et al. (1965) experimental gingivitis study proved which of the following, and what did it NOT prove?
A. It proved that gingivitis progresses to periodontitis in all cases
B. It proved that plaque accumulation causes gingivitis (and that gingivitis is reversible with plaque removal), but it did NOT prove that gingivitis progresses to periodontitis
C. It proved that periodontitis is caused by occlusal trauma
D. It proved that scaling and root planing reverses bone loss
E. It proved that antibiotics prevent gingivitis
Correct Answer: B

This is a Fleisher-flagged exam trap from your memory. Löe 1965 proved that when oral hygiene is suspended, plaque accumulates and gingivitis develops — and when hygiene resumes, gingivitis resolves. That's ALL it proved: plaque → gingivitis, remove plaque → gingivitis resolves. It did NOT prove that gingivitis progresses to periodontitis. That's a separate question entirely, and the answer comes from Socransky (1984) and the episodic burst theory: only ~12% of sites lose significant attachment, progression is unpredictable, and prior history at a site doesn't predict future breakdown (random burst hypothesis). The Eke prevalence study showed 56% periodontitis prevalence with 6-site methodology — NOT 47% (3-site), which is the exam trap answer.

Why A is wrong: This is THE exam trap — Löe 1965 did NOT prove gingivitis→perio progression. Why C is wrong: Occlusal trauma wasn't studied. Why D is wrong: SRP wasn't part of the Löe study. Why E is wrong: Antibiotics weren't part of the study.

Q226 What are the specific criteria for a coronally advanced flap (CAF) according to Bernimoulin et al. (1981)?
A. Any recession depth, any tissue thickness, no keratinized tissue required
B. Minimum tissue thickness of 0.8mm, shallow recession (<4mm), Miller Class I, keratinized attached tissue >3mm, minimal to no flap tension, flap placed 2.5mm coronal to CEJ
C. Only for Miller Class III and IV, tissue thickness >2mm
D. Minimum 5mm of keratinized tissue, deep recession (>6mm), any Miller class
E. No specific criteria exist — the CAF can be used in any clinical situation
Correct Answer: B

Directly from your slides (Bernimoulin et al. 1981): the six CAF criteria are (1) minimum tissue thickness 0.8mm, (2) shallow recession <4mm, (3) Miller Class I, (4) keratinized attached tissue >3mm, (5) minimal to no flap tension, and (6) flap should be placed 2.5mm coronal to CEJ. The 0.8mm tissue thickness connects to the biotype concept — GT <1mm is associated with reduced probability for complete root coverage (from your phenotype slides). The >3mm KT requirement is different from the general gingival health minimum (2mm KT per Lang & Löe) — the CAF needs MORE KT because the tissue is being mobilized coronally. Per Cortellini & Pini Prato 2012, when residual KT is thick, CAF alone may suffice; when thin, add a graft (CTG), EMD, or ADM.

Why A is wrong: Every criterion listed is specific and required. Why C is wrong: Miller III/IV are NOT indicated for CAF alone. Why D is wrong: 5mm KT is the restoration requirement (Maynard & Wilson), not CAF. Why E is wrong: Very specific criteria exist.

Q227 Which of the following conditions can NOT be ascribed to periodontitis when evaluating clinical attachment loss for a periodontitis case definition (2018)?
A. Attachment loss from plaque-induced inflammation at multiple sites
B. Gingival recession of traumatic origin, dental caries extending in the cervical area, CAL on the distal of a second molar associated with third molar malposition/extraction, an endodontic lesion draining through the marginal periodontium, and a vertical root fracture
C. Generalized attachment loss with radiographic bone loss and BOP
D. Attachment loss at >2 non-adjacent teeth with interdental CAL
E. Buccal CAL >3mm with pocketing >3mm at >2 teeth
Correct Answer: B

Directly from your slides — the 2018 periodontitis case definition requires interdental CAL detectable at >2 non-adjacent teeth OR buccal/lingual CAL >3mm with pocketing >3mm at >2 teeth. BUT the CAL CANNOT be ascribed to these 5 non-periodontitis causes: (1) gingival recession of traumatic origin, (2) dental caries extending in the cervical area, (3) CAL on the distal of a 2nd molar from 3rd molar malposition/extraction, (4) an endo lesion draining through the marginal periodontium, (5) a vertical root fracture. This matters clinically: if you see isolated deep probing on the distal of #15 and #18 was recently extracted, that's NOT periodontitis — it's a local factor. Similarly, a "healthy but reduced periodontium" has attachment loss but PD ≤3mm and no BOP — diagnose accordingly, don't automatically call it periodontitis.

Why A is wrong: Plaque-induced attachment loss at multiple sites IS periodontitis. Why C is wrong: This IS consistent with periodontitis. Why D is wrong: This IS the periodontitis case definition. Why E is wrong: This IS the alternative pathway for periodontitis diagnosis.

CROWN LENGTHENING (8)
Q198 According to Gargiulo et al. (1961), what is biologic width and what is the approximate total dimension from the alveolar crest to the gingival margin?
A. Biologic width is the zone of enamel at the CEJ; total dimension is 1.0mm
B. Biologic width is the zone of root surface coronal to the alveolar crest to which connective tissue and junctional epithelium are attached; total dimension from crest to gingival margin is approximately 2.73mm
C. Biologic width is the distance from the CEJ to the root apex; total dimension is 10mm
D. Biologic width is the probing depth in health; total dimension is 3.5mm
E. Biologic width is the width of the PDL space; total dimension is 0.25mm
Correct Answer: B
A. Biologic width is the zone of enamel at the CEJ; total dimension is 1.0mm
B. Biologic width is the zone of root surface coronal to the alveolar crest to which connective tissue and junctional epithelium are attached; total dimension from crest to gingival margin is approximately 2.73mm
C. Biologic width is the distance from the CEJ to the root apex; total dimension is 10mm
D. Biologic width is the probing depth in health; total dimension is 3.5mm
E. Biologic width is the width of the PDL space; total dimension is 0.25mm

Gargiulo et al. (1961) defined biologic width as "that zone of root surface coronal to the alveolar crest, to which the connective tissue and junctional epithelium are attached." The total length from osseous crest to gingival margin is approximately 2.73mm (broken down as: ~1.07mm CT attachment + ~0.97mm JE + ~0.69mm sulcus depth). The essay material emphasizes that "some people have more, and some have less" — biologic width is different for every individual. This is why bone sounding is important before crown lengthening — you need to know YOUR patient's biologic width, not just the average.

Why A is wrong: Biologic width involves soft tissue attachment, not enamel. Why C is wrong: That describes root length, not biologic width. Why D is wrong: Probing depth and biologic width are different measurements. Why E is wrong: PDL width is a separate dimension (~0.15-0.38mm).

Q199 After removing a temporary crown, you observe bleeding and ulceration of the sulcus. Before determining that crown lengthening is needed, what should you do FIRST?
A. Immediately schedule crown lengthening surgery
B. Make a new temporary, remove any excess cement, reinforce oral hygiene, and have the patient return in a few weeks to reassess
C. Extract the tooth and place an implant
D. Prescribe antibiotics and reassess in 6 months
E. Place the final restoration immediately to stabilize the tissue
Correct Answer: B
A. Immediately schedule crown lengthening surgery
B. Make a new temporary, remove any excess cement, reinforce oral hygiene, and have the patient return in a few weeks to reassess
C. Extract the tooth and place an implant
D. Prescribe antibiotics and reassess in 6 months
E. Place the final restoration immediately to stabilize the tissue

Don't jump to crown lengthening — first rule out other causes. The essay material is clear: make a new temp (the old one may have poor margins), remove any excess cement (cement left in the sulcus causes massive inflammation), reinforce OH, and have the patient return in a few weeks. If the tissue heals — the problem was the temp, the cement, or poor hygiene. If the tissue is STILL inflamed after eliminating those variables, THEN it's likely a biologic width violation and crown lengthening is indicated. Other causes of these symptoms include: bad temp margins, retained cement, food impaction from poor contact with adjacent teeth.

Why A is wrong: You must rule out simpler causes before committing to surgery. Why C is wrong: Extraction is premature without first identifying the cause. Why D is wrong: Antibiotics don't address the underlying mechanical/biologic cause. Why E is wrong: Placing a final restoration on inflamed tissue guarantees failure.

Q200 Which of the following is an INDICATION for crown lengthening?
A. Poor crown-to-root ratio
B. Tooth decay at or below the gingival margin with adequate remaining periodontal support
C. Loss of periodontal support on adjacent teeth
D. Furcation involvement at the proposed restorative margin
E. Better alternative treatment available
Correct Answer: B
A. Poor crown-to-root ratio
B. Tooth decay at or below the gingival margin with adequate remaining periodontal support
C. Loss of periodontal support on adjacent teeth
D. Furcation involvement at the proposed restorative margin
E. Better alternative treatment available

Indications for crown lengthening from the essay material: (1) tooth decay at or below the gingival margin, (2) tooth fracture below the gingival margin with adequate remaining support, (3) teeth with excessive wear, (4) insufficient interocclusal space, and (5) delayed passive eruption. All of the OTHER choices (A, C, D, E) are actually CONTRAINDICATIONS. The key thread: crown lengthening is indicated when you need MORE tooth structure exposed for restorative purposes, provided the tooth has adequate remaining support and favorable anatomy.

Why A is wrong: Poor crown-to-root ratio is a CONTRAINDICATION — removing more bone would worsen it. Why C is wrong: Loss of adjacent tooth support is a CONTRAINDICATION. Why D is wrong: Furcation location near the proposed margin is a CONTRAINDICATION. Why E is wrong: If a better alternative exists, CL is contraindicated.

Q201 Which of the following is a CONTRAINDICATION for crown lengthening?
A. Tooth decay below the gingival margin
B. Delayed passive eruption
C. Poor crown-to-root ratio
D. Excessive tooth wear requiring restoration
E. Insufficient interocclusal space
Correct Answer: C
A. Tooth decay below the gingival margin
B. Delayed passive eruption
C. Poor crown-to-root ratio
D. Excessive tooth wear requiring restoration
E. Insufficient interocclusal space

Contraindications from the essay material: (1) poor crown-to-root ratio — removing bone would make the ratio even worse, potentially making the tooth non-restorable. (2) Loss of periodontal support on adjacent teeth. (3) Furcation location near the proposed margin. (4) Inability to keep the area clean after restoration. (5) Better alternative treatments available. (6) Poor long-term prognosis. The overarching principle: if crown lengthening would create MORE problems than it solves (compromising adjacent teeth, worsening support, exposing furcations), it's contraindicated.

Why A is wrong: Subgingival decay IS an indication for CL. Why B is wrong: Delayed passive eruption IS an indication. Why D is wrong: Excessive wear IS an indication. Why E is wrong: Insufficient interocclusal space IS an indication.

Q202 When is an external bevel gingivectomy appropriate for crown lengthening versus a flap procedure with bone removal?
A. Gingivectomy is always preferred regardless of bone level
B. Gingivectomy is appropriate when there is sufficient keratinized tissue AND bone is already at an appropriate distance from the planned margin; a flap with bone removal is required when bone is too close to the planned margin (biologic width violation would occur)
C. Flap with bone removal is never indicated for crown lengthening
D. Gingivectomy is only for posterior teeth; flap procedures are only for anteriors
E. The choice is purely based on patient preference
Correct Answer: B
A. Gingivectomy is always preferred regardless of bone level
B. Gingivectomy is appropriate when there is sufficient keratinized tissue AND bone is already at an appropriate distance from the planned margin; a flap with bone removal is required when bone is too close to the planned margin (biologic width violation would occur)
C. Flap with bone removal is never indicated for crown lengthening
D. Gingivectomy is only for posterior teeth; flap procedures are only for anteriors
E. The choice is purely based on patient preference

Two clinical scenarios for CL from the essay material: (1) External gingivectomy is appropriate when there's sufficient KT AND the bone level is already at an appropriate distance from the planned restorative margin — think altered passive eruption or drug-induced gingival hyperplasia where the excess tissue is the problem, not the bone. (2) A flap with bone removal is required when bone is too close to the planned margin — you need to reduce bone levels to create adequate biologic width for the restoration without violation. This decision tree is fundamentally about bone position relative to the planned margin.

Why A is wrong: Gingivectomy alone fails if bone is too close to the margin. Why C is wrong: Flap + bone removal is frequently indicated. Why D is wrong: Location doesn't determine the technique — bone position does. Why E is wrong: The choice is based on anatomic assessment, not preference.

Q203 How does crown lengthening healing time differ for anterior teeth versus posterior teeth?
A. Both heal at the same rate — 4 weeks is sufficient for all teeth
B. Posterior (e.g., first molars) can be restored at 6–7 weeks; anterior teeth require longer (at least 8 weeks, often ~16 weeks) because it is important to know where the final gingival margin will settle for esthetic reasons
C. Anterior teeth heal faster (4 weeks); posterior teeth take 12+ weeks
D. All crown lengthening cases require 6 months before restoration regardless of location
E. Healing time depends only on patient age, not tooth location
Correct Answer: B
A. Both heal at the same rate — 4 weeks is sufficient for all teeth
B. Posterior (e.g., first molars) can be restored at 6–7 weeks; anterior teeth require longer (at least 8 weeks, often ~16 weeks) because it is important to know where the final gingival margin will settle for esthetic reasons
C. Anterior teeth heal faster (4 weeks); posterior teeth take 12+ weeks
D. All crown lengthening cases require 6 months before restoration regardless of location
E. Healing time depends only on patient age, not tooth location

From the essay material: "For the restoration of first molars, you can wait 6–7 weeks and then restore. However, for teeth in the anterior region where it is important to know where the gingival margin will end up, you need to wait more than 8 weeks, probably around 16 weeks." The difference isn't biologic healing rate — it's ESTHETIC predictability. In the anterior zone, the final gingival margin position directly impacts the restoration's esthetics. If you restore too early and the margin shifts, you'll have an exposed margin or an esthetic failure. Posteriors are less esthetically demanding, so earlier restoration is acceptable.

Why A is wrong: 4 weeks is too early for either location. Why C is wrong: The reverse is true — anteriors need MORE time. Why D is wrong: 6 months is excessive for posterior cases. Why E is wrong: Location matters significantly due to esthetic demands.

Q204 What are common complications of crown lengthening and their management?
A. There are no complications associated with crown lengthening
B. Complications include bleeding (manage with sutures/diet modification), pain (NSAIDs/analgesics), swelling (NSAIDs/ice), and root sensitivity (periodontal packing, stannous fluoride toothpaste, varnishes, Gluma, Super Seal)
C. The only complication is tooth loss
D. Complications include permanent numbness in all cases
E. Complications are limited to infection only
Correct Answer: B
A. There are no complications associated with crown lengthening
B. Complications include bleeding (manage with sutures/diet modification), pain (NSAIDs/analgesics), swelling (NSAIDs/ice), and root sensitivity (periodontal packing, stannous fluoride toothpaste, varnishes, Gluma, Super Seal)
C. The only complication is tooth loss
D. Complications include permanent numbness in all cases
E. Complications are limited to infection only

Four complications from the essay material with their specific management: (1) Bleeding — place sutures, avoid hard foods, avoid irritating the wound. (2) Pain — NSAIDs and analgesics. (3) Swelling — NSAIDs or ice pack. (4) Root sensitivity — protect the area post-surgery with peri packing, then during healing use OTC stannous fluoride toothpastes, varnishes, Gluma, or Super Seal for desensitization. Root sensitivity is especially common because crown lengthening exposes previously covered root surface, which has open dentinal tubules.

Why A is wrong: All surgical procedures have potential complications. Why C is wrong: Tooth loss is extremely rare with proper technique. Why D is wrong: Permanent numbness is not a standard complication. Why E is wrong: Multiple complications exist beyond infection.

Q224 According to Coslet (1977), altered passive eruption is classified into how many types and subtypes, and what are they based on?
A. 3 types based on probing depth
B. 2 types based on the relationship between keratinized gingiva and the tooth's CEJ, each divided into 2 subtypes based on the alveolar crest-CEJ relationship (1A, 1B, 2A, 2B)
C. 4 types based on Miller recession classification
D. 1 type with no subtypes
E. 2 types based on tooth mobility
Correct Answer: B
A. 3 types based on probing depth
B. 2 types based on the relationship between keratinized gingiva and the tooth's CEJ, each divided into 2 subtypes based on the alveolar crest-CEJ relationship (1A, 1B, 2A, 2B)
C. 4 types based on Miller recession classification
D. 1 type with no subtypes
E. 2 types based on tooth mobility

Directly from your slides (Coslet 1977): "Two types of altered passive eruption according to relationship between keratinized gingiva and tooth's CEJ and each type divided into two subtypes on the basis of the alveolar crest-CEJ relationship" — giving you 1A, 1B, 2A, 2B. This is directly relevant to crown lengthening planning: Type 1 = gingival margin is incisal to the CEJ with adequate KT width. Type 2 = gingival margin is at the CEJ with narrow KT width. Subtype A = alveolar crest is at a normal distance from the CEJ (~1.5-2mm). Subtype B = alveolar crest is AT the CEJ level. The subtype determines your surgical approach — A subtypes may only need gingivectomy, while B subtypes need osseous reduction (flap + bone removal). Delayed passive eruption is listed as an INDICATION for crown lengthening on your CL slides.

Why A is wrong: Not based on probing depth. Why C is wrong: Unrelated to Miller. Why D is wrong: There are multiple types and subtypes. Why E is wrong: Not based on mobility.

GTR / GBR (22)
Q31 What is the initial incision technique used in guided tissue regeneration (GTR)?
A. External bevel gingivectomy incision
B. Intrasulcular incision with removal of all pocket epithelium
C. Internal bevel incision preserving the pocket epithelium
D. Semilunar incision 2mm from the papilla tips
E. Crestal incision with vertical releasing incisions only
Correct Answer: B
A. External bevel gingivectomy incision
B. Intrasulcular incision with removal of all pocket epithelium
C. Internal bevel incision preserving the pocket epithelium
D. Semilunar incision 2mm from the papilla tips
E. Crestal incision with vertical releasing incisions only

GTR requires an intrasulcular incision combined with complete removal of all pocket epithelium. This makes total sense when you think about the GTR principle — you're trying to exclude epithelial cells from the healing equation (they're the fastest migrators and they win "the race" to the root surface). If you leave pocket epithelium behind, you've already defeated the purpose of placing a membrane. You need a clean connective tissue environment so that PDL cells can repopulate the root surface and generate true new attachment rather than repair (long junctional epithelium).

Why A is wrong: External bevel gingivectomy removes tissue from the outside — not appropriate for GTR access. Why C is wrong: Preserving pocket epithelium completely defeats the purpose of GTR. Why D is wrong: Semilunar incision is for the Tarnow coronally positioned flap, not GTR. Why E is wrong: A crestal incision alone doesn't address pocket epithelium removal.

Q32 What is the ideal closure technique for a GORE-TEX (ePTFE) membrane in GTR?
A. The membrane should be flush with the coronal aspect of the flap, with vertical incisions closed first
B. The membrane should be 2–3mm below the coronal aspect of the flap, with interproximal closure first and vertical releasing incisions closed last
C. The membrane should be exposed above the flap margin for guided healing
D. The membrane should be 5mm below the flap margin with continuous sling sutures only
E. Complete membrane exposure is acceptable if the patient maintains chlorhexidine rinse
Correct Answer: B
A. The membrane should be flush with the coronal aspect of the flap, with vertical incisions closed first
B. The membrane should be 2–3mm below the coronal aspect of the flap, with interproximal closure first and vertical releasing incisions closed last
C. The membrane should be exposed above the flap margin for guided healing
D. The membrane should be 5mm below the flap margin with continuous sling sutures only
E. Complete membrane exposure is acceptable if the patient maintains chlorhexidine rinse

The ideal closure places the GORE-TEX membrane 2–3mm below the coronal aspect of the flap. You close the interproximal areas FIRST, then the vertical releasing incisions LAST. The sequence matters — by closing interproximal first, you establish the primary seal over the membrane, then the verticals lock everything in place. That 2–3mm submergence is critical because membrane exposure is the #1 complication of GTR — it leads to bacterial contamination, infection, and failure of regeneration. You need that tissue buffer zone to protect the membrane.

Why A is wrong: Flush positioning gives zero safety margin against exposure. Why C is wrong: Intentional exposure guarantees contamination and failure. Why D is wrong: 5mm submergence is excessive and not described in the technique. Why E is wrong: Even with CHX, membrane exposure significantly compromises outcomes.

Q33 How long should a GORE-TEX (ePTFE) membrane ideally remain in place before removal?
A. 2 weeks
B. 4 weeks
C. 6 weeks
D. 3 months
E. It is resorbable and does not require removal
Correct Answer: C
A. 2 weeks
B. 4 weeks
C. 6 weeks
D. 3 months
E. It is resorbable and does not require removal

Clinically, the GORE-TEX membrane CAN be left for up to 3 months, but ideal healing occurs between 4–6 weeks, so the recommendation is to remove it at 6 weeks. GORE-TEX is a non-resorbable ePTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) membrane — it's the same medical-grade stretched Teflon used in vascular surgery and artificial ligaments. Because it's non-resorbable, it MUST be surgically removed. Leaving it too long increases the risk of exposure and infection; removing it too early doesn't allow adequate time for PDL cell repopulation and new attachment formation.

Why A is wrong: 2 weeks is way too early — regeneration hasn't had adequate time. Why B is wrong: 4 weeks is within the healing window but the ideal target is 6 weeks. Why D is wrong: 3 months is the maximum, not the ideal — too long increases exposure risk. Why E is wrong: GORE-TEX is non-resorbable and absolutely requires a second surgery for removal.

Q44 What is the key molecule responsible for bone morphogenesis?
A. Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)
B. Enamel matrix derivative (EMD)
C. Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs)
D. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)
E. Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β)
Correct Answer: C
A. Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)
B. Enamel matrix derivative (EMD)
C. Bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs)
D. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)
E. Transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β)

BMPs — bone morphogenetic proteins — are the key to bone morphogenesis. Your slides state that BMPs are "a group of regulatory glycoproteins which stimulate differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into osteoblasts." The biologic basis was shown by Marshall Urist, who discovered that demineralized, lyophilized segments of bone induced new bone formation when implanted in muscle pouches in rabbits (published 1965 in Science). Urist proposed the name "Bone Morphogenetic Protein" in the Journal of Dental Research in 1971. Much of periodontal research has focused on BMP-2, BMP-3 (osteogenin), and BMP-7 (OP-1).

Why A is wrong: PDGF promotes chemotaxis and mitogenesis but doesn't directly drive bone morphogenesis like BMPs do. Why B is wrong: EMD mimics developmental processes but isn't the key bone morphogenesis molecule. Why D is wrong: VEGF drives angiogenesis, not bone formation per se. Why E is wrong: TGF-β is involved in wound healing broadly but BMPs are the specific bone morphogenesis drivers.

Q45 What is piezocision and how does it work at the tissue level?
A. Ultrasonic bone cutting that permanently removes cortical bone segments
B. A technique that alternates between compression and expansion of hydroxyapatite crystals to accelerate orthodontic movement
C. Laser-assisted bone ablation for implant site preparation
D. Mechanical vibration therapy applied to teeth to increase PDL blood flow
E. Piezoelectric osteotomy used exclusively for ridge augmentation
Correct Answer: B
A. Ultrasonic bone cutting that permanently removes cortical bone segments
B. A technique that alternates between compression and expansion of hydroxyapatite crystals to accelerate orthodontic movement
C. Laser-assisted bone ablation for implant site preparation
D. Mechanical vibration therapy applied to teeth to increase PDL blood flow
E. Piezoelectric osteotomy used exclusively for ridge augmentation

Piezocision uses piezoelectric vibrations to create micro-incisions in cortical bone. At the tissue level, it works by alternating between compression and expansion of hydroxyapatite crystals in the bone. This creates controlled micro-damage to the cortical plate, triggering a RAP response (localized bone remodeling burst) that temporarily reduces bone density and allows faster orthodontic tooth movement. The piezoelectric device selectively cuts mineralized tissue while preserving soft tissue — it won't cut nerves, vessels, or mucosa — making it safer than rotary instruments.

Why A is wrong: Piezocision doesn't permanently remove bone segments — it makes micro-cuts. Why C is wrong: This describes a different procedure entirely. Why D is wrong: Mechanical vibration (like AcceleDent) is a different technology. Why E is wrong: Piezocision is used for orthodontic acceleration, not ridge augmentation.

Q46 When PDL cells grow into cementum and form new inserting fibers on a previously diseased root surface, this is classified as:
A. Repair
B. Reattachment
C. New attachment
D. Ankylosis
E. Long junctional epithelium formation
Correct Answer: C
A. Repair
B. Reattachment
C. New attachment
D. Ankylosis
E. Long junctional epithelium formation

This is NEW attachment, not reattachment. The distinction is critical and directly from your slides. Reattachment refers to reunion of connective tissue with a root surface from which it was NOT pathologically separated — like reattaching a flap to a root that was exposed during surgery but never had disease on it. NEW attachment is the formation of new cementum with inserting collagen fibers on a root surface that WAS previously exposed to the oral environment and diseased. Your GTR slides confirm this — the Nyman et al. studies showed that PDL cells possess the capability to re-establish connective tissue attachment (new cementum with inserting fibers) on previously diseased root surfaces when given the opportunity via membrane exclusion of other cell types.

Why A is wrong: Repair is junctional epithelial adhesion — no connective tissue fibers into cementum. Why B is wrong: Reattachment is reconnection to a surface that was never pathologically detached. Why D is wrong: Ankylosis is direct bone-to-root fusion without PDL — a pathologic outcome. Why E is wrong: Long junctional epithelium is the repair outcome, not new attachment.

Q47 What does the term "bone regeneration" specifically refer to in the context of GBR (guided bone regeneration)?
A. Replacement of bone with fibrous connective tissue
B. Appositional bone growth added to an edentulous area
C. Internal remodeling of existing cortical bone
D. Formation of a long junctional epithelium over bone
E. Resorption of existing bone to create space for implant placement
Correct Answer: B
A. Replacement of bone with fibrous connective tissue
B. Appositional bone growth added to an edentulous area
C. Internal remodeling of existing cortical bone
D. Formation of a long junctional epithelium over bone
E. Resorption of existing bone to create space for implant placement

Bone regeneration in the GBR context specifically means appositional growth — new bone being ADDED to an edentulous area. This is the major conceptual difference between GTR and GBR that your slides highlight: GTR is about regenerating the periodontium around TEETH (new cementum, PDL, bone), while GBR is about growing NEW bone in edentulous areas for implant placement, extraction site preservation, or ridge augmentation. GBR uses membranes with the same principle as GTR — exclude soft tissue cells so osteogenic cells can populate the space and form bone.

Why A is wrong: Fibrous tissue replacement is repair, not regeneration. Why C is wrong: Internal remodeling isn't the same as adding new bone to an edentulous area. Why D is wrong: Junctional epithelium formation is repair. Why E is wrong: Resorption is the opposite of regeneration.

Q48 A material that facilitates new bone formation from existing bone by acting as a scaffold is described as:
A. Osteoinductive
B. Osteoconductive
C. Osteogenic
D. Osteointegrative
E. Osteoclastic
Correct Answer: B
A. Osteoinductive
B. Osteoconductive
C. Osteogenic
D. Osteointegrative
E. Osteoclastic

Osteoconductive — directly from your slides: "when a material facilitates new bone formation from existing bone, essentially acting as a scaffold." Think of it as the material being a trellis that existing bone grows ALONG. It doesn't create bone from nothing — it needs existing bone at the margins to serve as the source. Contrast this with osteoinductive: "when a material can induce new bone formation from undifferentiated cells, or cells other than osteocytes." Osteoinduction is more powerful — it can actually recruit stem cells and convert them into osteoblasts, creating bone where there was none.

Why A is wrong: Osteoinductive means the material can induce bone from undifferentiated cells — that's induction, not scaffolding. Why C is wrong: Osteogenic means the material contains living bone cells that directly form bone — only autografts are truly osteogenic. Why D is wrong: Osteointegration describes implant-to-bone interface, not a material property. Why E is wrong: Osteoclastic refers to bone resorption, the opposite of formation.

Q49 A material that can induce new bone formation from undifferentiated cells or cells other than osteocytes is described as:
A. Osteoconductive
B. Osteoinductive
C. Osteogenic
D. Biocompatible
E. Bioinert
Correct Answer: B
A. Osteoconductive
B. Osteoinductive
C. Osteogenic
D. Biocompatible
E. Bioinert

Osteoinductive — per your slides: "when a material can induce new bone formation, from undifferentiated cells, or cells other than osteocytes." This is the more impressive property because the material can actually RECRUIT undifferentiated mesenchymal stem cells and CONVERT them into bone-forming osteoblasts. Marshall Urist demonstrated this principle when he showed that demineralized bone matrix (which contains BMPs) could induce bone formation even in muscle pouches — an ectopic site with no existing bone. This discovery is the foundation of DFDBA's theoretical superiority over FDBA.

Why A is wrong: Osteoconductive only provides a scaffold — needs existing bone nearby. Why C is wrong: Osteogenic means containing living cells — only fresh autograft qualifies. Why D is wrong: Biocompatible means the material doesn't cause adverse reactions — doesn't address bone induction. Why E is wrong: Bioinert means the material doesn't interact with tissue at all.

Q50 Which type of vital osseous graft material has the best osteogenic potential?
A. Cortical bone from the mandibular ramus
B. Freeze-dried bone allograft (FDBA)
C. Vital cancellous bone with hematopoietic marrow (e.g., tuberosity)
D. Anorganic bovine bone (Bio-Oss)
E. Beta-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP)
Correct Answer: C
A. Cortical bone from the mandibular ramus
B. Freeze-dried bone allograft (FDBA)
C. Vital cancellous bone with hematopoietic marrow (e.g., tuberosity)
D. Anorganic bovine bone (Bio-Oss)
E. Beta-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP)

Vital cancellous bone with hematopoietic marrow — such as from the tuberosity or a recent extraction site — has the best osteogenic potential. Your slides state this directly: "Vital cancellous bone contains hematopoietic marrow, such as bone marrow from a tuberosity, or from a recent extraction site, providing better osteogenic potential." Cancellous bone is spongy, highly vascularized, and full of marrow cells including osteogenic progenitors. Your slides also note that "cortical grafts would have less osteogenic potential than cancellous grafts" — so the ramus (cortical) is inferior.

Why A is wrong: Cortical bone has less osteogenic potential than cancellous — your slides explicitly state this. Why B is wrong: FDBA is a non-vital allograft and is osteoconductive, not osteogenic. Why D is wrong: Bio-Oss is a non-vital xenograft — osteoconductive scaffold only. Why E is wrong: β-TCP is a synthetic alloplast — no osteogenic cells present.

Q51 According to Urist, what happens when cortical allografts are demineralized, and what did Schwartz find regarding this?
A. Demineralization destroys all biologic activity; Schwartz confirmed this
B. Demineralization exposes BMPs and an inductive factor known to increase bone formation; Schwartz found that not all DFDBA samples were osteoinductive
C. Demineralization converts cortical bone into cancellous bone; Schwartz showed all samples were equally effective
D. Demineralization removes all organic components; Schwartz showed it was superior to autograft
E. Demineralization has no effect on allografts; Schwartz confirmed osteoconductivity only
Correct Answer: B
A. Demineralization destroys all biologic activity; Schwartz confirmed this
B. Demineralization exposes BMPs and an inductive factor known to increase bone formation; Schwartz found that not all DFDBA samples were osteoinductive
C. Demineralization converts cortical bone into cancellous bone; Schwartz showed all samples were equally effective
D. Demineralization removes all organic components; Schwartz showed it was superior to autograft
E. Demineralization has no effect on allografts; Schwartz confirmed osteoconductivity only

Urist showed that demineralization of cortical allografts exposes BMP and an inductive factor known to increase bone formation — this was the groundbreaking discovery published in Science in 1965. However, Schwartz's finding is the critical caveat: NOT all DFDBA samples are osteoinductive.
