This is a huge clinical concern because it means the quality of DFDBA from tissue banks is variable — some batches have good osteoinductive potential and others don't. Factors like donor age, processing methods, and particle size all affect the biologic activity of DFDBA. This variability is why some clinicians prefer other graft materials with more consistent properties.

Why A is wrong: Demineralization doesn't destroy activity — it EXPOSES BMPs. Why C is wrong: Demineralization doesn't physically change bone type from cortical to cancellous. Why D is wrong: Demineralization removes the MINERAL component, not the organic component — the organic matrix (including BMPs) is what's preserved. Why E is wrong: Demineralization absolutely affects the biologic properties.

Q52 What is Bio-Oss?
A. A demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft (DFDBA)
B. A synthetic calcium phosphate alloplast
C. A highly purified anorganic natural bone mineral xenograft
D. An autogenous cancellous bone graft
E. A genetically engineered bone morphogenetic protein preparation
Correct Answer: C
A. A demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft (DFDBA)
B. A synthetic calcium phosphate alloplast
C. A highly purified anorganic natural bone mineral xenograft
D. An autogenous cancellous bone graft
E. A genetically engineered bone morphogenetic protein preparation

Bio-Oss is a highly purified anorganic natural bone mineral xenograft — directly from your study guide. It's derived from bovine (cow) bone that has been processed to remove all organic components, leaving behind only the mineralized hydroxyapatite scaffold. This makes it osteoconductive — it provides an excellent scaffold for new bone to grow along — but it's NOT osteoinductive (no BMPs or growth factors remain after processing). Your GBR slides show Bio-Oss being used in combination with PDGF (like in GEM 21S) precisely because it provides the scaffold while the growth factor provides the biologic signal.

Why A is wrong: DFDBA is a human allograft, not bovine. Why B is wrong: Bio-Oss is natural (bovine-derived), not synthetic. Why D is wrong: Autogenous means from the same patient — Bio-Oss comes from a cow. Why E is wrong: Bio-Oss contains no genetically engineered proteins.

Q53 By how much does a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) preparation concentrate platelets compared to whole blood?
A. 50–100%
B. 100–200%
C. 200–330%
D. 330–900%
E. 1000–2000%
Correct Answer: D
A. 50–100%
B. 100–200%
C. 200–330%
D. 330–900%
E. 1000–2000%

PRP preparation concentrates platelets by 330–900% compared to whole blood baseline. That's a massive concentration of growth factors — platelets contain PDGF, TGF-β, VEGF, and other cytokines that drive wound healing. The PRP is spun from the patient's own blood using a centrifuge, creating a concentrated platelet gel that can be mixed with bone graft materials. Your slides show PRP gel combined with bone graft as one of the approaches to enhance regenerative outcomes.

Why A is wrong: 50–100% would be barely more than baseline — not clinically significant. Why B is wrong: Still too low for PRP technology. Why C is wrong: 200–330% underestimates the concentration capacity. Why E is wrong: 1000–2000% exceeds what standard PRP preparation achieves.

Q54 What is GEM 21S, and what clinical advantage does it provide?
A. A collagen membrane that prevents epithelial downgrowth and improves pocket depth reduction
B. A combination of recombinant human PDGF-BB (rhPDGF) with β-TCP that provides improved bone formation and faster healing but NOT greater bone volume
C. A BMP-2 infused allograft that produces significantly greater bone volume
D. An enamel matrix derivative that promotes cementum formation only
E. A PRP gel used alone without any scaffold material
Correct Answer: B
A. A collagen membrane that prevents epithelial downgrowth and improves pocket depth reduction
B. A combination of recombinant human PDGF-BB (rhPDGF) with β-TCP that provides improved bone formation and faster healing but NOT greater bone volume
C. A BMP-2 infused allograft that produces significantly greater bone volume
D. An enamel matrix derivative that promotes cementum formation only
E. A PRP gel used alone without any scaffold material

GEM 21S (Growth-factor Enhanced Matrix) combines a bioactive protein — highly purified recombinant human PDGF-BB (rhPDGF-BB) — with an osteoconductive matrix of beta-tricalcium phosphate (β-TCP). Your slides explain that after implantation, PDGF is released from the β-TCP matrix, binds to cell surface receptors, and initiates chemotaxis and mitogenesis of osteoblasts, PDL fibroblasts, and cementoblasts, leading to new bone, PDL, and cementum formation. The important clinical caveat: it provides improved bone formation and faster healing but does NOT produce greater bone volume. The β-TCP also serves to bind and localize PDGF to the wound site.

Why A is wrong: GEM 21S is a graft material, not a membrane. Why C is wrong: GEM 21S uses PDGF, not BMP-2, and doesn't produce greater bone volume. Why D is wrong: EMD (Emdogain) is a separate product from GEM 21S. Why E is wrong: GEM 21S specifically combines PRP/PDGF WITH a scaffold (β-TCP).

Q81 Which type of bone graft material is NOT scientifically proven to produce osteogenic properties?
A. Autograft
B. Allograft (vital, cryopreserved)
C. Xenograft
D. Alloplast
E. Both C and D
Correct Answer: D
A. Autograft
B. Allograft (vital, cryopreserved)
C. Xenograft
D. Alloplast
E. Both C and D

Alloplasts are NOT scientifically proven to have osteogenic properties. Alloplasts are synthetic materials — calcium sulfate, calcium ceramics, hydroxyapatite, tri-calcium phosphate, bioactive glass polymers. Your slides explicitly state that alloplasts are "inert biologic fillers" and are "unlikely to result in true regeneration." They are osteoconductive at best (providing a scaffold), but they contain no living cells (no osteogenic potential) and have no BMPs (no osteoinductive potential). They fill space and guide bone growth along their surface but cannot generate bone on their own. Autografts are osteogenic (contain living cells), vital allografts can be osteogenic, and even non-vital allografts (DFDBA) can be osteoinductive.

Why A is wrong: Autografts are the gold standard for osteogenic potential — they contain living bone cells. Why B is wrong: Vital cryopreserved allografts can contain osteogenic cells. Why C is wrong: Xenografts aren't osteogenic either, but the specific answer from the study guide targets alloplasts. Why E is wrong: While xenografts also lack osteogenic properties, the study guide specifically identifies alloplasts as the answer.

Q205 In GTR, a full-thickness flap is reflected and a membrane is placed. How many tissue types compete for space at the root surface, and which tissue type "wins the race" if no barrier is placed?
A. 2 tissue types compete; bone cells win
B. 3 tissue types compete; PDL cells win
C. 4 tissue types compete (gingival CT, epithelium, bone cells, PDL cells); epithelium wins without a barrier
D. 5 tissue types compete; cementoblasts win
E. Only 1 tissue type participates in healing
Correct Answer: C
A. 2 tissue types compete; bone cells win
B. 3 tissue types compete; PDL cells win
C. 4 tissue types compete (gingival CT, epithelium, bone cells, PDL cells); epithelium wins without a barrier
D. 5 tissue types compete; cementoblasts win
E. Only 1 tissue type participates in healing

From the essay material: "After surgery, there are 4 tissue types that compete for space adjacent to the tooth and without interference the epithelium will win." The four types are: gingival connective tissue, epithelium, bone cells, and PDL cells. Epithelium migrates at 0.5mm/day (fastest of all) and colonizes the root surface first, forming a long junctional epithelium (repair) instead of true new attachment (regeneration). The GTR membrane excludes the two unwanted fast-movers (epithelium and gingival CT) while giving the slower PDL and bone cells time to repopulate the root surface.

Why A is wrong: There are 4 types, not 2, and bone cells cause ankylosis, not proper healing. Why B is wrong: 4 types compete, and PDL cells are actually the slowest (but produce the BEST outcome). Why D is wrong: 4 types, not 5, and cementoblasts aren't listed as a separate competing cell. Why E is wrong: Multiple tissue types participate.

Q206 According to the landmark GTR studies, what happens when each of the four tissue types contacts the root surface directly?
A. All four produce identical healing outcomes
B. Gingival CT causes root resorption; epithelium forms long junctional epithelium (no true attachment); bone cells cause ankylosis; PDL cells produce regeneration (new cementum with inserting collagen fibers)
C. All four produce regeneration
D. Only epithelium produces healing; the other three cause resorption
E. Only bone cells produce useful healing
Correct Answer: B
A. All four produce identical healing outcomes
B. Gingival CT causes root resorption; epithelium forms long junctional epithelium (no true attachment); bone cells cause ankylosis; PDL cells produce regeneration (new cementum with inserting collagen fibers)
C. All four produce regeneration
D. Only epithelium produces healing; the other three cause resorption
E. Only bone cells produce useful healing

From the essay material and lecture slides: (1) Gingival CT causes a resorptive process — root resorption. (2) Epithelium forms a long junctional epithelium — you get healing but NOT true attachment ("you don't get true attachment"). (3) Bone cells cause ankylosis — direct fusion of bone to root without PDL (pathologic). (4) PDL cells produce true regeneration — new cementum with inserting collagen fibers, which was proven by Nyman et al. 1982 ("PDL cells possess the ability to re-establish CT attachment"). This is WHY GTR membranes are designed to keep out gingival CT and epithelium while allowing PDL cells access.

Why A is wrong: Each tissue type produces a distinctly different healing outcome. Why C is wrong: Only PDL cells produce regeneration. Why D is wrong: Epithelium produces repair, not the best healing, and the others don't all cause resorption. Why E is wrong: Bone cells cause the pathologic outcome of ankylosis.

Q207 In the Isidor et al. (1986) study, what happened when PDL cells were prevented from migrating coronally (tight elastic) versus when they were allowed to migrate (loose elastic)?
A. Tight elastic produced better regeneration than loose elastic
B. Both tight and loose elastic produced identical results
C. When PDL cells were prevented from migrating coronally (tight elastic), there was NO new attachment; when PDL cells were allowed to migrate (loose elastic), new attachment occurred
D. Tight elastic caused ankylosis; loose elastic caused root resorption
E. Neither condition produced any healing
Correct Answer: C
A. Tight elastic produced better regeneration than loose elastic
B. Both tight and loose elastic produced identical results
C. When PDL cells were prevented from migrating coronally (tight elastic), there was NO new attachment; when PDL cells were allowed to migrate (loose elastic), new attachment occurred
D. Tight elastic caused ankylosis; loose elastic caused root resorption
E. Neither condition produced any healing

Isidor et al. (1986) — "The Significance of Coronal Growth of PDL Tissue for New Attachment Formation": angular defects were created to mid-root level, PDL and cementum removed. In half the teeth, a tight elastic was placed (preventing PDL cell migration). In the other half, a loose elastic was placed (allowing migration). Result: tight elastic = NO new attachment. Loose elastic = new attachment. This proved that coronal migration of PDL cells is ESSENTIAL for regeneration. If you block PDL cells, you block healing. This study is one of the foundational pillars proving that PDL cells are the key to regeneration.

Why A is wrong: The tight elastic PREVENTED new attachment. Why B is wrong: Results were dramatically different. Why D is wrong: Tight elastic prevented attachment entirely — not specifically ankylosis in this study. Why E is wrong: The loose elastic group DID achieve new attachment.

Q208 How does GTR differ from GBR in terms of the number of competing cell types and the type of tissue regenerated?
A. GTR has 3 competing cell types and produces bone only; GBR has 4 and produces PDL
B. GTR has 4 competing cell types (including PDL cells) and creates new PDL around TEETH; GBR has 3 competing cell types (no PDL cells) and creates new BONE in edentulous areas
C. Both have identical cell competition and produce the same tissue
D. GTR has 2 cell types; GBR has 5 cell types
E. GTR only works in edentulous areas; GBR only works around teeth
Correct Answer: B
A. GTR has 3 competing cell types and produces bone only; GBR has 4 and produces PDL
B. GTR has 4 competing cell types (including PDL cells) and creates new PDL around TEETH; GBR has 3 competing cell types (no PDL cells) and creates new BONE in edentulous areas
C. Both have identical cell competition and produce the same tissue
D. GTR has 2 cell types; GBR has 5 cell types
E. GTR only works in edentulous areas; GBR only works around teeth

From the essay material: "Guided tissue regeneration takes place around a tooth and creates a new PDL, while guided bone regeneration takes place in an edentulous area and only new bone forms. Guided tissue regeneration also has 4 different cell types competing, while guided bone regeneration has 3 different cell types competing because no PDL cells." This is the major conceptual difference your lecture slides ask about. In GBR, there are no PDL cells because there's no tooth/PDL — so only 3 cell types compete (epithelium, connective tissue, bone cells). The goal in GBR is simply bone formation for implant placement or ridge augmentation.

Why A is wrong: The cell numbers and tissue types are reversed. Why C is wrong: They differ in both cell competition and tissue outcome. Why D is wrong: GTR has 4, GBR has 3. Why E is wrong: GTR is around teeth; GBR is in edentulous areas — the reverse of this choice.

Q209 What are common complications of GTR/GBR procedures?
A. No complications are possible with regenerative procedures
B. Pain/swelling (manage with NSAIDs), membrane exposure (trim back to 2–3mm), infection (antibiotics + OH + CHX rinses), perforation of soft tissue (proper suturing + tension-free closure), recession/flap sloughing (tension-free primary closure + proper flap design)
C. The only complication is tooth loss
D. Complications are limited to post-operative pain only
E. GTR/GBR complications are the same as those for extractions
Correct Answer: B
A. No complications are possible with regenerative procedures
B. Pain/swelling (manage with NSAIDs), membrane exposure (trim back to 2–3mm), infection (antibiotics + OH + CHX rinses), perforation of soft tissue (proper suturing + tension-free closure), recession/flap sloughing (tension-free primary closure + proper flap design)
C. The only complication is tooth loss
D. Complications are limited to post-operative pain only
E. GTR/GBR complications are the same as those for extractions

Five GTR/GBR complications from the essay material with specific remedies: (1) Pain/swelling — NSAIDs. (2) Membrane exposure — the #1 complication; trim the exposed membrane back to 2–3mm below the tissue (the same principle as the 2–3mm submergence during initial placement). (3) Infection — antibiotics, ensure good OH, CHX rinses. (4) Soft tissue perforation — use proper suturing technique, tension-free closure, make sure bone surfaces are smooth (sharp bone edges can poke through). (5) Recession/flap sloughing — tension-free primary closure and proper flap design are the keys to prevention.

Why A is wrong: All surgical procedures have potential complications. Why C is wrong: Tooth loss is not the typical complication. Why D is wrong: Multiple complications exist beyond pain. Why E is wrong: GTR/GBR has unique complications specific to membrane procedures.

Q210 Regarding regenerative barriers, what is the primary advantage of non-resorbable membranes (Gore-Tex) and the primary advantage of resorbable membranes?
A. Non-resorbable: cheaper and easier; Resorbable: more predictable outcomes
B. Non-resorbable: excellent space maintenance, long-term support, more predictable outcome; Resorbable: no second procedure required, more tissue compatible, resorption timing can be regulated
C. Non-resorbable: no surgery needed; Resorbable: better space maintenance
D. Both have identical advantages
E. Non-resorbable: faster healing; Resorbable: stronger barrier function
Correct Answer: B
A. Non-resorbable: cheaper and easier; Resorbable: more predictable outcomes
B. Non-resorbable: excellent space maintenance, long-term support, more predictable outcome; Resorbable: no second procedure required, more tissue compatible, resorption timing can be regulated
C. Non-resorbable: no surgery needed; Resorbable: better space maintenance
D. Both have identical advantages
E. Non-resorbable: faster healing; Resorbable: stronger barrier function

From the essay material — Non-resorbable (Gore-Tex) advantages: excellent space maintenance, long-term support, more predictable outcome. Disadvantages: requires a second procedure for removal, risk of inflammation/infection, need for tac (tack) fixation, may be exposed during healing. Resorbable (collagen membrane, synthetic polymers) advantages: no second procedure required, more tissue compatible, timing for resorption can be regulated. Disadvantage: unpredictable outcome. The tradeoff is clear: non-resorbable gives you MORE control and predictability but at the cost of a second surgery and exposure risk.

Why A is wrong: Non-resorbable is actually more expensive and technically demanding. Why C is wrong: Both require surgery for placement. Why D is wrong: They have distinctly different advantage profiles. Why E is wrong: Non-resorbable doesn't heal faster, and resorbable doesn't have stronger barrier function.

Q211 What is Enamel Matrix Derivative (EMD), and how does its biologic effect differ from bone morphogenetic proteins?
A. EMD is osteoinductive, just like BMPs
B. EMD is harvested from porcine tooth buds and is "osteopromotive" (stimulates bone formation when combined with DFDBA) but is NOT osteoinductive; BMPs ARE osteoinductive (stimulate differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into osteoblasts)
C. EMD directly forms bone; BMPs only form soft tissue
D. EMD and BMPs are identical products
E. EMD is synthetic; BMPs are harvested from porcine sources
Correct Answer: B
A. EMD is osteoinductive, just like BMPs
B. EMD is harvested from porcine tooth buds and is "osteopromotive" (stimulates bone formation when combined with DFDBA) but is NOT osteoinductive; BMPs ARE osteoinductive (stimulate differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into osteoblasts)
C. EMD directly forms bone; BMPs only form soft tissue
D. EMD and BMPs are identical products
E. EMD is synthetic; BMPs are harvested from porcine sources

Critical distinction from the essay material: EMD is harvested from porcine tooth buds and contains low molecular weight proteins. It is "osteopromotive" — meaning it stimulates bone formation WHEN COMBINED with DFDBA — but it is NOT osteoinductive on its own. It enhances PDL fibroblast cell proliferation and protein production and stimulates periodontal tissue reconstruction around teeth. BMPs, in contrast, ARE truly osteoinductive — they stimulate differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into osteoblasts independently. The exam trap: EMD promotes bone formation but cannot INDUCE it from undifferentiated cells the way BMPs can.

Why A is wrong: EMD is specifically NOT osteoinductive — it's osteopromotive. Why C is wrong: EMD doesn't directly form bone — it promotes it. Why D is wrong: They are completely different products with different mechanisms. Why E is wrong: EMD is from porcine sources; some BMPs are genetically engineered.

NON-SURGICAL / SURGICAL THERAPY (24)
Q82 Clinical attachment level (CAL) is measured from:
A. The CEJ to the bottom of the pocket
B. The CEJ to the gingival margin
C. The bottom of the pocket to the gingival margin
D. The alveolar crest to the bottom of the pocket
E. The gingival margin to the alveolar crest
Correct Answer: A
A. The CEJ to the bottom of the pocket
B. The CEJ to the gingival margin
C. The bottom of the pocket to the gingival margin
D. The alveolar crest to the bottom of the pocket
E. The gingival margin to the alveolar crest

CAL is measured from the CEJ to the bottom (base) of the pocket. This is THE most important clinical measurement in periodontology because it tells you the cumulative amount of attachment that has been lost over time — it doesn't change with swelling or recession like probing depth does. Probing depth (choice C) measures gingival margin to base of pocket, which can increase from swelling without any true attachment loss. The CEJ is a fixed anatomic landmark, making CAL the reliable, reproducible measure of disease severity.

Why B is wrong: CEJ to gingival margin measures the amount of recession (or pseudo-pocket depth if margin is coronal to CEJ). Why C is wrong: That's probing depth, not CAL. Why D is wrong: Crest to pocket base is a radiographic/surgical measurement, not CAL. Why E is wrong: This isn't a standard periodontal measurement.

Q86 What is the most important factor in determining the long-term success of periodontal treatment?
A. The skill of the operator
B. Compliance of the patient with recall visits
C. The patient's oral hygiene practices
D. The type of surgical technique used
E. The choice of graft material
Correct Answer: C
A. The skill of the operator
B. Compliance of the patient with recall visits
C. The patient's oral hygiene practices
D. The type of surgical technique used
E. The choice of graft material

The patient's oral hygiene practices are the single most important factor for long-term success of periodontal treatment. You can perform the most technically perfect surgery in the world, but if the patient goes home and doesn't brush or floss, plaque re-accumulates and disease recurs. This is why Phase I therapy (OHI, SRP) always comes FIRST before any surgical intervention — you need to establish that the patient CAN and WILL maintain their mouth. Operator skill and recall compliance matter, but daily home care is the constant variable that determines success.

Why A is wrong: Technical skill matters but is secondary to daily patient behavior. Why B is wrong: Recall visits happen 2–4x/year — oral hygiene happens 365 days/year. Why D is wrong: Surgical technique is important but maintenance is what sustains results. Why E is wrong: Graft material choice has minimal impact compared to patient hygiene compliance.

Q87 A tooth has 5mm probing depth and 2mm recession. What is the clinical attachment level (CAL)?
A. 3mm
B. 5mm
C. 7mm
D. 2mm
E. 10mm
Correct Answer: C
A. 3mm
B. 5mm
C. 7mm
D. 2mm
E. 10mm

When recession is present, CAL = probing depth + recession. So 5mm + 2mm = 7mm CAL. Think about it anatomically: the gingival margin has already receded 2mm apical to the CEJ, and then you're probing 5mm deeper from that receded margin — so the total distance from the CEJ to the base of the pocket is 7mm. The opposite scenario applies with gingival overgrowth (pseudopocket): if there's 3mm of overgrowth, you SUBTRACT it from the probing depth. CAL always references the CEJ as the fixed landmark, regardless of where the gingival margin sits.

Why A is wrong: 3mm would be subtraction (5-2), which is the formula for overgrowth, not recession. Why B is wrong: 5mm is just the probing depth — doesn't account for recession. Why D is wrong: 2mm is just the recession measurement. Why E is wrong: 10mm would be 5\u00d72, which has no clinical basis.

Q91 During the re-evaluation phase (4–6 weeks after scaling), which of the following should NOT be performed?
A. Evaluating the effectiveness of procedures already completed
B. Evaluating patient compliance with oral hygiene instructions
C. Assessing esthetic requirements and planning cosmetic procedures
D. Re-probing to assess tissue response
E. Determining if additional treatment phases are needed
Correct Answer: C
A. Evaluating the effectiveness of procedures already completed
B. Evaluating patient compliance with oral hygiene instructions
C. Assessing esthetic requirements and planning cosmetic procedures
D. Re-probing to assess tissue response
E. Determining if additional treatment phases are needed

During re-evaluation at 4–6 weeks post-scaling, you evaluate what you DID (was SRP effective?), assess patient compliance (are they brushing and flossing?), re-probe to check tissue response, and determine next steps. Esthetic requirements and cosmetic procedures are NOT part of the re-evaluation phase — those belong in later treatment phases after disease is controlled. You don't plan cosmetic work while you're still assessing whether the foundational therapy (Phase I) was successful. First control disease, then worry about aesthetics.

Why A is wrong: Evaluating completed procedures IS a core re-evaluation activity. Why B is wrong: Assessing patient compliance IS essential during re-evaluation. Why D is wrong: Re-probing IS the primary clinical activity at re-evaluation. Why E is wrong: Determining additional treatment needs IS the purpose of re-evaluation.

Q92 What is the primary goal of maintenance therapy (supportive periodontal therapy)?
A. To perform additional surgery
B. To prevent recurrence of periodontal disease
C. To evaluate the results of all procedures done
D. To complete any remaining restorative work
E. To taper the patient off chlorhexidine rinse
Correct Answer: B
A. To perform additional surgery
B. To prevent recurrence of periodontal disease
C. To evaluate the results of all procedures done
D. To complete any remaining restorative work
E. To taper the patient off chlorhexidine rinse

The primary goal of maintenance therapy (SPT) is to prevent recurrence of periodontal disease. Once active treatment is complete and disease is controlled, maintenance visits (typically every 3–4 months) are designed to keep the disease from coming back. SPT includes professional debridement, reinforcement of oral hygiene, monitoring for disease recurrence, and managing any new or recurring sites. Your slides on SPT emphasize that periodontal disease is chronic and requires lifelong management — the battle is never truly "won," only controlled.

Why A is wrong: Surgery is part of active treatment phases, not maintenance. Why C is wrong: Evaluating results is part of re-evaluation, which occurs before maintenance begins. Why D is wrong: Restorative work is a separate treatment phase. Why E is wrong: CHX management isn't the goal of SPT.

Q93 When can you probe an area that was scaled and root planed without encountering immature (healing) fibers?
A. 3 weeks
B. 5 weeks
C. 8 weeks (2 months) for moderate to severe cases
D. 12 weeks for mild to moderate cases
E. Both C and D are correct depending on severity
Correct Answer: E
A. 3 weeks
B. 5 weeks
C. 8 weeks (2 months) for moderate to severe cases
D. 12 weeks for mild to moderate cases
E. Both C and D are correct depending on severity

The timing depends on disease severity. For mild-to-moderate cases, you can safely re-probe at about 12 weeks (3 months) without disrupting immature fibers. For moderate-to-severe cases, healing takes longer and 8 weeks (2 months) may be the minimum, though many clinicians wait the full 12 weeks. Your laser lecture slides (Dr. Ahn) also noted that you "should not re-probe before 3 months post therapy because healing in sulcus begins at bottom of pocket which can be damaged by probe" and recommended "probing with light touch at 3 months." The general principle: don't probe too early or you'll tear apart the healing connective tissue attachment.

Why A is wrong: 3 weeks is far too early — fibers are still immature. Why B is wrong: 5 weeks is still within the active healing window for most cases. Why C alone is incomplete: 8 weeks applies to some cases but not all. Why D alone is incomplete: 12 weeks applies to milder cases but the question asks about both scenarios.

Q94 A patient with severe periodontitis would most likely be scheduled for re-evaluation at what time interval after initial therapy?
A. 1–2 days
B. 2–4 weeks
C. 6–8 weeks
D. 3–4 months
E. 6 months
Correct Answer: C
A. 1–2 days
B. 2–4 weeks
C. 6–8 weeks
D. 3–4 months
E. 6 months

For severe periodontitis, re-evaluation is typically scheduled at 6–8 weeks after initial therapy (SRP). This gives enough time for significant tissue healing — soft tissue maturation, reduction of inflammation, pocket depth reduction — while not waiting so long that disease progression goes unmonitored. Mild cases might be re-evaluated at 4–6 weeks, but severe cases need the extra healing time because there was more tissue destruction and a greater inflammatory burden to resolve. At re-evaluation, you re-probe, reassess, and determine if surgical intervention is needed.

Why A is wrong: 1–2 days is way too early for any meaningful healing to have occurred. Why B is wrong: 2–4 weeks is too early for severe cases — tissue is still actively healing. Why D is wrong: 3–4 months is the maintenance/SPT interval, not the re-evaluation window. Why E is wrong: 6 months is far too long to wait before assessing treatment response.

Q95 Probing depth measurements are affected by which of the following?
A. The force applied by the clinician
B. Age and gender of the patient
C. The degree of inflammation in the tissues
D. Both A and C
E. A, B, and C
Correct Answer: D
A. The force applied by the clinician
B. Age and gender of the patient
C. The degree of inflammation in the tissues
D. Both A and C
E. A, B, and C

Probing depth is affected by both the force applied and the degree of tissue inflammation. Higher probing force = deeper readings (the probe pushes farther into inflamed, weakened tissue). Inflamed tissue is more permeable — the probe tip can penetrate through the junctional epithelium into the connective tissue, overestimating the true pocket depth. In healthy tissue, the probe stops at the base of the sulcus/junctional epithelium. This is why standardized probing force (~25g, about the weight of a nickel) is important. Age and gender do NOT directly affect probing depth measurements — they may affect disease prevalence but not the measurement itself.

Why A alone is incomplete: Force matters but so does inflammation. Why B is wrong: Age and gender don't directly affect probe penetration. Why C alone is incomplete: Inflammation matters but so does force. Why E is wrong: Age and gender are not factors that affect the probing measurement itself.

Q96 What is the primary goal of scaling and root planing (SRP)?
A. Eliminate all pathogenic bacteria from the oral cavity
B. Eliminate all spirochetes
C. Alter the subgingival plaque composition to a health-compatible biofilm
D. Eliminate the dental pellicle
E. Sterilize the root surface
Correct Answer: C
A. Eliminate all pathogenic bacteria from the oral cavity
B. Eliminate all spirochetes
C. Alter the subgingival plaque composition to a health-compatible biofilm
D. Eliminate the dental pellicle
E. Sterilize the root surface

The primary goal of SRP is to alter the plaque composition — shifting the subgingival microbiome from a pathogenic, anaerobic, gram-negative dominated biofilm to a health-compatible, aerobic, gram-positive dominated one. You CANNOT eliminate all pathogenic bacteria (choice A) — that's impossible. You CANNOT sterilize the root surface (choice E) — recolonization begins within hours. What you CAN do is mechanically disrupt the biofilm, remove calculus (the bacterial reservoir), and create an environment that favors recolonization by health-associated organisms rather than pathogens.

Why A is wrong: Complete elimination of all pathogens is biologically impossible. Why B is wrong: Targeting only spirochetes is too narrow — you want to shift the entire ecology. Why D is wrong: Pellicle is an acellular protein film that reforms immediately — removing it isn't the goal. Why E is wrong: Sterilization is impossible in the oral environment.

Q134 Regarding SRP (scaling and root planing), which of the following statements is CORRECT?
A. SRP can be performed without anesthesia if the patient has a high pain threshold
B. SRP should never be started if the patient has not demonstrated adequate plaque removal; the goals are both technical (calculus-free surfaces) and biological (reducing bacterial load); root planing continues until a smooth, glassy surface is achieved
C. SRP only needs to remove supragingival calculus
D. SRP goals are limited to removing visible calculus — root surface smoothness is not important
E. SRP can be performed before oral hygiene instruction
Correct Answer: B
A. SRP can be performed without anesthesia if the patient has a high pain threshold
B. SRP should never be started if the patient has not demonstrated adequate plaque removal; the goals are both technical (calculus-free surfaces) and biological (reducing bacterial load); root planing continues until a smooth, glassy surface is achieved
C. SRP only needs to remove supragingival calculus
D. SRP goals are limited to removing visible calculus — root surface smoothness is not important
E. SRP can be performed before oral hygiene instruction

Your notes hit several SRP principles: "All SRP needs anesthesia" (it's a surgical procedure involving instrumentation below the gingival margin). "Never start sx if there is no adequate plaque removal" — Phase I OHI must come first. "SRP goals: technical, free of calculus; biological, taking the bacteria low, killing them." "We root planing until we get a smooth glassy surface." And the pocket contains "bacteria, calculus, endotoxins" — all of which must be addressed. The smooth, glassy surface after root planing removes endotoxin-contaminated cementum and creates a biocompatible surface for connective tissue reattachment.

Why A is wrong: Your notes explicitly state ALL SRP needs anesthesia. Why C is wrong: SRP specifically targets SUBgingival calculus and root deposits. Why D is wrong: Root surface smoothness IS a critical endpoint — you plane until smooth and glassy. Why E is wrong: OHI and plaque control must be established BEFORE SRP.

Q135 A patient has undergone multiple episodes of SRP with no improvement. Which of the following statements is MOST accurate?
A. Continue with additional rounds of SRP until improvement is seen
B. Multiple episodes of SRP without improvement indicates non-surgical therapy is ineffective and surgical intervention should be considered
C. Switch to a different curette type and repeat SRP
D. Increase the interval between SRP sessions to allow more healing time
E. Add systemic antibiotics and repeat SRP indefinitely
Correct Answer: B
A. Continue with additional rounds of SRP until improvement is seen
B. Multiple episodes of SRP without improvement indicates non-surgical therapy is ineffective and surgical intervention should be considered
C. Switch to a different curette type and repeat SRP
D. Increase the interval between SRP sessions to allow more healing time
E. Add systemic antibiotics and repeat SRP indefinitely

If repeated rounds of SRP aren't working, continuing to do the same thing won't change the outcome. This is when you transition to surgical therapy — open flap debridement, osseous surgery, or regenerative procedures — to gain direct access to root surfaces and bony defects that closed instrumentation can't reach. Remember from earlier: SRP has a maximum effective depth of about 6.2mm, and 60% of furcation entrances are narrower than the Gracey blade. Some defects simply can't be resolved non-surgically.

Why A is wrong: Repeating an ineffective treatment is the definition of insanity in clinical practice. Why C is wrong: Changing instrument type won't overcome anatomic limitations. Why D is wrong: Spacing out sessions won't improve access to deep defects. Why E is wrong: Antibiotics are adjunctive, not a substitute for surgical access when SRP fails.

Q141 What is the probing depth at which calculus and plaque can be 100% efficiently removed with hand instrumentation?
A. 1.5mm
B. 2.5mm
C. 3.7mm
D. 5.0mm
E. 6.2mm
Correct Answer: C
A. 1.5mm
B. 2.5mm
C. 3.7mm
D. 5.0mm
E. 6.2mm

At 3.7mm probing depth, calculus and plaque can be removed with 100% efficiency using hand instruments. Beyond this depth, efficiency drops progressively — by 6.2mm you've reached the absolute maximum depth that SRP can physically access (as covered in Q72). This number helps explain why non-surgical therapy alone works beautifully for shallow-to-moderate pockets but becomes increasingly inadequate for deep pockets. It's also why surgical access (flap elevation) dramatically improves debridement efficiency in deeper defects.

Why A is wrong: 1.5mm is well within easy access — not the threshold. Why B is wrong: 2.5mm is still very manageable. Why D is wrong: At 5mm, efficiency has already dropped below 100%. Why E is wrong: 6.2mm is the absolute maximum reach, not the 100% efficiency point.

Q146 At what probing depth is surgical therapy MOST effective compared to non-surgical therapy (SRP)?
A. 1–3mm
B. 3–4mm
C. 5–6mm
D. 7–8mm
E. Surgery is never more effective than SRP
Correct Answer: C
A. 1–3mm
B. 3–4mm
C. 5–6mm
D. 7–8mm
E. Surgery is never more effective than SRP

Surgical therapy is most effective at 5–6mm probing depth compared to non-surgical therapy. At shallower depths (1–4mm), SRP alone is generally sufficient and surgery offers no significant advantage. At 5–6mm, you hit the "sweet spot" where surgical access provides substantially better debridement outcomes than closed instrumentation. Remember: SRP is 100% efficient at 3.7mm and maxes out at 6.2mm — so the 5–6mm range is exactly where surgical access starts to dramatically outperform closed scaling.

Why A is wrong: At 1–3mm, SRP is fully adequate — surgery is unnecessary and may even cause attachment loss. Why B is wrong: At 3–4mm, SRP still handles the job. Why D is wrong: 7–8mm benefits from surgery but 5–6mm is the range where the RELATIVE advantage over non-surgical is most demonstrated. Why E is wrong: Surgery IS more effective at appropriate depths.

Q147 After initial SRP, which finding most reliably indicates that the periodontal condition will NOT improve with continued non-surgical therapy?
A. Bleeding on probing at 3mm sites
B. Patient reports sensitivity to cold
C. Residual probing depth greater than 6mm
D. Mild gingival redness at 4mm sites
E. Slight tooth mobility (Grade 1)
Correct Answer: C
A. Bleeding on probing at 3mm sites
B. Patient reports sensitivity to cold
C. Residual probing depth greater than 6mm
D. Mild gingival redness at 4mm sites
E. Slight tooth mobility (Grade 1)

Probing depth ≥6mm after SRP is the red flag that tells you the problem won't resolve non-surgically. Your notes state this directly: "After initial therapy, what makes it likely that there is no improvement/attachment loss? — probing depth > 6mm." At these depths, you've exceeded the effective reach of hand instruments (max 6.2mm), and the persistent pocket depth means the environment remains favorable for anaerobic pathogen recolonization. These sites need surgical intervention — open flap debridement at minimum.

Why A is wrong: BOP at 3mm sites may just indicate residual gingivitis that can resolve. Why B is wrong: Sensitivity is common after SRP and isn't a prognostic indicator. Why D is wrong: Mild redness at 4mm may resolve with continued healing. Why E is wrong: Grade 1 mobility alone doesn't indicate failure of non-surgical therapy.

Q148 When a tooth has both endodontic and periodontal pathology, which treatment should be performed FIRST?
A. Periodontal therapy first, then endodontic therapy
B. Both simultaneously
C. Endodontic (pulp) treatment first, then periodontal therapy
D. Neither — extract the tooth
E. Periodontal therapy only — the endo problem will resolve
Correct Answer: C
A. Periodontal therapy first, then endodontic therapy
B. Both simultaneously
C. Endodontic (pulp) treatment first, then periodontal therapy
D. Neither — extract the tooth
E. Periodontal therapy only — the endo problem will resolve

Pulp treatment comes first. Your notes state: "Do pulp treatment first and then perio." The rationale is that the infected pulp may be contributing to the periodontal breakdown via accessory canals (especially in the furcation area) and the apical foramen. By treating the endo first, you eliminate the endodontic contribution to the periodontal lesion, which may allow partial resolution of the perio component. If you did perio first, the ongoing endo infection would continue to undermine healing.

Why A is wrong: Perio first doesn't address the ongoing endo infection. Why B is wrong: While possible in some cases, the standard teaching is endo first. Why D is wrong: Combined endo-perio lesions aren't automatic extractions if both can be treated. Why E is wrong: The endo problem will NOT resolve spontaneously from perio therapy alone.

Q150 What is PerioChip, what does it contain, and what is the primary contraindication?
A. Resorbable chip containing 2.5mg doxycycline; contraindicated in renal failure
B. Resorbable chip containing 2.5mg chlorhexidine gluconate; contraindicated in patients with sensitivity to chlorhexidine
C. Non-resorbable chip containing metronidazole; contraindicated in pregnancy
D. Resorbable chip containing minocycline; contraindicated in liver damage
E. Non-resorbable chip requiring surgical removal; no contraindications
Correct Answer: B
A. Resorbable chip containing 2.5mg doxycycline; contraindicated in renal failure
B. Resorbable chip containing 2.5mg chlorhexidine gluconate; contraindicated in patients with sensitivity to chlorhexidine
C. Non-resorbable chip containing metronidazole; contraindicated in pregnancy
D. Resorbable chip containing minocycline; contraindicated in liver damage
E. Non-resorbable chip requiring surgical removal; no contraindications

PerioChip contains 2.5mg of chlorhexidine gluconate in a resorbable gelatin matrix that's placed directly into the periodontal pocket for sustained local delivery. The contraindication is sensitivity/allergy to chlorhexidine. Your notes specifically clarify: "PerioChip should not be used in any patient w/ sensitivity to chlorhexidine" and note that the exam answer was "none of the above" when liver damage was listed (liver damage is NOT a contraindication for PerioChip).

Why A is wrong: PerioChip contains CHX, not doxycycline, and renal failure isn't the contraindication. Why C is wrong: It's resorbable and contains CHX, not metronidazole. Why D is wrong: Contains CHX, not minocycline, and liver damage is NOT the contraindication (your notes confirm this was a wrong answer on a prior exam). Why E is wrong: It IS resorbable and DOES have a contraindication.

Q151 What is the sub-antimicrobial dose of doxycycline used in Periostat, and how is it dosed?
A. 50mg once daily
B. 100mg twice daily
C. 20mg twice daily (bid)
D. 10mg three times daily
E. 200mg loading dose then 100mg daily
Correct Answer: C
A. 50mg once daily
B. 100mg twice daily
C. 20mg twice daily (bid)
D. 10mg three times daily
E. 200mg loading dose then 100mg daily

Periostat is doxycycline at 20mg bid (twice daily). This is a SUB-antimicrobial dose — meaning it's below the concentration needed to kill bacteria. At this dose, doxycycline acts as a host modulation agent by inhibiting matrix metalloproteinases (collagenase), thereby reducing connective tissue destruction. It doesn't target bacteria directly at this dose. It's used as an adjunct to SRP to reduce the host's destructive inflammatory response — the doxycycline + SRP combination increases the treatment effect beyond SRP alone.

Why A is wrong: 50mg is not the Periostat dose. Why B is wrong: 100mg bid is the ANTIMICROBIAL dose for infections, not the sub-antimicrobial host-modulation dose. Why D is wrong: 10mg tid isn't a recognized dosing regimen. Why E is wrong: That's the loading dose regimen for acute infections, not for Periostat.

Q155 What is Arrestin, and what is its active agent and delivery form?
A. Chlorhexidine in a gel form
B. Doxycycline in a polymer matrix
C. Minocycline hydrochloride in microspheres
D. Tetracycline in a fiber form
E. Metronidazole in a chip form
Correct Answer: C
A. Chlorhexidine in a gel form
B. Doxycycline in a polymer matrix
C. Minocycline hydrochloride in microspheres
D. Tetracycline in a fiber form
E. Metronidazole in a chip form

Arrestin (Arestin) contains minocycline hydrochloride delivered in microsphere form. The microspheres are placed directly into periodontal pockets after SRP for sustained local antibiotic delivery. The maximum duration of Arestin is 14 days — after that, the microspheres have fully dissolved and released their antibiotic content. This is different from PerioChip (CHX gluconate chip), Atridox (42mg doxycycline in a polymer gel), and Periostat (20mg doxycycline systemic).

Why A is wrong: That would describe PerioChip's CHX, and it's not a gel. Why B is wrong: Doxycycline polymer is Atridox, not Arrestin. Why D is wrong: Tetracycline fiber (Actisite) is an older product, not Arrestin. Why E is wrong: Metronidazole chip isn't Arrestin.

Q185 What is Atridox, and what does it contain?
A. 2.5mg chlorhexidine gluconate in a chip
B. 42mg doxycycline hyclate in a resorbable polymer gel
C. Minocycline microspheres
D. 20mg doxycycline tablets for systemic use
E. Metronidazole in a fiber delivery system
Correct Answer: B
A. 2.5mg chlorhexidine gluconate in a chip
B. 42mg doxycycline hyclate in a resorbable polymer gel
C. Minocycline microspheres
D. 20mg doxycycline tablets for systemic use
E. Metronidazole in a fiber delivery system

Atridox contains 42mg of doxycycline hyclate in a resorbable polymer gel (liquid syringe delivery) that's placed directly into periodontal pockets. The polymer solidifies upon contact with crevicular fluid, forming a sustained-release matrix. Important: Atridox should NOT be used in children or nursing women. This is different from Periostat (20mg doxycycline tablets taken systemically), PerioChip (2.5mg CHX chip), and Arestin (minocycline microspheres).

Why A is wrong: That's PerioChip. Why C is wrong: That's Arestin. Why D is wrong: That's Periostat (systemic sub-antimicrobial dose doxycycline). Why E is wrong: Metronidazole fiber isn't Atridox.

Q193 How does root planing specifically differ from scaling in terms of what is being removed?
A. Root planing removes calculus from root surfaces; scaling removes plaque from crowns only
B. Root planing removes diseased cementum and endotoxins to create a smooth root surface — it has nothing to do with calculus; scaling removes soft and hard deposits (plaque and calculus) from both crown and root
C. Root planing and scaling are identical procedures with no difference
D. Root planing removes dentin; scaling removes enamel
E. Root planing is performed only supragingivally; scaling is performed subgingivally
Correct Answer: B
A. Root planing removes calculus from root surfaces; scaling removes plaque from crowns only
B. Root planing removes diseased cementum and endotoxins to create a smooth root surface — it has nothing to do with calculus; scaling removes soft and hard deposits (plaque and calculus) from both crown and root
C. Root planing and scaling are identical procedures with no difference
D. Root planing removes dentin; scaling removes enamel
E. Root planing is performed only supragingivally; scaling is performed subgingivally

This is a critical distinction from the essay material: root planing is the removal of diseased root surfaces (contaminated cementum containing endotoxins) to create a smooth, noncontaminated surface — it has NOTHING to do with calculus. Scaling is the removal of soft and hard deposits (plaque and tartar) adhering to the tooth surface, from both crown and root. Think of it this way: scaling deals with what's ON the tooth, root planing deals with the tooth SURFACE itself. You scale off the deposits, then you plane the diseased cementum underneath.

Why A is wrong: Scaling removes deposits from both crown AND root, not just crowns. Why C is wrong: They are distinctly different procedures. Why D is wrong: Root planing removes cementum, not dentin (ideally). Why E is wrong: Both can be performed subgingivally.

Q194 According to Harper and Robinson (1987), SRP reduces motile microbes and spirochetes for what duration, and according to Caffesse et al. (1986), what percentage of the time do clinicians fail to adequately debride root surfaces?
A. SRP eliminates all bacteria permanently; clinicians succeed 90% of the time
B. SRP reduces motile microbes and spirochetes for a limited period of time; clinicians fail to adequately debride 65% of the time
C. SRP has no effect on microbial composition; clinicians fail 25% of the time
D. SRP eliminates anaerobes for 6 months; clinicians fail 10% of the time
E. SRP only affects aerobic bacteria; clinicians fail 50% of the time
Correct Answer: B
A. SRP eliminates all bacteria permanently; clinicians succeed 90% of the time
B. SRP reduces motile microbes and spirochetes for a limited period of time; clinicians fail to adequately debride 65% of the time
C. SRP has no effect on microbial composition; clinicians fail 25% of the time
D. SRP eliminates anaerobes for 6 months; clinicians fail 10% of the time
E. SRP only affects aerobic bacteria; clinicians fail 50% of the time

Harper & Robinson (1987) showed that SRP reduces motile microbes and spirochetes for a LIMITED period — meaning bacterial recolonization occurs, which is why maintenance every 3 months is essential. Caffesse et al. (1986) demonstrated that clinicians fail to adequately debride root surfaces 65% of the time — a staggering number that reinforces why (1) surgical access is sometimes necessary for complete debridement, and (2) adjunctive antimicrobials (Arestin, Atridox, systemic antibiotics) have a legitimate role in enhancing bacterial elimination beyond what SRP alone achieves.

Why A is wrong: SRP does NOT permanently eliminate bacteria, and 90% success is too optimistic. Why C is wrong: SRP absolutely affects microbial composition. Why D is wrong: The reduction isn't limited to anaerobes only, and the time frame isn't specified as 6 months. Why E is wrong: SRP affects the entire subgingival biofilm, not just aerobes.

Q195 What clinical outcomes indicate that NON-SURGICAL periodontal therapy has been successful?
A. Increased probing depths and continued bleeding on probing
B. Decreased probing depths with "a gain" in clinical attachment, decreased gingival inflammation, and decreased bleeding on probing
C. Tooth extraction and implant placement
D. Complete regeneration of lost alveolar bone
E. Elimination of all bacteria from the oral cavity
Correct Answer: B
A. Increased probing depths and continued bleeding on probing
B. Decreased probing depths with "a gain" in clinical attachment, decreased gingival inflammation, and decreased bleeding on probing
C. Tooth extraction and implant placement
D. Complete regeneration of lost alveolar bone
E. Elimination of all bacteria from the oral cavity

Successful non-surgical therapy produces: (1) decreased probing depths, (2) a "gain" in clinical attachment (the key metric — means the JE has moved coronally and/or the pocket has shrunk), (3) decreased gingival inflammation, and (4) decreased bleeding on probing. Notice what's NOT listed: bone regeneration. Non-surgical therapy reduces soft tissue inflammation and probing depths but doesn't predictably regenerate bone — that requires surgical/regenerative approaches. The "gain" in clinical attachment from SRP comes primarily from resolution of inflammation (tissue shrinkage) and reattachment of the junctional epithelium, not from true new connective tissue attachment.

Why A is wrong: These are signs of treatment FAILURE, not success. Why C is wrong: Extraction isn't a success metric for non-surgical therapy. Why D is wrong: Non-surgical therapy doesn't produce complete bone regeneration. Why E is wrong: Complete bacterial elimination is biologically impossible.

Q196 What ADDITIONAL outcomes does successful SURGICAL periodontal therapy achieve beyond what non-surgical therapy provides?
A. No additional outcomes — surgical and non-surgical produce identical results
B. Restoration of physiologic gingival and osseous contours, plus the potential for reattachment and regeneration
C. Only improved esthetics, no clinical benefit
D. Permanent elimination of all periodontal pockets
E. Reversal of systemic disease effects
Correct Answer: B
A. No additional outcomes — surgical and non-surgical produce identical results
B. Restoration of physiologic gingival and osseous contours, plus the potential for reattachment and regeneration
C. Only improved esthetics, no clinical benefit
D. Permanent elimination of all periodontal pockets
E. Reversal of systemic disease effects

Surgical therapy achieves everything non-surgical therapy does (decreased probing depths, attachment gain, decreased inflammation/BOP) PLUS two additional outcomes: (1) restoration of physiologic gingival and osseous contours — through resective osseous surgery you can re-establish positive architecture and eliminate reverse architecture, and (2) the potential for reattachment and regeneration — through GTR/bone grafting, you can potentially achieve true new attachment (new cementum, PDL, bone) rather than just repair. These additional outcomes are only achievable through surgical access and regenerative techniques.

Why A is wrong: Surgery achieves additional outcomes beyond non-surgical therapy. Why C is wrong: The benefits are functional and regenerative, not just esthetic. Why D is wrong: "Permanent" elimination is unrealistic — maintenance is always needed. Why E is wrong: Surgery doesn't reverse systemic disease.

Q197 What assumptions are clinicians making when they decide that periodontal treatment is indicated?
A. Only that the patient has insurance coverage
B. That the disease is currently active and will progress without intervention; that treatment will help and not worsen things; and that the patient will be compliant with oral hygiene
C. That all teeth will survive regardless of treatment
D. That surgery is always necessary
E. That the patient's age determines treatment need
Correct Answer: B
A. Only that the patient has insurance coverage
B. That the disease is currently active and will progress without intervention; that treatment will help and not worsen things; and that the patient will be compliant with oral hygiene
C. That all teeth will survive regardless of treatment
D. That surgery is always necessary
E. That the patient's age determines treatment need

Three critical assumptions from the essay material: (1) The disease is currently active and without intervention, it WILL progress — this is the fundamental justification for intervening rather than watching. (2) Treatment will help the patient and not worsen things — we assume the benefits outweigh the risks (remember: SRP at shallow sites can actually cause attachment loss). (3) The patient will be compliant and keep up oral hygiene — if the patient won't brush, the most brilliant surgery is pointless because disease will recur. These assumptions should be explicitly considered for every treatment plan.

Why A is wrong: Insurance isn't a clinical assumption for treatment indication. Why C is wrong: Not all teeth will survive — prognosis varies. Why D is wrong: Surgery is not always necessary — many cases resolve with SRP alone. Why E is wrong: Age doesn't determine treatment need (as established in the chronic perio/age discussion).

OCCLUSAL TRAUMA (12)
Q142 What is the major purpose of splinting teeth in periodontal treatment?
A. To regenerate bone around mobile teeth
B. To permanently fix teeth in place for esthetics
C. For patient comfort and to dissipate occlusal forces across multiple teeth
D. To eliminate periodontal pockets
E. To replace missing teeth like a fixed partial denture
Correct Answer: C
A. To regenerate bone around mobile teeth
B. To permanently fix teeth in place for esthetics
C. For patient comfort and to dissipate occlusal forces across multiple teeth
D. To eliminate periodontal pockets
E. To replace missing teeth like a fixed partial denture

Splinting serves two purposes: (1) patient comfort — mobile teeth are uncomfortable to function on, and splinting eliminates that discomfort, and (2) dissipating occlusal forces across multiple teeth — by connecting mobile teeth to more stable adjacent teeth, the occlusal load is distributed over a larger root surface area, reducing the force per tooth. Splinting does NOT regenerate bone or cure periodontal disease — it's a supportive measure that manages the consequences of attachment loss (mobility) while definitive treatment addresses the underlying disease.

Why A is wrong: Splinting doesn't regenerate bone — it's a mechanical support. Why B is wrong: The primary purpose is functional, not esthetic. Why D is wrong: Splinting has no effect on pocket depth. Why E is wrong: Splinting stabilizes existing teeth, it doesn't replace missing ones.

Q164 Which of the following statements about occlusal trauma is CORRECT?
A. Occlusal trauma causes progressive attachment loss and deepening of periodontal pockets
B. Occlusal trauma causes mobility and changes in bone density but does NOT cause progressive attachment loss
C. Occlusal trauma causes gingival recession
D. Occlusal trauma causes apical migration of the junctional epithelium
E. Occlusal trauma is the primary cause of periodontitis
Correct Answer: B
A. Occlusal trauma causes progressive attachment loss and deepening of periodontal pockets
B. Occlusal trauma causes mobility and changes in bone density but does NOT cause progressive attachment loss
C. Occlusal trauma causes gingival recession
D. Occlusal trauma causes apical migration of the junctional epithelium
E. Occlusal trauma is the primary cause of periodontitis

Your notes are clear: "Occlusal trauma does NOT cause progressive attachment loss. (It causes mobility)" and separately "Occlusal trauma causes: change in bone density." Occlusal trauma can widen the PDL space (visible radiographically as a widened PDL), cause mobility, change trabecular bone patterns, and even cause angular/vertical bone defects — but it does NOT by itself cause the apical migration of junctional epithelium that defines true periodontal attachment loss. Attachment loss requires bacterial infection. Occlusal trauma can WORSEN existing periodontitis (secondary occlusal trauma) but cannot initiate it.

Why A is wrong: Occlusal trauma does NOT cause progressive attachment loss — this is the key point. Why C is wrong: Recession is caused by toothbrushing and plaque-induced inflammation, not occlusal trauma per se. Why D is wrong: JE migration requires bacterial inflammation, not mechanical force. Why E is wrong: Bacteria cause periodontitis, not occlusal forces.

Q165 "Functional loading" of a dental implant results in:
A. Bone loss around the implant
B. Implant mobility
C. Increased bone-implant interface (improved osseointegration)
D. Peri-implantitis
E. No change in the bone-implant relationship
Correct Answer: C
A. Bone loss around the implant
B. Implant mobility
C. Increased bone-implant interface (improved osseointegration)
D. Peri-implantitis
E. No change in the bone-implant relationship

Functional loading of an implant causes increased bone-implant interface — meaning the bone around a loaded implant becomes denser and more intimately connected to the implant surface. This is Wolff's Law applied to implant dentistry: bone responds to functional stress by becoming stronger. Controlled occlusal loading stimulates bone remodeling that improves osseointegration over time. This is the opposite of what EXCESSIVE/traumatic loading does (which can cause peri-implant bone loss). The key word is "functional" — meaning physiologic, within normal limits.

Why A is wrong: Functional (physiologic) loading strengthens bone — only EXCESSIVE loading causes loss. Why B is wrong: A properly loaded, osseointegrated implant should not be mobile. Why D is wrong: Functional loading doesn't cause peri-implantitis. Why E is wrong: Loading absolutely changes the bone-implant interface — positively.

Q181 What is the limit of NORMAL physiological tooth mobility, and what are the mobility grades?
A. Normal = 0.5mm or less; Grade 1 = 0.5–1.0mm; Grade 2 = 1.0–2.0mm; Grade 3 = >2.0mm
B. Normal = 0.2mm or less; Grade 1 = 0.2–1.0mm; Grade 2 = 1.0–2.0mm; Grade 3 = >2.0mm
C. Normal = 0mm (no movement); Grade 1 = any detectable movement; Grade 2 = 1mm; Grade 3 = 2mm+
D. Normal = 1.0mm or less; Grade 1 = 1.0–2.0mm; Grade 2 = 2.0–3.0mm; Grade 3 = >3.0mm
E. There is no normal physiological mobility — any movement is pathological
Correct Answer: B
A. Normal = 0.5mm or less; Grade 1 = 0.5–1.0mm; Grade 2 = 1.0–2.0mm; Grade 3 = >2.0mm
B. Normal = 0.2mm or less; Grade 1 = 0.2–1.0mm; Grade 2 = 1.0–2.0mm; Grade 3 = >2.0mm
C. Normal = 0mm (no movement); Grade 1 = any detectable movement; Grade 2 = 1mm; Grade 3 = 2mm+
D. Normal = 1.0mm or less; Grade 1 = 1.0–2.0mm; Grade 2 = 2.0–3.0mm; Grade 3 = >3.0mm
E. There is no normal physiological mobility — any movement is pathological

Normal physiological mobility is 0.2mm or less. Your notes lay out the grading: Physiologic = 0.2mm or less. Grade 1 = 0.2–1.0mm. Grade 2 = 1.0–2.0mm. Grade 3 = >2.0mm (often with vertical depressibility). ALL teeth have some degree of physiologic mobility due to the PDL acting as a shock absorber — 0.2mm of movement is completely normal. Only when mobility exceeds this threshold does it become clinically significant.

Why A is wrong: 0.5mm is already into Grade 1 territory, not normal. Why C is wrong: Zero mobility is impossible — all teeth move slightly. Why D is wrong: 1.0mm is NOT normal — that's clearly pathological. Why E is wrong: Physiological mobility absolutely exists and is normal.

Q182 What are the radiographic signs supporting a diagnosis of occlusal trauma?
A. Horizontal bone loss only
B. Widened PDL space, loss of lamina dura, angular osseous defects, root resorption, and altered trabecular pattern
C. Periapical radiolucency only
D. External root resorption only
E. No radiographic changes are ever associated with occlusal trauma
Correct Answer: B
A. Horizontal bone loss only
B. Widened PDL space, loss of lamina dura, angular osseous defects, root resorption, and altered trabecular pattern
C. Periapical radiolucency only
D. External root resorption only
E. No radiographic changes are ever associated with occlusal trauma

The radiographic signs of occlusal trauma are: (1) widened PDL space, (2) loss of lamina dura, (3) angular osseous defects, (4) root resorption, and (5) altered trabecular pattern. Plus clinical signs include increasing mobility and wear facets/crazing. The widened PDL is the most classic finding — the bone remodels to accommodate excessive forces, creating a wider space around the root. Loss of lamina dura indicates the compact bone lining the socket is being resorbed. Angular defects occur because forces are distributed unevenly.

Why A is wrong: Horizontal bone loss is associated with periodontitis, not specifically occlusal trauma. Why C is wrong: Periapical radiolucency is an endodontic finding. Why D is wrong: Root resorption is only ONE of the multiple signs. Why E is wrong: Occlusal trauma absolutely produces radiographic changes.

Q183 What is fremitus?
A. The sound produced when a tooth is percussed
B. Tooth movement detected by the patient's own occlusal forces (functional movement)
C. The degree of calculus accumulation on a tooth
D. Vibration of the tongue during speech
E. Bleeding from the interdental papilla
Correct Answer: B
A. The sound produced when a tooth is percussed
B. Tooth movement detected by the patient's own occlusal forces (functional movement)
C. The degree of calculus accumulation on a tooth
D. Vibration of the tongue during speech
E. Bleeding from the interdental papilla

Fremitus is tooth movement detected when the patient applies their OWN functional occlusal forces — you feel the tooth vibrate or move when the patient taps or grinds their teeth together. It's checked by placing a finger on the buccal surface of each tooth while the patient opens and closes, slides laterally, and protrudes. Fremitus is a clinical sign of occlusal trauma — it tells you that tooth is receiving excessive forces during function. It's different from mobility testing (where the CLINICIAN applies force with instruments).

Why A is wrong: That describes percussion testing. Why C is wrong: Calculus accumulation is unrelated to fremitus. Why D is wrong: Tongue vibration isn't a periodontal finding. Why E is wrong: Papillary bleeding is a sign of inflammation, not fremitus.

Q212 What is trauma from occlusion?
A. A reversible gingival condition caused by bacterial plaque
B. A pathologic lesion in the attachment apparatus established by excessive or abnormal biting forces that exceed the adaptive capacity of the tissues
C. Tooth fracture from traumatic injury
D. Damage to the oral mucosa from orthodontic appliances
E. Carious lesions caused by acid erosion
Correct Answer: B
A. A reversible gingival condition caused by bacterial plaque
B. A pathologic lesion in the attachment apparatus established by excessive or abnormal biting forces that exceed the adaptive capacity of the tissues
C. Tooth fracture from traumatic injury
D. Damage to the oral mucosa from orthodontic appliances
E. Carious lesions caused by acid erosion

The precise definition from the essay material: "A pathologic lesion in the attachment apparatus established by excessive or abnormal biting forces that exceed the adaptive capacity of the tissues." Key elements: (1) it's a PATHOLOGIC LESION (not just force — it must produce tissue damage), (2) it occurs in the ATTACHMENT APPARATUS (cementum, PDL, bone — NOT the gingiva), (3) it's caused by forces that EXCEED the adaptive capacity (below the adaptive threshold, the PDL can accommodate the forces; above it, damage occurs). This definition is critical for understanding why occlusal trauma doesn't cause gingival recession or attachment loss.

Why A is wrong: Occlusal trauma isn't caused by plaque and doesn't affect gingiva. Why C is wrong: Tooth fracture is a structural failure, not occlusal trauma in the periodontal sense. Why D is wrong: Mucosal damage from appliances isn't occlusal trauma. Why E is wrong: Caries is a completely different disease process.

Q213 How do you clinically and radiographically diagnose PRIMARY versus SECONDARY occlusal trauma?
A. Both present identically and cannot be distinguished
B. Primary: increasing mobility, migration, fremitus on a tooth with normal periodontal support; radiographically shows widened PDL and possible angular bone loss. Secondary: attachment loss is ALREADY present with bone loss; normal or heavy forces on a reduced periodontium
C. Primary: bone loss always present; Secondary: no bone loss ever
D. Primary: only diagnosed by patient symptoms; Secondary: only diagnosed by radiographs
E. Primary: involves only posterior teeth; Secondary: involves only anterior teeth
Correct Answer: B
A. Both present identically and cannot be distinguished
B. Primary: increasing mobility, migration, fremitus on a tooth with normal periodontal support; radiographically shows widened PDL and possible angular bone loss. Secondary: attachment loss is ALREADY present with bone loss; normal or heavy forces on a reduced periodontium
C. Primary: bone loss always present; Secondary: no bone loss ever
D. Primary: only diagnosed by patient symptoms; Secondary: only diagnosed by radiographs
E. Primary: involves only posterior teeth; Secondary: involves only anterior teeth

From the essay material — Primary occlusal trauma: excessive force on a tooth with NORMAL periodontal support. Clinical signs: increasing mobility, migration, fremitus. Radiographic signs: widened PDL space, possible angular bone loss. The periodontium is healthy but the forces are too much. Secondary occlusal trauma: "You must have attachment loss to have secondary occlusal trauma." Normal or even heavy forces on a REDUCED periodontium — the support has been lost to periodontitis, and now even normal biting forces exceed what the remaining support can handle. Treatment differs: primary = reduce the force (occlusal adjustment); secondary = compensate for lost support (splinting).

Why A is wrong: They have distinctly different clinical presentations and treatment. Why C is wrong: Primary doesn't always show bone loss initially; secondary always has pre-existing bone loss. Why D is wrong: Both are diagnosed by a combination of clinical and radiographic findings. Why E is wrong: Both can occur on any tooth.

Q214 According to Glickman and Smulow (1962), what happens when periodontal disease coexists with occlusal trauma?
A. Occlusal trauma completely replaces plaque as the cause of attachment loss
B. Trauma from occlusion redirects inflammatory exudate from the gingival unit to the attachment apparatus, exacerbating the progression of periodontal disease — but attachment loss with co-destruction is still predominantly caused by plaque inflammation
C. Occlusal trauma protects against periodontal disease progression
D. The combination has no additional effect beyond periodontitis alone
E. Occlusal trauma causes gingivitis independent of plaque
Correct Answer: B
A. Occlusal trauma completely replaces plaque as the cause of attachment loss
B. Trauma from occlusion redirects inflammatory exudate from the gingival unit to the attachment apparatus, exacerbating the progression of periodontal disease — but attachment loss with co-destruction is still predominantly caused by plaque inflammation
C. Occlusal trauma protects against periodontal disease progression
D. The combination has no additional effect beyond periodontitis alone
E. Occlusal trauma causes gingivitis independent of plaque

Glickman & Smulow (1962) described the zone of co-destruction: in the presence of periodontal disease, trauma from occlusion REDIRECTS inflammatory exudate from the gingival unit to the attachment apparatus. This means the inflammatory products that would normally be confined to the gingiva now penetrate deeper, accelerating destruction of the attachment apparatus. The essay material emphasizes: "Periodontal breakdown with co-destruction is still predominantly caused by plaque inflammation, while that caused by occlusal trauma is minor." Translation: plaque is STILL the main driver — occlusal trauma is the ACCELERANT, not the ignitor.

Why A is wrong: Plaque remains the predominant cause of attachment loss. Why C is wrong: Occlusal trauma worsens, not protects against, periodontal disease. Why D is wrong: The combination IS worse than periodontitis alone. Why E is wrong: Occlusal trauma doesn't cause gingivitis.

Q215 What is the treatment for PRIMARY occlusal trauma versus SECONDARY occlusal trauma?
A. Both are treated with extraction only
B. Primary: reduce excessive forces (occlusal adjustment) to a level acceptable to the attachment apparatus. Secondary: splinting to compensate for lost bone support that has left the tooth unable to withstand even normal forces
C. Primary: bone graft; Secondary: root canal therapy
D. Both are treated with antibiotics
E. Primary: splinting; Secondary: occlusal adjustment
Correct Answer: B
A. Both are treated with extraction only
B. Primary: reduce excessive forces (occlusal adjustment) to a level acceptable to the attachment apparatus. Secondary: splinting to compensate for lost bone support that has left the tooth unable to withstand even normal forces
C. Primary: bone graft; Secondary: root canal therapy
D. Both are treated with antibiotics
E. Primary: splinting; Secondary: occlusal adjustment

Treatment logically follows from the cause — Primary: the problem is EXCESSIVE FORCE on normal support, so treatment = reduce the force through occlusal adjustment, equilibration, or removal of premature contacts. Get the forces back within the adaptive capacity of the normal periodontium. Secondary: the problem is REDUCED SUPPORT under normal forces, so treatment = splinting to distribute forces across multiple teeth, compensating for the support deficiency. The essay material states: "Splinting will compensate for the loss of support which has left the tooth unable to withstand even normal forces."

Why A is wrong: Neither type automatically requires extraction. Why C is wrong: Bone grafting and RCT aren't the primary treatments for occlusal trauma. Why D is wrong: Antibiotics don't address mechanical force problems. Why E is wrong: The treatments are reversed — primary needs force reduction, secondary needs splinting.

Q216 Does mobility always indicate disease and always require treatment?
A. Yes — all mobility is pathologic and must be treated immediately
B. No — mobility can indicate disease but alone does not confirm it; a certain increase in mobility can be accepted and does not need to be treated, provided it doesn't disturb masticatory function or patient comfort
C. Mobility only needs treatment if it exceeds Grade 3
D. Mobility is always caused by periodontitis
E. All healthy teeth are completely immobile (0.0mm movement)
Correct Answer: B
A. Yes — all mobility is pathologic and must be treated immediately
B. No — mobility can indicate disease but alone does not confirm it; a certain increase in mobility can be accepted and does not need to be treated, provided it doesn't disturb masticatory function or patient comfort
C. Mobility only needs treatment if it exceeds Grade 3
D. Mobility is always caused by periodontitis
E. All healthy teeth are completely immobile (0.0mm movement)

From the essay material: "Mobility can indicate disease, but alone it does not indicate disease." And: "A certain increase in mobility can be accepted and does not need to be treated, provided the mobile tooth does not disturb the masticatory function or the comfort of the patient. Most healthy teeth have some sort of mobility, so unless the mobile teeth affect masticatory function or cause discomfort to the patient they do not need to be treated." Remember from Q181: normal physiological mobility is 0.2mm or less. Mobility becomes clinically relevant when it's progressive (getting worse over time) or functional (affecting chewing or comfort).

Why A is wrong: Not all mobility is pathologic — physiological mobility exists. Why C is wrong: Treatment depends on function and comfort, not a specific grade threshold. Why D is wrong: Mobility can be caused by occlusal trauma, inflammation, pregnancy, and other non-perio causes. Why E is wrong: All teeth have physiological mobility of up to 0.2mm.

Q217 Does trauma from occlusion cause attachment loss?
A. Yes — occlusal trauma is the primary cause of attachment loss in periodontitis
B. No — trauma from occlusion does NOT cause attachment loss because the effects of occlusal force on the periodontium are limited to the attachment apparatus; gingival soft tissues coronal to bone are not damaged by excessive force
C. Yes — occlusal trauma directly causes apical migration of the junctional epithelium
D. No — occlusal trauma has no effect on any periodontal tissue
E. Yes — occlusal trauma causes both attachment loss and gingival recession
Correct Answer: B
A. Yes — occlusal trauma is the primary cause of attachment loss in periodontitis
B. No — trauma from occlusion does NOT cause attachment loss because the effects of occlusal force on the periodontium are limited to the attachment apparatus; gingival soft tissues coronal to bone are not damaged by excessive force
C. Yes — occlusal trauma directly causes apical migration of the junctional epithelium
D. No — occlusal trauma has no effect on any periodontal tissue
E. Yes — occlusal trauma causes both attachment loss and gingival recession

From the essay material: "Trauma from occlusion does not cause attachment loss because the effects of occlusal force on the periodontium are limited to the attachment apparatus. Thus, gingival soft tissues coronal to bone are not damaged by excessive force on a tooth." This is the definitive statement. Occlusal forces affect the PDL, bone, and cementum (the attachment apparatus), causing widening of PDL space, bone density changes, and mobility — but the junctional epithelium and gingival connective tissue (which define attachment level) are NOT affected by mechanical forces. Attachment loss requires bacterial-induced inflammation.

Why A is wrong: Occlusal trauma does NOT cause attachment loss — plaque-induced inflammation does. Why C is wrong: JE migration requires bacterial inflammation, not mechanical force. Why D is wrong: OT DOES affect the attachment apparatus (PDL, bone) — it just doesn't cause attachment LOSS as measured by CAL. Why E is wrong: OT causes neither attachment loss nor gingival recession.

MUCOGINGIVAL SURGERY (32)
Q1 Which teeth have the highest correlation between root prominence and gingival recession?
A. Maxillary central incisors
B. Mandibular first premolars
C. Upper and lower canines
D. Maxillary first molars
E. Mandibular second premolars
Correct Answer: C
A. Maxillary central incisors
B. Mandibular first premolars
C. Upper and lower canines
D. Maxillary first molars
E. Mandibular second premolars

Canines — both upper and lower — have the most prominent roots in the arch, which means the overlying bone and soft tissue are naturally thinner on the facial. That thin bony housing (often a dehiscence) makes them the most susceptible teeth to recession when root prominence is the driving factor. The other teeth listed have less prominent root eminences relative to the alveolar housing.

Why A is wrong: Central incisors have relatively flat labial roots compared to canines. Why B is wrong: Premolars can get recession from brushing but are not the highest *root prominence* correlation. Why D is wrong: Molars have thick buccal bone generally and aren't associated with root prominence recession. Why E is wrong: Same logic as B — not the strongest root prominence relationship.

Q2 After orthodontic treatment, which areas are most commonly affected by gingival recession?
A. Maxillary canines and mandibular first premolars
B. Lower incisors and the mesiobuccal root of the maxillary first molar
C. Upper central incisors and mandibular canines
D. Mandibular second premolars and maxillary lateral incisors
E. Maxillary canines and mandibular second molars
Correct Answer: B
A. Maxillary canines and mandibular first premolars
B. Lower incisors and the mesiobuccal root of the maxillary first molar
C. Upper central incisors and mandibular canines
D. Mandibular second premolars and maxillary lateral incisors
E. Maxillary canines and mandibular second molars

Ortho moves teeth through bone — and when you push a tooth labially through the cortical plate, you create a bone dehiscence (Steiner et al. 1981; Karring et al. 1982). Your slides explicitly state that bodily tooth movement in a labial direction toward and through the cortical plate creates a labial bone dehiscence, and no bone formation will take place in front of the tooth.
