Lower incisors are thin-boned and commonly proclined during treatment, and the MB root of the upper first molar is the most prominent buccal root of that tooth — both are high-risk sites post-ortho.

Why A is wrong: Canines are recession-prone generally but not the classic ortho-associated pair. Why C is wrong: Upper centrals aren't the #1 ortho target. Why D/E are wrong: These pairings don't match the established post-orthodontic recession pattern from lecture.

Q3 Which periodontal biotype correlates with the gingival margin being located at the CEJ?
A. Thin scalloped biotype
B. Thick scalloped biotype
C. Thick flat biotype
D. Thin flat biotype
E. There is no correlation between biotype and gingival margin position
Correct Answer: C
A. Thin scalloped biotype
B. Thick scalloped biotype
C. Thick flat biotype
D. Thin flat biotype
E. There is no correlation between biotype and gingival margin position

Per your slides, the thick and flat biotype (Weisgold 1997; Olson & Lindhe 1991) is the one where the gingival margin sits right at the CEJ. This makes clinical sense — thick, flat tissue tends to have a broad zone of keratinized gingiva, minimal scalloping, and the margin stays put at the CEJ rather than sitting coronal to it or receding apically. Thin scalloped biotypes have more delicate tissue that's prone to recession, meaning the margin is more likely to be *apical* to the CEJ. Your slides also note that inflammation leads to pocket formation in thick tissue but recession in thin tissue.

Why A is wrong: Thin scalloped tissue recedes easily — margin is often apical to CEJ. Why B is wrong: Thick scalloped has more scalloping so the margin follows a more undulating pattern. Why D is wrong: This combination isn't a recognized biotype category in the lecture classification. Why E is wrong: There absolutely is a correlation — it's directly from your slides.

Q4 Gingival recession caused by aggressive toothbrushing most commonly affects which teeth?
A. Teeth on the same side as the dominant hand
B. Maxillary and mandibular incisors bilaterally
C. Canines and premolars on the opposite side of the dominant hand
D. Mandibular molars on the dominant hand side
E. Maxillary canines and premolars on the same side as the dominant hand
Correct Answer: C
A. Teeth on the same side as the dominant hand
B. Maxillary and mandibular incisors bilaterally
C. Canines and premolars on the opposite side of the dominant hand
D. Mandibular molars on the dominant hand side
E. Maxillary canines and premolars on the same side as the dominant hand

This is a classic factoid. When you brush with your right hand, you apply the most force on the LEFT side of the mouth (and vice versa). The canines and premolars are the teeth that receive the most direct, horizontal scrubbing force because of their position in the arch. So it's always the *opposite* dominant hand canines and premolars. Think about it mechanically — you cross your arm over, and the bristle pressure is greatest on the contralateral side.

Why A is wrong: It's the opposite side, not the same side. Why B is wrong: Incisors get hit but aren't the *most* commonly affected. Why D is wrong: Molars are further back and don't take the same scrubbing angle. Why E is wrong: Same side is incorrect — it's the contralateral side.

Q5 According to Albander and Kingman (WHO data), what is the prevalence of greater than 1mm gingival recession in people over 30 years of age?
A. 38%
B. 47%
C. 58%
D. 67%
E. 78%
Correct Answer: C
A. 38%
B. 47%
C. 58%
D. 67%
E. 78%

Straight from your study guide material — Albander and Kingman reported 58% prevalence of >1mm gingival recession in adults over 30, with prevalence increasing with age. This is a pure memorization number. The key takeaway is that recession is incredibly common in the adult population — more than half of people over 30 have clinically significant recession. This number helps justify why mucogingival therapy is such an important part of perio practice.

Why A is wrong: Too low — that's not from this study. Why B is wrong: 47% is the old Eke periodontitis prevalence number (3-site), don't cross your wires. Why D is wrong: 67% is the worsening rate for 3mm recession (Serino) — different stat entirely. Why E is wrong: No study reports this figure for overall recession prevalence.

Q6 According to Serino et al. (1994), once gingival recession is present, what percentage of the time does 3mm recession worsen, and what percentage for 4mm recession?
A. 3mm = 47%, 4mm = 78%
B. 3mm = 58%, 4mm = 90%
C. 3mm = 67%, 4mm = 98%
D. 3mm = 75%, 4mm = 95%
E. 3mm = 50%, 4mm = 85%
Correct Answer: C
A. 3mm = 47%, 4mm = 78%
B. 3mm = 58%, 4mm = 90%
C. 3mm = 67%, 4mm = 98%
D. 3mm = 75%, 4mm = 95%
E. 3mm = 50%, 4mm = 85%

Serino et al. 1994 — directly on your slides: 3mm recession worsened 67% of the time, 4mm recession worsened 98% of the time. This is a critical clinical concept: recession doesn't just stay where it is. Once you hit 4mm, it's almost guaranteed to get worse. This supports the rationale for early surgical intervention (root coverage procedures) before recession becomes severe. Chambrone & Tatakis 2016 further confirmed that untreated facial recession in patients with even good oral hygiene is highly likely to increase over long-term follow-up.

Why all other options are wrong: These are exact numbers from the Serino study — no other combination is correct. The 67/98 pairing is the only one supported by the literature cited in your lectures.

Q7 What is the minimum amount of keratinized tissue required to maintain gingival health?
A. 1mm keratinized tissue (0.5mm attached + 0.5mm free)
B. 2mm keratinized tissue (1mm attached + 1mm free)
C. 3mm keratinized tissue (2mm attached + 1mm free)
D. 4mm keratinized tissue (2mm attached + 2mm free)
E. 5mm keratinized tissue (3mm attached + 2mm free)
Correct Answer: B
A. 1mm keratinized tissue (0.5mm attached + 0.5mm free)
B. 2mm keratinized tissue (1mm attached + 1mm free)
C. 3mm keratinized tissue (2mm attached + 1mm free)
D. 4mm keratinized tissue (2mm attached + 2mm free)
E. 5mm keratinized tissue (3mm attached + 2mm free)

Lang & Löe 1972 established this: a minimum of 2mm of keratinized tissue — broken down as 1mm of attached gingiva plus 1mm of free gingiva — is needed to maintain gingival health. This is directly on your slides. However, your slides also note the counterpoint from Maynard & Wilson 1979: if there is good oral hygiene, a lack of attached gingiva does NOT necessarily result in recession. So the 2mm number is the threshold for health maintenance, but it's not an absolute death sentence if you're below it with pristine hygiene.

Why A is wrong: Too little — not supported by any study. Why C is wrong: 3mm KT is the requirement for a coronally advanced flap (Bernimoulin), not general health. Why D is wrong: Not a recognized threshold. Why E is wrong: 5mm KT is the requirement *around restorations* (Maynard & Wilson 1979), not for general gingival health.

Q8 How much keratinized tissue is required around a restoration to maintain gingival health?
A. 2mm keratinized tissue (1mm attached + 1mm free)
B. 3mm keratinized tissue (2mm attached + 1mm free)
C. 4mm keratinized tissue (2mm attached + 2mm free)
D. 5mm keratinized tissue (3mm attached + 2mm free)
E. 6mm keratinized tissue (4mm attached + 2mm free)
Correct Answer: D
A. 2mm keratinized tissue (1mm attached + 1mm free)
B. 3mm keratinized tissue (2mm attached + 1mm free)
C. 4mm keratinized tissue (2mm attached + 2mm free)
D. 5mm keratinized tissue (3mm attached + 2mm free)
E. 6mm keratinized tissue (4mm attached + 2mm free)

Maynard & Wilson 1979, directly from your slides: 5mm of keratinized tissue is needed around restorations, consisting of 2mm of free gingiva and 3mm of attached gingiva. This is a higher threshold than the general health minimum (2mm) because subgingival restorations create an additional inflammatory challenge. Your slides also cite Ericsson & Lindhe 1984 showing that subgingival restorations placed in areas with narrow KT may, in the presence of subgingival plaque, favor recession.

Why A is wrong: 2mm is the general health minimum, not the restoration requirement. Why B/C are wrong: Not the recognized threshold from Maynard & Wilson. Why E is wrong: No study supports 6mm as the threshold.

Q9 How does widening of the attached gingiva benefit the patient? (Select the three correct answers)
A. Enhances plaque control around the gingival margin
B. Improves esthetics
C. Reduces inflammation around restored teeth
D. Increases bone regeneration potential
E. Prevents root caries formation
Correct Answer: A, B, C
A. Enhances plaque control around the gingival margin
B. Improves esthetics
C. Reduces inflammation around restored teeth
D. Increases bone regeneration potential
E. Prevents root caries formation

Directly from your slides — widening of attached gingiva helps the patient in three specific ways: (1) enhances plaque control around the gingival margin, (2) improves esthetics, and (3) reduces inflammation around restored teeth. Wider attached gingiva gives the patient a more stable, resilient tissue margin to brush against, looks better cosmetically, and creates a better seal around restorations that minimizes inflammatory breakdown.

Why D is wrong: Gingival augmentation doesn't directly increase bone regeneration — that's a GTR/GBR concept. Why E is wrong: While recession correction indirectly reduces root caries risk, "prevents root caries formation" is not one of the three listed benefits from the slides.

Q10 Which of the following are indications for gingival augmentation?
A. Gingival inflammation, progressive soft tissue recession, no attached gingiva
B. Root caries, dentin hypersensitivity, esthetic concerns
C. Shallow pocketing, bleeding on probing, mobility
D. Furcation involvement, bone loss, tooth migration
E. Occlusal trauma, fremitus, gingival enlargement
Correct Answer: A
A. Gingival inflammation, progressive soft tissue recession, no attached gingiva
B. Root caries, dentin hypersensitivity, esthetic concerns
C. Shallow pocketing, bleeding on probing, mobility
D. Furcation involvement, bone loss, tooth migration
E. Occlusal trauma, fremitus, gingival enlargement

The three indications for gingival augmentation from your study guide are: (1) gingival inflammation that is worsened by lack of attached tissue, (2) progressive soft tissue recession, and (3) absence of attached gingiva. These are the clinical scenarios where augmenting the attached gingiva will actually change the disease trajectory. Choice B lists *consequences* of recession (which your slides cover under "Management of Gingival Recession — Consequences"), not indications for augmentation per se.

Why B is wrong: These are consequences/symptoms of recession, not indications for augmentation surgery. Why C is wrong: These are signs of periodontitis requiring different treatment. Why D is wrong: These require osseous/regenerative therapy, not soft tissue augmentation. Why E is wrong: Occlusal trauma is managed with occlusal adjustment, not gingival augmentation.

Q11 In the Miller Classification (1985), which class is defined as recession extending to or beyond the mucogingival junction with NO loss of interproximal bone or soft tissue?
A. Class I
B. Class II
C. Class III
D. Class IV
E. None of the above — all classes beyond Class I have interproximal loss
Correct Answer: B
A. Class I
B. Class II
C. Class III
D. Class IV
E. None of the above — all classes beyond Class I have interproximal loss

Directly from your slides — Miller Class II: "Marginal tissue recession extends to or beyond the MGJ. No periodontal attachment loss (bone or soft tissue) in the interdental area." The key differentiator between Class I and Class II is the MGJ: Class I doesn't reach the MGJ, Class II reaches or passes it — but BOTH have intact interproximal attachment. Class III and IV both have interproximal attachment loss, with IV being more severe (extending apical to the extent of the marginal recession).

Why A is wrong: Class I recession does NOT extend to the MGJ. Why C is wrong: Class III extends to/beyond MGJ but HAS interproximal attachment loss (though coronal to the apical extent of the buccal recession). Why D is wrong: Class IV has SEVERE interproximal loss extending apical to the buccal recession. Why E is wrong: Both Class I and II have no interproximal loss.

Q12 In the Miller Classification, which classes of recession allow for complete root coverage, partial root coverage, and no root coverage respectively?
A. Complete = Class I only; Partial = Class II; None = Class III and IV
B. Complete = Class I and II; Partial = Class III; None = Class IV
C. Complete = Class I, II, and III; Partial = none; None = Class IV
D. Complete = Class I; Partial = Class II and III; None = Class IV
E. Complete = Class II; Partial = Class I and III; None = Class IV
Correct Answer: B
A. Complete = Class I only; Partial = Class II; None = Class III and IV
B. Complete = Class I and II; Partial = Class III; None = Class IV
C. Complete = Class I, II, and III; Partial = none; None = Class IV
D. Complete = Class I; Partial = Class II and III; None = Class IV
E. Complete = Class II; Partial = Class I and III; None = Class IV

This is the prognosis framework for root coverage: Miller Class I and II = complete (100%) root coverage is predictable because there's no interproximal bone loss. Miller Class III = only partial root coverage is possible because there IS interproximal attachment loss, but it's coronal to the buccal recession (so some root coverage can be achieved). Miller Class IV = no root coverage is possible because the interproximal loss is severe and extends apical to the buccal recession — there's no tissue foundation to support coverage.

Why A is wrong: Class II also allows complete coverage. Why C is wrong: Class III only allows partial, not complete. Why D is wrong: Class II allows complete coverage, not just partial. Why E is wrong: Class I also allows complete coverage.

Q13 A rotational flap is best described as which of the following?
A. A free soft tissue graft harvested from the palate and sutured to the recipient site
B. A pedicle graft that moves coronally to cover recession
C. A pedicle soft tissue graft that moves laterally while rotating around a pivot point, used for root coverage
D. A full-thickness flap positioned apically to preserve keratinized tissue
E. A split-thickness flap tunneled under the papillae for root coverage
Correct Answer: C
A. A free soft tissue graft harvested from the palate and sutured to the recipient site
B. A pedicle graft that moves coronally to cover recession
C. A pedicle soft tissue graft that moves laterally while rotating around a pivot point, used for root coverage
D. A full-thickness flap positioned apically to preserve keratinized tissue
E. A split-thickness flap tunneled under the papillae for root coverage

Your slides list rotational flaps under "Pedicle Grafts" and include the laterally repositioned flap (Grupe & Warren 1956) and the double papilla flap (Cohen & Ross 1968). These flaps maintain a blood supply through their pedicle base and are rotated laterally around a pivot point to cover an adjacent area of recession. They're effective for covering small areas of recession when an adequate donor site is available adjacent to the defect. The key feature is the lateral + rotational movement, distinguishing them from advanced flaps that move coronally.

Why A is wrong: That's a free gingival graft — no pedicle attachment. Why B is wrong: That's an advanced flap (coronally positioned), not rotational. Why D is wrong: That's an apically positioned flap. Why E is wrong: That describes a tunnel technique, which is different from a rotational flap.

Q14 An advanced flap used for root coverage is best described as:
A. A laterally repositioned pedicle flap
B. A coronally positioned pedicle soft tissue graft
C. A free gingival graft positioned over the recession defect
D. A split-thickness flap moved apically past the MGJ
E. A connective tissue graft placed beneath a tunnel
Correct Answer: B
A. A laterally repositioned pedicle flap
B. A coronally positioned pedicle soft tissue graft
C. A free gingival graft positioned over the recession defect
D. A split-thickness flap moved apically past the MGJ
E. A connective tissue graft placed beneath a tunnel

Per your slides, advanced flaps are the second category of pedicle grafts (after rotational flaps) and their defining movement is coronal positioning. The mucosal flap is raised beyond the MGJ and moved coronally because of the elasticity of the tissue (directly from slides). This category includes the coronally advanced flap (Bernimoulin et al. 1975; Allen & Miller 1989) and the semilunar coronally positioned flap (Tarnow 1986). Single or multiple defects can be covered, and the technique can be combined with EMD, autogenous grafts, or allografts.

Why A is wrong: That's a rotational flap. Why C is wrong: FGG is not a pedicle graft. Why D is wrong: Apical movement is the opposite direction. Why E is wrong: That's the tunnel + CTG technique.

Q15 Which of the following are indications for an apically positioned flap?
A. Root coverage, increasing vestibular depth, elimination of frenum pull, gummy smile correction
B. Increasing attached gingiva, deepening the vestibule, eliminating pocket depth, gummy smile correction
C. Root coverage, increasing keratinized tissue width, reducing pocket depth, increasing vestibular depth
D. Increasing attached gingiva, root coverage, pocket elimination, increasing vestibular depth
E. Crown lengthening only
Correct Answer: B
A. Root coverage, increasing vestibular depth, elimination of frenum pull, gummy smile correction
B. Increasing attached gingiva, deepening the vestibule, eliminating pocket depth, gummy smile correction
C. Root coverage, increasing keratinized tissue width, reducing pocket depth, increasing vestibular depth
D. Increasing attached gingiva, root coverage, pocket elimination, increasing vestibular depth
E. Crown lengthening only

Four indications for the apically positioned flap directly from your study material: (1) increase attached gingiva, (2) deepen the vestibule, (3) eliminate pocket depth, and (4) gummy smile correction. Note that root coverage is NOT an indication — the APF moves tissue *apically*, which would expose MORE root, not cover it. The APF is a subtractive procedure that preserves keratinized tissue by repositioning it apically while eliminating pockets. Your midterm slides also confirm that apical positioning of the flap can be used to preserve keratinized tissue.

Why A is wrong: Root coverage is NOT an APF indication — APF moves tissue apically. Why C is wrong: Root coverage is wrong again. Why D is wrong: Root coverage doesn't belong here. Why E is wrong: Crown lengthening often involves an APF but the APF has more indications than just CL.

Q16 A free gingival graft (FGG) is also known as:
A. Subepithelial connective tissue graft
B. Epithelialized soft tissue graft
C. Pedicle rotational graft
D. Alloderm acellular dermal matrix graft
E. Tunnel connective tissue graft
Correct Answer: B
A. Subepithelial connective tissue graft
B. Epithelialized soft tissue graft
C. Pedicle rotational graft
D. Alloderm acellular dermal matrix graft
E. Tunnel connective tissue graft

From your slides, the FGG is also called an "epithelialized gingival graft" — the technique listing under "Techniques for Root Coverage / Gingival Augmentation" lists "epithelialized gingival grafts" as the alternative name. The FGG is called "epithelialized" because it includes the surface epithelium from the palatal donor site (unlike a CTG which is deepithelialized). This epithelial layer is why FGGs have poorer color match compared to CTGs — the palatal epithelium retains its palatal keratinization pattern and lighter color.

Why A is wrong: That's the CTG, not the FGG. Why C is wrong: Pedicle grafts maintain a blood supply base — FGGs are completely detached free grafts. Why D is wrong: Alloderm is an acellular dermal matrix allograft, completely different. Why E is wrong: Tunnel technique uses a CTG, not an FGG.

Q17 What are the three indications for a free gingival graft (FGG)?
A. Root coverage, pocket elimination, bone regeneration
B. Increase width/thickness of gingiva, increase vestibular depth, cover exposed roots
C. Increase vestibular depth, frenectomy, bone augmentation
D. Root coverage, increase attached gingiva, crown lengthening
E. Increase keratinized tissue, bone regeneration, esthetic improvement
Correct Answer: B
A. Root coverage, pocket elimination, bone regeneration
B. Increase width/thickness of gingiva, increase vestibular depth, cover exposed roots
C. Increase vestibular depth, frenectomy, bone augmentation
D. Root coverage, increase attached gingiva, crown lengthening
E. Increase keratinized tissue, bone regeneration, esthetic improvement

Three FGG indications from your study material: (1) increase width and thickness of gingiva, (2) increase vestibular depth, and (3) cover exposed roots. Your slides also list the advantages of FGG as "rapid and predictable" and "not as technically challenging" and "may be more easily combined with a frenectomy." The disadvantages include poor color match/esthetics and two surgical sites. So while FGG *can* cover roots, its primary strength is really in increasing the zone and thickness of keratinized tissue — root coverage is more predictably achieved with CTG.

Why A is wrong: Pocket elimination and bone regeneration aren't FGG indications. Why C is wrong: Bone augmentation is not an FGG indication. Why D is wrong: Crown lengthening is a different procedure entirely. Why E is wrong: Bone regeneration is not related to FGG.

Q18 Which thickness of free gingival graft is appropriate for covering exposed roots?
A. Thin (0.5–0.8mm)
B. Average (0.9–1.4mm)
C. Thick (1.5mm or greater)
D. Any thickness works equally well for root coverage
E. Ultra-thin (less than 0.5mm)
Correct Answer: C
A. Thin (0.5–0.8mm)
B. Average (0.9–1.4mm)
C. Thick (1.5mm or greater)
D. Any thickness works equally well for root coverage
E. Ultra-thin (less than 0.5mm)

Your study guide lays out the FGG thickness spectrum: Thin (0.5–0.8mm) is for increasing the amount of attached gingiva with the best color match. Average (0.9–1.4mm) is for increasing gingival dimension and vestibular depth. Thick (1.5mm+) is what you need to cover exposed roots. Your slides also note the recommended graft thickness for FGG is 0.75–1.25mm in general, but for root coverage specifically you need the thicker end. Root coverage requires a thick graft because the graft must survive over an avascular root surface — more thickness = more connective tissue volume = better plasmatic diffusion and survival.

Why A is wrong: Thin grafts are for increasing attached gingiva with best color match, not root coverage. Why B is wrong: Average thickness increases gingival dimension and vestibular depth but isn't thick enough for predictable root coverage. Why D is wrong: Thickness absolutely matters — root coverage demands thicker grafts. Why E is wrong: Ultra-thin grafts would have poor survival over root surfaces.

Q19 What are the two critical factors for soft tissue graft survival?
A. Graft thickness and suture technique
B. Blood supply and graft stability
C. Patient oral hygiene and smoking status
D. Recipient site width and palatal donor quality
E. Flap tension and graft color match
Correct Answer: B
A. Graft thickness and suture technique
B. Blood supply and graft stability
C. Patient oral hygiene and smoking status
D. Recipient site width and palatal donor quality
E. Flap tension and graft color match

Two factors: (1) Blood supply — don't place the graft above the CEJ because there's no bone there, so no periosteal blood supply to feed the graft. The graft gets its blood from the recipient bed (bone/periosteum), so no bone = no blood = graft death. (2) Stability — reduce graft mobility and eliminate dead spaces between the graft and root surface. Dead space allows blood clot disruption and prevents the intimate contact needed for plasmatic circulation (Phase 1 of FGG healing, per Gargiulo & Arocha 1967).

Why A is wrong: Graft thickness matters for outcomes but isn't one of the two named survival factors. Why C is wrong: These are patient risk factors, not direct graft survival factors. Why D is wrong: These influence outcomes but aren't the two named critical factors. Why E is wrong: Flap tension and color match relate to technique and esthetics, not survival per se.

Q20 Regarding the predictability of the free gingival graft for root coverage, which statement is most accurate?
A. Greatest success occurs in wide and deep recession defects, with an average predictability of 80%
B. Greatest success occurs in narrow and shallow recession defects, with predictability ranging from 0–90% and an average of 57%
C. Predictability is uniformly 90%+ regardless of defect morphology
D. Greatest success occurs in interproximal recession defects, with an average of 67%
E. FGG is not indicated for root coverage under any circumstances
Correct Answer: B
A. Greatest success occurs in wide and deep recession defects, with an average predictability of 80%
B. Greatest success occurs in narrow and shallow recession defects, with predictability ranging from 0–90% and an average of 57%
C. Predictability is uniformly 90%+ regardless of defect morphology
D. Greatest success occurs in interproximal recession defects, with an average of 67%
E. FGG is not indicated for root coverage under any circumstances

Per Wennstrom: FGG has the greatest success in narrow and shallow recession defects. The predictability range is wide — 0 to 90% — with an average of about 57%. That wide range tells you the FGG is not the most reliable tool for root coverage. This is exactly why the CTG became the gold standard — it's more predictable. The narrow/shallow preference makes sense: less root surface to cover = higher chance of getting full coverage with the graft.

Why A is wrong: Wide and deep defects are actually harder to cover — the opposite of greatest success. Why C is wrong: 90%+ would be way too optimistic for FGG root coverage. Why D is wrong: Interproximal recession is not where FGG shines, and 67% is the Serino recession worsening stat. Why E is wrong: FGG can be used for root coverage, it's just not as predictable as CTG.

Q21 A connective tissue graft (CTG) is also known as:
A. Epithelialized soft tissue graft
B. Subepithelial connective tissue graft
C. Free gingival graft
D. Acellular dermal matrix graft
E. Pedicle rotational graft
Correct Answer: B
A. Epithelialized soft tissue graft
B. Subepithelial connective tissue graft
C. Free gingival graft
D. Acellular dermal matrix graft
E. Pedicle rotational graft

Directly from your slides — the CTG is also called the subepithelial connective tissue graft. It was described by Langer & Langer 1985. The name tells you exactly what it is: you harvest tissue from *beneath* the epithelium of the palate. The donor site technique uses either a double incision (with epithelium) or a single incision (without epithelium) to take the CTG from the palate. The "subepithelial" distinction separates it from the FGG, which IS epithelialized.

Why A is wrong: That's the FGG. Why C is wrong: FGG and CTG are different grafts. Why D is wrong: Alloderm is an allograft, not autogenous. Why E is wrong: Pedicle grafts maintain a vascular base — CTG is a free graft.

Q22 What is the key difference between a partially covered CTG and a completely covered CTG?
A. Partially covered uses sutures; completely covered uses tissue glue
B. Partially covered leaves epithelium on the graft to increase keratinized tissue thickness and cannot be used on thin tissue; completely covered removes epithelium for use on thinner tissue
C. Partially covered is placed on bone; completely covered is placed on root only
D. There is no clinical difference between the two techniques
E. Partially covered is for Miller Class IV; completely covered is for Miller Class I
Correct Answer: B
A. Partially covered uses sutures; completely covered uses tissue glue
B. Partially covered leaves epithelium on the graft to increase keratinized tissue thickness and cannot be used on thin tissue; completely covered removes epithelium for use on thinner tissue
C. Partially covered is placed on bone; completely covered is placed on root only
D. There is no clinical difference between the two techniques
E. Partially covered is for Miller Class IV; completely covered is for Miller Class I

Directly from your slides on CTG technique — the graft can be: (1) completely covered, which allows thin grafts to survive and provides better esthetics, or (2) partially covered, which maintains the MGJ and allows for keratinization. Your study guide adds the critical detail: the partially covered approach leaves epithelium on the graft to increase thickness of keratinized tissue, but CAN'T be used on thin tissue. The completely covered approach removes the epithelium and is used for thinner tissue situations where you need the flap to nourish the graft from above.

Why A is wrong: Both use sutures. Why C is wrong: Placement site isn't the distinguishing feature. Why D is wrong: There's a significant clinical difference in indications and outcomes. Why E is wrong: Miller classification isn't the determining factor for coverage technique choice.

Q23 How does the predictability of the connective tissue graft (CTG) compare to the free gingival graft (FGG) for root coverage?
A. FGG is the gold standard and outperforms CTG
B. CTG and FGG have equivalent outcomes
C. CTG is the gold standard; most studies support CTG over FGG for root coverage
D. Neither graft provides predictable root coverage
E. CTG is only superior in mandibular teeth
Correct Answer: C
A. FGG is the gold standard and outperforms CTG
B. CTG and FGG have equivalent outcomes
C. CTG is the gold standard; most studies support CTG over FGG for root coverage
D. Neither graft provides predictable root coverage
E. CTG is only superior in mandibular teeth

Per Wennstrom, the CTG is the gold standard for root coverage — most studies support CTG over FGG. Your slides on CTG advantages include "good color blend," "can increase zone and thickness of KG," and "predictable root coverage in Miller Class I and II." The Cortellini & Pini Prato 2012 comparison charts from your slides also consistently rank CAF+CTG at or near the top for root coverage, amount of KT gain, long-term stability, and esthetics. The CTG gets dual blood supply (from the periosteal bed below AND from the flap covering it above), which gives it a survival advantage.

Why A is wrong: It's the reverse — CTG outperforms FGG. Why B is wrong: CTG is superior in most studies. Why D is wrong: Both provide root coverage; CTG just does it more predictably. Why E is wrong: CTG superiority is not limited to mandibular teeth.

Q24 What is "creeping attachment" and what type of graft is it associated with?
A. Gradual apical migration of the gingival margin after FGG; associated with thin grafts
B. Approximately 1mm of additional root coverage over a 1-year period after graft surgery; associated with a thick graft that replaces the gingival margin
C. Immediate coronal repositioning of the graft at the time of surgery; associated with CTG
D. Reattachment of PDL fibers after GTR membrane placement; associated with bone grafts
E. Migration of epithelium along the root surface after SRP; associated with no graft
Correct Answer: B
A. Gradual apical migration of the gingival margin after FGG; associated with thin grafts
B. Approximately 1mm of additional root coverage over a 1-year period after graft surgery; associated with a thick graft that replaces the gingival margin
C. Immediate coronal repositioning of the graft at the time of surgery; associated with CTG
D. Reattachment of PDL fibers after GTR membrane placement; associated with bone grafts
E. Migration of epithelium along the root surface after SRP; associated with no graft

Creeping attachment is the phenomenon where you get about 1mm of additional root coverage over a 1-year period AFTER graft surgery. It occurs with thick grafts that replace the gingival margin — the tissue slowly "creeps" coronally as it matures and contracts. This is a bonus: you might not get 100% root coverage at the time of surgery, but over the next year the tissue can gain another millimeter. It's one reason why final outcomes of soft tissue grafts should be assessed at 1 year, not immediately post-op.

Why A is wrong: Creeping attachment moves *coronally* (more coverage), not apically. Why C is wrong: Creeping attachment occurs over months, not immediately at surgery. Why D is wrong: This describes GTR regeneration, not creeping attachment. Why E is wrong: Epithelial migration after SRP is junctional epithelial reattachment (repair), not creeping attachment.

Q25 Which of the following are the two major causative factors in marginal tissue recession?
A. Amount of attached gingiva and tooth position
B. Occlusal trauma and oral hygiene habits
C. Toothbrushing trauma and plaque-induced periodontal inflammation
D. Genetic predisposition and smoking
E. Orthodontic treatment and subgingival restorations
Correct Answer: C
A. Amount of attached gingiva and tooth position
B. Occlusal trauma and oral hygiene habits
C. Toothbrushing trauma and plaque-induced periodontal inflammation
D. Genetic predisposition and smoking
E. Orthodontic treatment and subgingival restorations

This one comes with a critical "what ISN'T" trap from your study guide: the two major causative factors are (1) toothbrushing trauma and (2) plaque-induced periodontal inflammation. What is NOT a major causative factor? The amount of attached gingiva. This matters because students often assume that lack of attached gingiva *causes* recession, but your slides (Maynard & Wilson 1979) explicitly state that with good oral hygiene, a lack of attached gingiva does NOT result in recession. The amount of AG is a risk modifier, not a cause.

Why A is wrong: Amount of attached gingiva is explicitly NOT a major causative factor — this is the trap. Why B is wrong: Occlusal trauma causes bone loss patterns, not direct soft tissue recession. Why D is wrong: These are risk factors but not the two major causes. Why E is wrong: These are contributing factors but not the two primary causes listed in your material.

Q26 When subgingival restorations are present, which factor influences the development of recession over time, and which factor does NOT?
A. Does influence: apical-coronal height of gingiva; Does NOT influence: gingival thickness
B. Does influence: gingival thickness; Does NOT influence: apical-coronal height of gingiva
C. Does influence: amount of attached gingiva; Does NOT influence: biotype
D. Does influence: keratinized tissue width; Does NOT influence: probe depth
E. Both gingival thickness and apical-coronal height equally influence recession
Correct Answer: B
A. Does influence: apical-coronal height of gingiva; Does NOT influence: gingival thickness
B. Does influence: gingival thickness; Does NOT influence: apical-coronal height of gingiva
C. Does influence: amount of attached gingiva; Does NOT influence: biotype
D. Does influence: keratinized tissue width; Does NOT influence: probe depth
E. Both gingival thickness and apical-coronal height equally influence recession

Straight from your study guide: what DOES influence recession development over time with subgingival restorations is gingival thickness. What does NOT influence it is the apical-coronal height of the gingiva. This connects directly to the thick vs. thin biotype concept on your slides — thin tissue (GT <1mm) responds to inflammation with recession, while thick tissue responds with pocket formation. So around restorations, having thicker tissue is protective against recession. The vertical dimension of the gingiva (how tall it is) doesn't matter as much as how thick it is.

Why A is wrong: It's the exact reverse — thickness matters, height doesn't. Why C is wrong: These aren't the two factors being compared in this context. Why D is wrong: These aren't the paired comparison from lecture. Why E is wrong: They do NOT equally influence — thickness matters, height doesn't.

Q27 What are the two main indications for root coverage procedures?
A. Pocket elimination and bone regeneration
B. Esthetics and root sensitivity
C. Increasing keratinized tissue and vestibular depth
D. Preventing tooth mobility and occlusal trauma
E. Eliminating frenum pull and reducing inflammation
Correct Answer: B
A. Pocket elimination and bone regeneration
B. Esthetics and root sensitivity
C. Increasing keratinized tissue and vestibular depth
D. Preventing tooth mobility and occlusal trauma
E. Eliminating frenum pull and reducing inflammation

The two main indications for root coverage are (1) esthetics and (2) root sensitivity. These are the patient-driven reasons someone seeks treatment. Think about it from the patient's perspective: they either see an ugly long tooth (esthetics) or they feel pain when they drink cold water (sensitivity). Your slides under "Management of Gingival Recession — Consequences" list both dentin hypersensitivity and restoration of esthetics as key consequences that drive the need for root coverage procedures.

Why A is wrong: Pocket elimination uses resective surgery, not root coverage. Why C is wrong: These are gingival augmentation goals, not the primary root coverage indications. Why D is wrong: Mobility and occlusal trauma aren't treated with root coverage. Why E is wrong: Frenum elimination is a frenectomy indication, not root coverage.

Q28 The free gingival graft (FGG) is ideal for increasing which two parameters?
A. Root coverage and vestibular depth
B. Amount of keratinized tissue and gingival thickness
C. Bone height and pocket depth reduction
D. Esthetics and color match
E. PDL regeneration and new attachment
Correct Answer: B
A. Root coverage and vestibular depth
B. Amount of keratinized tissue and gingival thickness
C. Bone height and pocket depth reduction
D. Esthetics and color match
E. PDL regeneration and new attachment

FGG is ideal for increasing (1) the amount of keratinized tissue and (2) gingival thickness. This is the FGG's sweet spot — it's essentially a tissue-volume procedure. Your slides list FGG advantages as "rapid and predictable" and "not as technically challenging." The tradeoff is poor color match/esthetics. So FGG is your go-to when you need more keratinized tissue bulk, NOT when you need the prettiest result. For esthetic root coverage, you'd use a CTG instead.

Why A is wrong: Root coverage is possible but not what FGG is *ideal* for — that's CTG territory. Why C is wrong: FGG doesn't directly affect bone height or pocket depth. Why D is wrong: The opposite — FGG has POOR color match, which is listed as a disadvantage on your slides. Why E is wrong: Regeneration is a GTR concept, not FGG.

Q29 In periodontal wound healing, what is "repair" and when does it occur?
A. Formation of new cementum, PDL, and bone; occurs after GTR membrane placement
B. Junctional epithelial cell adhesion to a root surface deprived of its periodontal ligament, preventing connective tissue attachment; occurs during flap procedures or after SRP
C. Complete regeneration of all periodontal tissues; occurs after bone grafting
D. Ankylosis of the root surface to alveolar bone; occurs after tooth replantation
E. Formation of granulation tissue only; occurs after extraction
Correct Answer: B
A. Formation of new cementum, PDL, and bone; occurs after GTR membrane placement
B. Junctional epithelial cell adhesion to a root surface deprived of its periodontal ligament, preventing connective tissue attachment; occurs during flap procedures or after SRP
C. Complete regeneration of all periodontal tissues; occurs after bone grafting
D. Ankylosis of the root surface to alveolar bone; occurs after tooth replantation
E. Formation of granulation tissue only; occurs after extraction

Directly from your slides: "REPAIR — A junctional epithelial cell adhesion with a root surface which has been deprived of its periodontal ligament; preventing a connective tissue attachment." This is the healing outcome you get after a standard flap procedure or SRP — epithelial cells are the fastest to migrate (they win the race to the root surface), so they form a long junctional epithelial attachment rather than true new connective tissue attachment. This is fundamentally different from REGENERATION, which is "the biologic process by which the architecture and function of the lost tissue is completely returned" (Melcher 1969). The whole concept of GTR was born from trying to prevent repair and promote regeneration.

Why A is wrong: That describes regeneration, not repair. Why C is wrong: Complete return of all tissues is regeneration. Why D is wrong: Ankylosis is a pathologic healing outcome, not repair. Why E is wrong: Granulation tissue is part of the wound healing process but repair specifically refers to the junctional epithelial adhesion.

Q30 What are the four cell types that have the potential to participate in the healing process after periodontal surgery?
A. Osteoclasts, fibroblasts, macrophages, neutrophils
B. Connective tissue cells from the PDL, connective tissue cells from the inner aspect of the flap, bone cells, and epithelial cells from the gingiva
C. Stem cells, red blood cells, platelets, epithelial cells
D. Cementoblasts, ameloblasts, odontoblasts, osteoblasts
E. Keratinocytes, chondrocytes, myocytes, endothelial cells
Correct Answer: B
A. Osteoclasts, fibroblasts, macrophages, neutrophils
B. Connective tissue cells from the PDL, connective tissue cells from the inner aspect of the flap, bone cells, and epithelial cells from the gingiva
C. Stem cells, red blood cells, platelets, epithelial cells
D. Cementoblasts, ameloblasts, odontoblasts, osteoblasts
E. Keratinocytes, chondrocytes, myocytes, endothelial cells

Your slides ask the question directly: "What are the different cell types which have the potential to be involved in the healing process after surgery?" The four cell types are: (1) CT cells from the PDL, (2) CT cells from the inner aspect of the flap, (3) bone cells, and (4) epithelial cells from the gingiva. This is the FOUNDATIONAL concept behind GTR. Each cell type produces a different healing outcome: epithelial cells = long junctional epithelium (repair), bone cells = root resorption/ankylosis, CT from flap = fibrous adhesion, and PDL cells = TRUE regeneration (new cementum, new PDL, new bone). GTR works by excluding the unwanted cell types (epithelium and gingival CT) with a membrane, giving PDL cells time to repopulate the root surface.

Why A is wrong: These are inflammatory/immune cells, not the four healing cell types from the GTR framework. Why C is wrong: This is a random assortment of cell types not specific to the periodontal healing model. Why D is wrong: Ameloblasts and odontoblasts are involved in tooth formation, not periodontal healing. Why E is wrong: Chondrocytes and myocytes aren't involved in periodontal wound healing.

Q113 When harvesting a free gingival graft from the palatal donor site, how far from the teeth should the graft be taken, and what is the ideal graft thickness?
A. 1mm from teeth; 0.5–0.75mm thick
B. 2mm apically from teeth; 0.75–1.25mm thick
C. 3mm from teeth; 1.5–2.0mm thick
D. 4mm from teeth; 0.25–0.50mm thick
E. At the gingival margin of teeth; 1.0–1.5mm thick
Correct Answer: B
A. 1mm from teeth; 0.5–0.75mm thick
B. 2mm apically from teeth; 0.75–1.25mm thick
C. 3mm from teeth; 1.5–2.0mm thick
D. 4mm from teeth; 0.25–0.50mm thick
E. At the gingival margin of teeth; 1.0–1.5mm thick

Directly from your slides on FGG technique: "The graft should be taken 2mm apically from teeth" and "The graft should be 0.75–1.25mm in thickness and can be placed at the recipient site (with no dead space) using sling sutures." The 2mm distance from teeth avoids damaging the gingival attachment of the palatal teeth. The 0.75–1.25mm thickness range sits within the "average" zone from the thickness spectrum you already know — thick enough to survive but thin enough to revascularize efficiently. The "no dead space" instruction connects to the graft survival factor of stability.

Why A is wrong: 1mm is too close to the teeth and 0.5–0.75mm is below the recommended range. Why C is wrong: 3mm is farther than necessary and 1.5–2.0mm is at the thick end for root coverage, not the standard FGG. Why D is wrong: 4mm is too far and 0.25–0.50mm is too thin to survive. Why E is wrong: Harvesting at the gingival margin would damage the palatal teeth's attachment.

Q114 When harvesting a connective tissue graft (CTG) from the palate, which two incision techniques can be used at the donor site?
A. Full-thickness incision only; no alternative technique exists
B. Double incision (with epithelium) or single incision (without epithelium)
C. Semilunar incision or crestal incision
D. External bevel gingivectomy or internal bevel gingivectomy
E. Intrasulcular incision or mid-crestal incision
Correct Answer: B
A. Full-thickness incision only; no alternative technique exists
B. Double incision (with epithelium) or single incision (without epithelium)
C. Semilunar incision or crestal incision
D. External bevel gingivectomy or internal bevel gingivectomy
E. Intrasulcular incision or mid-crestal incision

Directly from your slides: "Donor site: A double incision (with epithelium) or single incision (without epithelium) of the palate is made to take the CTG." The double incision technique makes two parallel incisions through the palatal mucosa, creating a strip that includes the surface epithelium — the surgeon then removes the epithelium from the graft chairside. The single incision technique (trap-door approach) accesses the connective tissue underneath the epithelium through one incision, leaving the palatal epithelium intact as a "bandage" over the donor site — less donor site morbidity and faster healing.

Why A is wrong: There are two established techniques, not just one. Why C is wrong: Semilunar incisions are for coronally positioned flaps, not palatal harvest. Why D is wrong: Gingivectomy incisions aren't used for palatal CTG harvest. Why E is wrong: Intrasulcular incisions are for GTR/flap surgery, not palatal donor harvest.

FURCATION & ROOT RESECTION (26)
Q55 What is the width of a new Gracey curette blade, and what percentage of furcation entrances are narrower than this?
A. Gracey blade = 1.0mm; 40% of furcation entrances are narrower
B. Gracey blade = 0.75mm; 60% of furcation entrances are narrower
C. Gracey blade = 0.50mm; 80% of furcation entrances are narrower
D. Gracey blade = 1.5mm; 90% of furcation entrances are narrower
E. Gracey blade = 0.75mm; 30% of furcation entrances are narrower
Correct Answer: B
A. Gracey blade = 1.0mm; 40% of furcation entrances are narrower
B. Gracey blade = 0.75mm; 60% of furcation entrances are narrower
C. Gracey blade = 0.50mm; 80% of furcation entrances are narrower
D. Gracey blade = 1.5mm; 90% of furcation entrances are narrower
E. Gracey blade = 0.75mm; 30% of furcation entrances are narrower

A new Gracey curette blade is 0.75mm wide, and 60% of furcation entrances are narrower than 0.75mm. Let that sink in — your primary hand instrument for SRP DOESN'T FIT into the majority of furcation entrances. This is exactly why furcation-involved teeth have such poor prognosis with non-surgical therapy alone and why open flap debridement, ultrasonic instrumentation (with thinner tips), and sometimes root resection or extraction become necessary. It's also why furcation involvement is such a critical prognostic factor in the 2018 classification grading system.

Why A is wrong: 1.0mm is too wide for a Gracey, and 40% is too low. Why C is wrong: 0.50mm is too thin for a standard Gracey blade. Why D is wrong: 1.5mm is way too wide. Why E is wrong: The 30% figure is too low — it's 60%.

Q56 How do the root trunk lengths compare among the mandibular molars?
A. First molar > second molar > third molar
B. Third molar > second molar > first molar
C. All mandibular molars have equal root trunk lengths
D. Second molar > first molar > third molar
E. First molar > third molar > second molar
Correct Answer: B
A. First molar > second molar > third molar
B. Third molar > second molar > first molar
C. All mandibular molars have equal root trunk lengths
D. Second molar > first molar > third molar
E. First molar > third molar > second molar

Root trunk length comparison: 3rd molar > 2nd molar > 1st molar (3M > 2M > 1M). This means the first molar has the SHORTEST root trunk, which means its furcation entrance is closest to the CEJ and most accessible to periodontal disease. Shorter root trunk = earlier furcation involvement = worse prognosis when disease is present. This is another reason why the first molar is the most commonly lost tooth to perio — its furcation is exposed to disease earliest. The third molar's longer root trunk is somewhat protective, but its position makes hygiene nearly impossible.

Why A is wrong: This is completely reversed — 1M has the shortest trunk, not the longest. Why C is wrong: They are definitively NOT equal. Why D is wrong: Incorrect order. Why E is wrong: Incorrect order.

Q57 At what distance from the CEJ are the furcation entrances located on maxillary molars for the mesial, buccal, and distal surfaces?
A. Mesial = 2mm, Buccal = 3mm, Distal = 4mm
B. Mesial = 3mm, Buccal = 3.5mm, Distal = 5mm
C. Mesial = 4mm, Buccal = 4mm, Distal = 4mm
D. Mesial = 5mm, Buccal = 3mm, Distal = 3.5mm
E. Mesial = 3.5mm, Buccal = 5mm, Distal = 3mm
Correct Answer: B
A. Mesial = 2mm, Buccal = 3mm, Distal = 4mm
B. Mesial = 3mm, Buccal = 3.5mm, Distal = 5mm
C. Mesial = 4mm, Buccal = 4mm, Distal = 4mm
D. Mesial = 5mm, Buccal = 3mm, Distal = 3.5mm
E. Mesial = 3.5mm, Buccal = 5mm, Distal = 3mm

Maxillary molar furcation entrances: Mesial = 3mm from CEJ, Buccal = 3.5mm from CEJ, Distal = 5mm from CEJ. The mesial furcation is closest to the CEJ (most vulnerable to early involvement), the buccal is intermediate, and the distal is farthest (most protected). This is clinically important: mesial furcation involvement happens first and is also the hardest to detect clinically because it's between the roots and requires a Nabers probe approached from the palatal. The buccal furcation is the easiest to detect and access clinically.

Why A is wrong: All measurements are too low. Why C is wrong: They're not all equal — each surface has a different distance. Why D is wrong: This reverses the mesial and distal values. Why E is wrong: Incorrect distribution of values.

Q58 Which root of the maxillary molar most commonly has more than one canal, and what is the prevalence?
A. Palatal root; 95%
B. Distobuccal root; 70%
C. Mesiobuccal root; 85%
D. All roots equally; 50% each
E. Mesiobuccal root; 50%
Correct Answer: C
A. Palatal root; 95%
B. Distobuccal root; 70%
C. Mesiobuccal root; 85%
D. All roots equally; 50% each
E. Mesiobuccal root; 50%

The mesiobuccal (MB) root of the maxillary molar has more than one canal approximately 85% of the time. This is the famous MB2 canal that's the bane of every endodontist's existence. Your study guide also notes that the mesial root of mandibular molars commonly has multiple canals as well. Knowing this is critical for both endo treatment planning (don't miss MB2!) and for perio — the MB root's complex anatomy also makes it the most challenging root for furcation debridement and potential resection planning.

Why A is wrong: Palatal roots are almost always single-canaled. Why B is wrong: The DB root is the simplest root of the max molar — rarely has 2 canals. Why D is wrong: Canal prevalence is NOT equal across roots. Why E is wrong: 50% significantly underestimates the MB root's dual-canal prevalence.

Q59 Which root of the maxillary molar is most frequently removed (resected)?
A. Mesiobuccal root
B. Distobuccal root
C. Palatal root
D. All roots are equally likely to be resected
E. Furcation involvement never requires root resection
Correct Answer: B
A. Mesiobuccal root
B. Distobuccal root
C. Palatal root
D. All roots are equally likely to be resected
E. Furcation involvement never requires root resection

The distobuccal (DB) root of the maxillary molar is the most frequently removed root. The DB root is the smallest, thinnest, and often shortest of the three maxillary molar roots, making it the most expendable. It also typically has a single canal, making endodontic preparation simpler. After DB root resection, you're left with the larger MB and palatal roots, which together provide a solid bipod support structure (like two legs of a tripod — still functional). The palatal root is the largest and provides the most support, so you almost never want to sacrifice it.

Why A is wrong: The MB root is large and important for support — not the most frequently resected. Why C is wrong: The palatal root is the largest and provides the most retention — removing it would be a last resort. Why D is wrong: Root resection frequency is NOT equal across roots. Why E is wrong: Root resection is absolutely a treatment option for furcation involvement.

Q60 Which root surfaces of maxillary and mandibular molars have the most significant concavities, and what are their depths and prevalences?
A. Distal of MB maxillary root: 0.3mm deep, 94%; Mesial of mandibular molar: 0.7mm deep, 100%
B. Mesial of MB maxillary root: 0.5mm deep, 80%; Distal of mandibular molar: 0.5mm deep, 90%
C. Palatal maxillary root: 0.7mm deep, 94%; Mesial of mandibular molar: 0.3mm deep, 100%
D. DB maxillary root: 0.3mm deep, 94%; Distal of mandibular molar: 0.7mm deep, 99%
E. All root surfaces have equal concavity depths of 0.5mm
Correct Answer: A
A. Distal of MB maxillary root: 0.3mm deep, 94%; Mesial of mandibular molar: 0.7mm deep, 100%
B. Mesial of MB maxillary root: 0.5mm deep, 80%; Distal of mandibular molar: 0.5mm deep, 90%
C. Palatal maxillary root: 0.7mm deep, 94%; Mesial of mandibular molar: 0.3mm deep, 100%
D. DB maxillary root: 0.3mm deep, 94%; Distal of mandibular molar: 0.7mm deep, 99%
E. All root surfaces have equal concavity depths of 0.5mm

Here are the root concavity stats from your study guide — these are the most clinically significant ones:

The distal surface of the MB root of the maxillary molar has a 0.3mm deep concavity present 94% of the time. The palatal root of the maxillary molar has a lingual-side concavity 17% of the time. The DB root of the maxillary molar has a concavity 31% of the time. The mesial root of the mandibular molar has a 0.7mm deep concavity present 100% of the time. The distal root of the mandibular molar has a 0.5mm deep concavity 99% of the time.

The mandibular mesial root concavity at 100% prevalence and 0.7mm depth is the deepest and most universal — this is why the mesial surface of mandibular molars is the hardest to debride thoroughly with hand instruments.

Why B is wrong: The measurements and locations don't match the data. Why C is wrong: Palatal concavity is 17% prevalence, not 94%, and the depths are reversed. Why D is wrong: The DB concavity is 31%, not 94%. Why E is wrong: Concavity depths are absolutely NOT equal — they vary significantly.

Q61 What are the furcation entrance locations and widths for mandibular molars?
A. Buccal = 3mm from CEJ, >0.75mm wide; Lingual = 3mm from CEJ, >0.75mm wide
B. Buccal = 3mm from CEJ, >0.75mm wide; Lingual = 4mm from CEJ, <0.75mm wide
C. Buccal = 4mm from CEJ, <0.75mm wide; Lingual = 3mm from CEJ, >0.75mm wide
D. Buccal = 5mm from CEJ, >0.75mm wide; Lingual = 5mm from CEJ, <0.75mm wide
E. Buccal = 2mm from CEJ, >0.75mm wide; Lingual = 2mm from CEJ, <0.75mm wide
Correct Answer: B
A. Buccal = 3mm from CEJ, >0.75mm wide; Lingual = 3mm from CEJ, >0.75mm wide
B. Buccal = 3mm from CEJ, >0.75mm wide; Lingual = 4mm from CEJ, <0.75mm wide
C. Buccal = 4mm from CEJ, <0.75mm wide; Lingual = 3mm from CEJ, >0.75mm wide
D. Buccal = 5mm from CEJ, >0.75mm wide; Lingual = 5mm from CEJ, <0.75mm wide
E. Buccal = 2mm from CEJ, >0.75mm wide; Lingual = 2mm from CEJ, <0.75mm wide

Mandibular molar furcation entrances: Buccal = 3mm from CEJ and WIDER than 0.75mm; Lingual = 4mm from CEJ and NARROWER than 0.75mm. This has huge clinical implications. The buccal furcation is closer to the CEJ (gets involved earlier) but is wider — so at least your Gracey curette (0.75mm) can get in there. The lingual furcation is farther from the CEJ (somewhat protected) but NARROWER than the Gracey blade — meaning once it IS involved, you literally can't instrument it effectively with hand instruments. This is why lingual furcation involvement on mandibular molars is a nightmare.

Why A is wrong: The lingual furcation is at 4mm, not 3mm, and is narrower, not wider. Why C is wrong: This reverses the buccal and lingual values. Why D is wrong: 5mm is the distal furcation of maxillary molars, not mandibular. Why E is wrong: 2mm is too close to the CEJ for either entrance.

Q62 What percentage of maxillary premolars have two root cones (bifurcated roots)?
A. 20%
B. 30%
C. 40%
D. 50%
E. 60%
Correct Answer: C
A. 20%
B. 30%
C. 40%
D. 50%
E. 60%

40% of maxillary premolars have two root cones. This is clinically significant because it means almost half of upper premolars have a furcation-like anatomy that can complicate both periodontal and endodontic treatment. When you're probing around a maxillary premolar and hit a deeper reading on the mesial or distal, consider the possibility of a root bifurcation. It also matters for extraction planning — a two-rooted upper premolar is more likely to fracture during extraction if you don't section it appropriately.

Why A is wrong: 20% underestimates the prevalence. Why B is wrong: 30% is still too low. Why D is wrong: 50% overestimates it. Why E is wrong: 60% is too high — it's 40%.

Q63 What is the mean distance from the CEJ to the furcation entrance, and where in the root does this typically place the furcation?
A. 4mm; coronal 1/3
B. 6mm; middle 1/3
C. 8mm; middle or apical 1/3
D. 10mm; apical 1/3
E. 3mm; cervical 1/3
Correct Answer: C
A. 4mm; coronal 1/3
B. 6mm; middle 1/3
C. 8mm; middle or apical 1/3
D. 10mm; apical 1/3
E. 3mm; cervical 1/3

The mean distance from the CEJ to the furcation entrance is 8mm, placing it in the middle or apical 1/3 of the root. This tells you that furcation involvement generally represents moderate-to-advanced disease — you need significant attachment loss before the furcation is even reached. It also means that shallow probing depths don't rule out furcation problems; the furcation could be well below the base of a 5-6mm pocket depending on recession. Always use a Nabers probe to specifically check furcations rather than relying on straight periodontal probe readings alone.

Why A is wrong: 4mm would place the furcation very coronally — too close to the CEJ. Why B is wrong: 6mm is closer but still underestimates the mean. Why D is wrong: 10mm would place the furcation extremely apically — past the typical root length for many teeth. Why E is wrong: 3mm is the distance to specific furcation entrances (like mesial of max molars), not the mean across all teeth.

Q64 According to Bender, what is the relationship between periodontal disease, caries, and the dental pulp?
A. Teeth with periodontal disease have normal pulp tissue regardless of caries status
B. Teeth with periodontal disease plus caries and/or restorations have histologically inflamed dental pulps
C. Only teeth with caries have inflamed pulps; periodontal disease alone does not affect the pulp
D. Pulp inflammation occurs only when the furcation is involved
E. Teeth with periodontal disease have necrotic pulps in all cases
Correct Answer: B
A. Teeth with periodontal disease have normal pulp tissue regardless of caries status
B. Teeth with periodontal disease plus caries and/or restorations have histologically inflamed dental pulps
C. Only teeth with caries have inflamed pulps; periodontal disease alone does not affect the pulp
D. Pulp inflammation occurs only when the furcation is involved
E. Teeth with periodontal disease have necrotic pulps in all cases

Bender showed that teeth with periodontal disease PLUS caries and/or restorations have histologically inflamed dental pulps. This is the endo-perio connection — the pulp and periodontium communicate through the apical foramen, lateral canals, and dentinal tubules. When you have BOTH perio disease and a carious/restored tooth, the combined insult from the periodontal pocket (bacteria traveling through lateral canals or exposed tubules) and from the restoration/caries (bacterial penetration through dentin) creates pulpal inflammation. This has treatment planning implications: a tooth with both perio and a deep restoration may need endo evaluation before definitive perio treatment.

Why A is wrong: Perio disease combined with caries/restorations absolutely affects pulp histology. Why C is wrong: Perio disease contributes to pulp changes when combined with other factors. Why D is wrong: Furcation involvement isn't the sole trigger — it's the combination of perio + caries/restorations. Why E is wrong: The pulps are inflamed, not necessarily necrotic.

Q65 Which site has the highest frequency of furcation involvement?
A. Mandibular first molar buccal furcation
B. Maxillary first molar mesial furcation
C. Maxillary first molar distal furcation
D. Mandibular second molar lingual furcation
E. Maxillary second molar buccal furcation
Correct Answer: C
A. Mandibular first molar buccal furcation
B. Maxillary first molar mesial furcation
C. Maxillary first molar distal furcation
D. Mandibular second molar lingual furcation
E. Maxillary second molar buccal furcation

The upper first molar distal furcation has the highest frequency of furcation involvement. This connects to what we covered in Q57 — the distal furcation of the maxillary molar is at 5mm from the CEJ (the farthest), so why is it the most commonly involved? Because the distal surface of the upper first molar is the interproximal area facing the second molar, and interproximal bone loss is the most common pattern of periodontal destruction. Plaque accumulates between the first and second molars, and the distal furcation sits right in the path of that bone loss. Also, the distal furcation can be very difficult to access for debridement.

Why A is wrong: Mandibular buccal furcation is commonly involved but not the #1 site. Why B is wrong: Mesial furcation is clinically important but not the highest frequency. Why D is wrong: Mandibular lingual furcation is problematic but not the most frequent. Why E is wrong: Second molar isn't the highest-frequency tooth for furcation involvement.

Q66 In the Glickman horizontal furcation classification, what defines each grade (1 through 4)?
A. Grade 1 = slight bone loss; Grade 2 = moderate bone loss; Grade 3 = severe bone loss; Grade 4 = tooth loss
B. Grade 1 = V-shaped notch at furcation entrance; Grade 2 = partial probe insertion into furcation; Grade 3 = probe penetrates completely with clear radiographic evidence; Grade 4 = probe penetrates completely with gingival recession and total furcation exposure
C. Grade 1 = 1mm horizontal loss; Grade 2 = 2mm; Grade 3 = 3mm; Grade 4 = 4mm+
D. Grade 1 = no furcation involvement; Grade 2 = incipient involvement; Grade 3 = moderate; Grade 4 = advanced
E. Grade 1 = buccal only; Grade 2 = buccal + lingual; Grade 3 = through-and-through; Grade 4 = tooth extraction indicated
Correct Answer: B
A. Grade 1 = slight bone loss; Grade 2 = moderate bone loss; Grade 3 = severe bone loss; Grade 4 = tooth loss
B. Grade 1 = V-shaped notch at furcation entrance; Grade 2 = partial probe insertion into furcation; Grade 3 = probe penetrates completely with clear radiographic evidence; Grade 4 = probe penetrates completely with gingival recession and total furcation exposure
C. Grade 1 = 1mm horizontal loss; Grade 2 = 2mm; Grade 3 = 3mm; Grade 4 = 4mm+
D. Grade 1 = no furcation involvement; Grade 2 = incipient involvement; Grade 3 = moderate; Grade 4 = advanced
E. Grade 1 = buccal only; Grade 2 = buccal + lingual; Grade 3 = through-and-through; Grade 4 = tooth extraction indicated

Glickman's horizontal classification: Grade 1 = V-shaped notch (you can feel the beginning of the furcation — the earliest detectable involvement, like a little divot). Grade 2 = partial probe insertion into the furcation (you get INTO it but can't push all the way through). Grade 3 = probe penetrates completely through the furcation with clear radiographic evidence of bone loss (through-and-through involvement but tissue still covers it). Grade 4 = probe penetrates completely, PLUS there's gingival recession exposing the furcation clinically — total furcation exposure (you can literally see through it).

Why A is wrong: These are vague severity terms, not the Glickman criteria. Why C is wrong: Glickman isn't measured in millimeters — that's more like Tarnow/Fletcher vertical. Why D is wrong: These are generic descriptors, not the specific Glickman definitions. Why E is wrong: Glickman doesn't classify by which surface is involved.

Q67 In the Lindhe horizontal furcation classification, what defines each degree (1 through 3)?
A. Degree 1 = V-notch only; Degree 2 = probe passes halfway; Degree 3 = full recession exposure
B. Degree 1 = loss of interradicular bone less than 1/3 of tooth width; Degree 2 = loss of interradicular bone but not all the way through; Degree 3 = complete through-and-through bone loss
C. Degree 1 = 1-2mm loss; Degree 2 = 3-4mm loss; Degree 3 = 5mm+ loss
D. Degree 1 = buccal furcation only; Degree 2 = buccal + lingual; Degree 3 = all furcations involved
E. Degree 1 = no radiographic changes; Degree 2 = slight radiolucency; Degree 3 = obvious radiolucency
Correct Answer: B
A. Degree 1 = V-notch only; Degree 2 = probe passes halfway; Degree 3 = full recession exposure
B. Degree 1 = loss of interradicular bone less than 1/3 of tooth width; Degree 2 = loss of interradicular bone but not all the way through; Degree 3 = complete through-and-through bone loss
C. Degree 1 = 1-2mm loss; Degree 2 = 3-4mm loss; Degree 3 = 5mm+ loss
D. Degree 1 = buccal furcation only; Degree 2 = buccal + lingual; Degree 3 = all furcations involved
E. Degree 1 = no radiographic changes; Degree 2 = slight radiolucency; Degree 3 = obvious radiolucency

Lindhe's classification uses three degrees based on the PROPORTION of interradicular bone lost horizontally. Degree 1 = loss of interradicular bone less than 1/3 of the tooth width. Degree 2 = loss of interradicular bone that extends more than 1/3 but NOT all the way through. Degree 3 = complete through-and-through bone destruction. Notice Lindhe uses 3 grades while Glickman uses 4 — the main difference is Glickman separates the "through-and-through with tissue coverage" (Grade 3) from "through-and-through with clinical exposure" (Grade 4), while Lindhe lumps both as Degree 3.

Why A is wrong: These are Glickman-style descriptors, not Lindhe's proportional system. Why C is wrong: Lindhe uses proportions (1/3 of tooth width), not absolute millimeters. Why D is wrong: Lindhe doesn't classify by surface involvement. Why E is wrong: Lindhe's system is clinically based, not purely radiographic.

Q68 In the Tarnow and Fletcher vertical furcation classification, what is measured and what are the subclasses?
A. Distance from the CEJ to the furcation entrance; A = 0-3mm, B = 4-6mm, C = 7+mm
B. Distance from the bottom of the defect to the fornix (roof) of the furcation; Subclass A = 0-3mm loss, Subclass B = 4-6mm loss, Subclass C = 7+mm loss
C. Distance from the alveolar crest to the root apex; A = coronal 1/3, B = middle 1/3, C = apical 1/3
D. Vertical probing depth within the furcation; A = shallow, B = moderate, C = deep
E. Distance from the gingival margin to the base of the pocket; A = 1-3mm, B = 4-6mm, C = 7+mm
Correct Answer: B
A. Distance from the CEJ to the furcation entrance; A = 0-3mm, B = 4-6mm, C = 7+mm
B. Distance from the bottom of the defect to the fornix (roof) of the furcation; Subclass A = 0-3mm loss, Subclass B = 4-6mm loss, Subclass C = 7+mm loss
C. Distance from the alveolar crest to the root apex; A = coronal 1/3, B = middle 1/3, C = apical 1/3
D. Vertical probing depth within the furcation; A = shallow, B = moderate, C = deep
E. Distance from the gingival margin to the base of the pocket; A = 1-3mm, B = 4-6mm, C = 7+mm

Tarnow and Fletcher's classification is the VERTICAL component of furcation assessment — it measures the distance from the bottom of the bony defect UP to the fornix (roof) of the furcation. Subclass A = 0–3mm of vertical bone loss. Subclass B = 4–6mm of vertical loss. Subclass C = 7+mm of vertical loss. This is used IN COMBINATION with the horizontal classifications (Glickman or Lindhe) to give a 3D picture of the furcation defect. A tooth with Glickman Grade 2, Tarnow Subclass C has a very different prognosis than Glickman Grade 2, Tarnow Subclass A — the vertical component tells you how deep the defect extends.

Why A is wrong: CEJ-to-entrance distance is a separate anatomic measurement, not Tarnow's classification. Why C is wrong: This describes root thirds, not the Tarnow system. Why D is wrong: These are vague descriptors, not the defined subclasses. Why E is wrong: This describes probing depth, not the vertical furcation measurement.

Q69 What percentage of molars have cervical enamel projections (CEPs), and what percentage of those with CEPs have furcation involvement?
A. 5% have CEPs; 50% of those have furcation involvement
B. 13% have CEPs; 82% of those have furcation involvement
C. 25% have CEPs; 60% of those have furcation involvement
D. 40% have CEPs; 90% of those have furcation involvement
E. 8% have CEPs; 100% of those have furcation involvement
Correct Answer: B
A. 5% have CEPs; 50% of those have furcation involvement
B. 13% have CEPs; 82% of those have furcation involvement
C. 25% have CEPs; 60% of those have furcation involvement
D. 40% have CEPs; 90% of those have furcation involvement
E. 8% have CEPs; 100% of those have furcation involvement

13% of molars have cervical enamel projections, and a whopping 82% of those with CEPs have furcation involvement. CEPs are ectopic extensions of enamel that project from the CEJ toward or into the furcation area. They prevent connective tissue attachment to the root surface in that area (because enamel can't support a CT attachment — only junctional epithelium attaches to enamel). This creates a natural weak point where periodontal breakdown can reach the furcation more easily. The 82% association is one of the strongest risk correlations in furcation disease. CEPs can be managed with odontoplasty — grinding them down and allowing CT to attach.

Why A is wrong: Both percentages are too low. Why C is wrong: 25% overestimates CEP prevalence. Why D is wrong: 40% is way too high for CEP prevalence. Why E is wrong: 8% is close but not exact, and 100% overstates the association.

Q70 What is the average distance from the pulp to the outer root surface in the mandibular molar furcation, and what is the clinical significance?
A. 1.5mm; inadequate for any restorative procedure in the furcation area
B. 2.8mm; adequate distance for odontoplasty to remove cervical enamel projections
C. 4.0mm; allows for post placement into the furcation area
D. 5.5mm; no clinical significance
E. 0.5mm; prevents any instrumentation in the furcation
Correct Answer: B
A. 1.5mm; inadequate for any restorative procedure in the furcation area
B. 2.8mm; adequate distance for odontoplasty to remove cervical enamel projections
C. 4.0mm; allows for post placement into the furcation area
D. 5.5mm; no clinical significance
E. 0.5mm; prevents any instrumentation in the furcation

Per Sterrett, the average distance from the pulp to the outer root surface in the mandibular molar furcation is 2.8mm, which is adequate for odontoplasty to remove CEPs. This is reassuring — when you encounter a CEP contributing to furcation involvement, you can safely grind it away without getting dangerously close to the pulp. With 2.8mm of dentin/enamel between the pulp and the furcation surface, you have enough room to remove the enamel projection (typically <1mm thick) and smooth the root surface to allow connective tissue attachment without risking pulp exposure.

Why A is wrong: 1.5mm is too thin and doesn't match the Sterrett data. Why C is wrong: 4.0mm overestimates the distance. Why D is wrong: 5.5mm is way too large, and there IS clinical significance. Why E is wrong: 0.5mm would be dangerously thin — fortunately that's not the case.

Q71 What is the prevalence and most common location of enamel pearls?
A. 10-15%; mandibular first molars near the root apex
B. 1.1-5.7%; mostly in maxillary second molars near the CEJ
C. 20-25%; maxillary premolars near the mid-root
D. 0.1-0.5%; mandibular canines near the CEJ
E. 8-12%; equally distributed among all posterior teeth
Correct Answer: B
A. 10-15%; mandibular first molars near the root apex
B. 1.1-5.7%; mostly in maxillary second molars near the CEJ
C. 20-25%; maxillary premolars near the mid-root
D. 0.1-0.5%; mandibular canines near the CEJ
E. 8-12%; equally distributed among all posterior teeth

Enamel pearls have a prevalence of 1.1–5.7% and are most commonly found on maxillary second molars near the CEJ. Enamel pearls are small, discrete nodules of ectopic enamel on the root surface — they're essentially little balls of enamel that shouldn't be there. Like CEPs, they prevent connective tissue attachment at their location and can predispose to localized periodontal breakdown and furcation involvement. They're different from CEPs in that they're discrete nodules rather than extensions from the CEJ, but the clinical consequence is similar — they create attachment-free zones on the root surface.

Why A is wrong: Prevalence is too high and location is wrong. Why C is wrong: Prevalence is way too high and premolars aren't the most common site. Why D is wrong: Canines aren't the typical location. Why E is wrong: Prevalence is too high and distribution isn't equal.

Q72 What class of furcation involvement can SRP (scaling and root planing) resolve, what is the efficiency depth, and what is the maximum treatable depth?
A. Resolves Class 2 furcation; efficiency at 6mm; max depth 8mm
B. Resolves Class 1 furcation; efficiency at 4mm; max depth 6.2mm
C. Resolves Class 3 furcation; efficiency at 3mm; max depth 5mm
D. Resolves Class 1 and 2 furcation; efficiency at 5mm; max depth 7mm
E. SRP cannot resolve any class of furcation involvement
Correct Answer: B
A. Resolves Class 2 furcation; efficiency at 6mm; max depth 8mm
B. Resolves Class 1 furcation; efficiency at 4mm; max depth 6.2mm
C. Resolves Class 3 furcation; efficiency at 3mm; max depth 5mm
D. Resolves Class 1 and 2 furcation; efficiency at 5mm; max depth 7mm
E. SRP cannot resolve any class of furcation involvement

SRP can resolve Class/Grade 1 furcation involvement only. The efficiency limit for SRP is 4mm (meaning instrumentation is most effective up to 4mm depth), and the absolute maximum depth SRP can reach is 6.2mm. Beyond that, you simply can't get adequate debridement with closed (non-surgical) instrumentation. This is why Grade 2 and 3 furcations require surgical access — open flap debridement at minimum, potentially with regenerative procedures (GTR/bone grafts) or root resection. Remember from Q55 that 60% of furcation entrances are narrower than the Gracey blade (0.75mm), compounding the difficulty.

Why A is wrong: SRP can't resolve Class 2 — only Class 1. Why C is wrong: Class 3 (through-and-through) is far beyond SRP capability. Why D is wrong: SRP cannot resolve Class 2. Why E is wrong: SRP CAN resolve Grade 1 furcation involvement.

Q73 What three factors influence the predictability of furcation regeneration?
A. Patient age, smoking status, and systemic disease
B. Horizontal morphology of the periodontal defect, anatomy of the furcation, and early phase of healing
C. Graft type, membrane selection, and suture technique
D. Tooth mobility, probing depth, and bleeding on probing
E. Root trunk length, number of roots, and root divergence angle
Correct Answer: B
A. Patient age, smoking status, and systemic disease
B. Horizontal morphology of the periodontal defect, anatomy of the furcation, and early phase of healing
C. Graft type, membrane selection, and suture technique
D. Tooth mobility, probing depth, and bleeding on probing
E. Root trunk length, number of roots, and root divergence angle

Three factors from your study guide: (1) horizontal morphology of the periodontal defect — the shape and dimensions of the bony defect determine how much containment the walls provide for graft/membrane stability; (2) anatomy of the furcation — root divergence, trunk length, concavities, and entrance width all affect access and regenerative potential; (3) early phase of healing — the initial clot stability, membrane integrity, and protection from mechanical disruption in the first weeks are critical for successful regeneration. These three factors together determine whether a GTR/graft procedure in a furcation will produce true regeneration vs. repair.

Why A is wrong: These are systemic risk factors, not the three specific predictability factors listed. Why C is wrong: These are procedural choices, not the three named factors. Why D is wrong: These are clinical parameters, not the specific predictability factors. Why E is wrong: These are anatomic details that fall UNDER "anatomy of the furcation" but aren't the three overarching factors.

Q74 What is the definition of root resection?
A. Extraction of an entire tooth
B. Removal of only the crown of a multirooted tooth
C. Surgical removal of all or a portion of tooth roots
D. Intentional replantation of an extracted root
E. Endodontic treatment of a root with furcation involvement
Correct Answer: C
A. Extraction of an entire tooth
B. Removal of only the crown of a multirooted tooth
C. Surgical removal of all or a portion of tooth roots
D. Intentional replantation of an extracted root
E. Endodontic treatment of a root with furcation involvement

Root resection is the surgical removal of all or a portion of tooth roots. It's the umbrella term that encompasses both root amputation and hemisection. The goal is to eliminate the diseased root(s) while preserving the healthy portion of the tooth for continued function and restoration. Root resection requires endodontic treatment FIRST (or simultaneously) to seal the remaining root canal(s), followed by surgical removal of the offending root, and then restorative rehabilitation of the remaining tooth structure.

Why A is wrong: Extraction removes the whole tooth — resection preserves part of it. Why B is wrong: Crown removal isn't root resection. Why D is wrong: Replantation puts a tooth BACK — resection takes root(s) away. Why E is wrong: Endo treats the canal system — resection physically removes root structure.

Q75 What is root amputation?
A. Surgical separation of a multirooted tooth through the furcation
B. Removal of a root from a multirooted tooth while maintaining the crown and remaining roots
C. Removal of the entire crown leaving only the roots
D. Extraction of a single-rooted tooth
E. Apicoectomy of a root tip
Correct Answer: B
A. Surgical separation of a multirooted tooth through the furcation
B. Removal of a root from a multirooted tooth while maintaining the crown and remaining roots
